why_important: It tests a general principle for foundation-model adaptation: when the pretrained representation provably lacks a feature class, inject it at the narrowest interface instead of fine-tuning deeper — a pattern reusable beyond SAM.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency-domain side-inputs exist in low-level vision; using them as a targeted representational patch for a frozen segmentation foundation model, with the dissociation-based validation, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: ViT encoders may retain more texture-spectral information than assumed, making the injection redundant and the dissociation absent.
default_community_belief: The pretrained encoder computes sufficient features; adaptation is about reweighting, not injecting new signal families.
falsifiable_prediction: On texture-boundary-heavy tasks the spectral branch will beat parameter-matched spatial adapters (extra LoRA rank) decisively, while on photometric-boundary tasks the two will tie — a double dissociation identifying what the encoder lacks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two texture-boundary datasets and two photometric-boundary controls; spectral branch vs extra-rank LoRA at matched parameters; per-boundary-type error analysis.
fastest_falsification: Linear-probe check first: can texture boundaries be decoded from frozen embeddings at all? Hours; if yes, the premise of missing information collapses.
main_risk: The neck may be an information bottleneck that clips injected features unless the decoder is also lightly tuned, complicating the parameter-matched comparison.

judge_flags.reason: SAM + FFT side-branch is a module pairing; the information-deficit premise is assumed.

one_line: The 'optical adapter': a single tuned 3x3 input convolution (dozens of parameters) matches encoder LoRA on intensity-remapped domains — the domain gap is at the sensor, fix it at the sensor
problem: For modality shifts that are approximately pointwise intensity transforms (different sensors, stains, exposure regimes), the community reflexively adapts deep layers, using thousands of times more parameters than the underlying transformation needs.
core_hypothesis: When the domain map is approximately a local pixel-space transformation, the minimal sufficient adapter is an input-space convolution that inverts it; a tuned 3x3 conv (possibly per-channel affine plus one nonlinearity) will match encoder LoRA on such domains and its failure signals that the shift is genuinely feature-level — a built-in diagnostic.
why_important: It establishes a 'fix at the lowest sufficient level' principle with the most extreme parameter efficiency possible, and doubles as a domain-gap classifier that costs one tiny training run.
why_possibly_novel: Input transformations are used as augmentations, not as trained adapters benchmarked against weight-space PEFT with a gap-classification interpretation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The encoder may be so robust to pointwise transforms already that neither the input conv nor LoRA shows gains, voiding the comparison.
default_community_belief: Meaningful adaptation happens in deep layers; input-space fixes are preprocessing hacks below research interest.
falsifiable_prediction: On intensity-remap shifts the input conv will reach LoRA-level IoU; the learned kernels will approximate the true transformation where known (verifiable on synthetic shifts); and on structural shifts it will fail early, cleanly classifying gap types by where adaptation succeeds.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three synthetic pointwise shifts (gamma, inversion, channel mix) plus two real sensor shifts; input-conv vs LoRA; kernel-recovery check on the synthetic cases.
fastest_falsification: One synthetic inversion shift, input-conv vs rank-1 LoRA: under a GPU-day.
main_risk: Real sensor shifts include spatial noise correlations and resolution differences that a pointwise-ish adapter cannot express, shrinking its winning regime.

one_line: Decoder prefix tokens as task identity: K learned virtual tokens prepended to prompts encode a task in ~8KB, enabling instant task switching and a measurable 'task capacity' of SAM's decoder
problem: Multi-task adaptation currently stores an adapter per task; the decoder's prompt interface suggests a cheaper mechanism — inject task identity as learned tokens — but its capacity and limits for segmentation are unmapped.
core_hypothesis: The decoder treats prompt tokens as a flexible instruction channel; a small set of learned prefix tokens can steer granularity, boundary conventions, and class-selectivity per task without any weight change, and the number of reliably separable tasks (capacity) is measurable and nontrivial (hypothesized >=10 tasks at <2 IoU cost each).
why_important: Kilobyte-scale task plugins that hot-swap at request time change the economics of serving many tenant-specific segmentation behaviors on shared frozen infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt/prefix tuning is standard in NLP; a quantitative task-capacity study of a segmentation decoder's prompt channel, including interpolation behavior, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM's decoder was trained with a fixed prompt vocabulary and may hard-ignore token patterns outside it, unlike language models trained on diverse contexts.
default_community_belief: Vision decoders lack the instruction-following flexibility of language models; task identity requires weight changes.
falsifiable_prediction: Prefix-token tuning will reach within a few IoU points of decoder-LoRA on label-convention and granularity tasks, capacity will degrade gracefully with task count, and prefix arithmetic (averaging related tasks' prefixes) will produce sensible interpolated behaviors.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Ten small tasks with distinct conventions; train K in {2,4,8} prefixes per task; measure per-task IoU vs decoder-LoRA, cross-task confusion, and interpolation behavior.
fastest_falsification: One convention-shift task, prefix vs LoRA: one GPU-day; total failure to move outputs kills the mechanism immediately.
main_risk: The decoder's prompt slots may be too few or too specialized for instruction-like steering, capping capacity at 1-2 behaviors.

judge_flags.reason: Prefix/prompt-tuning ported to SAM's decoder; as stated it is 'new PEFT method' framing.

one_line: Patch-embedding LoRA is disproportionately effective for sensor-statistics shifts: the cheapest layer nobody adapts because NLP-derived conventions skip it
problem: PEFT placement conventions inherited from language models target attention and FFN layers, skipping the patch-embedding projection where raw pixel statistics first meet the model — plausibly the exact site where sensor shifts (noise spectra, bit depth, color response) should be absorbed.
core_hypothesis: For shifts residing in low-level statistics, adapting the patch-embed projection (a single conv) redirects the entire downstream network cheaply; patch-embed LoRA will dominate parameter-matched attention LoRA on sensor shifts and be useless for semantic shifts, yielding a placement rule keyed to shift level.
why_important: One overlooked placement with a clear applicability rule simplifies practice, and the result would demonstrate that placement conventions ported from NLP mismatch vision's shift structure.
why_possibly_novel: Placement ablations rarely include patch-embed as a serious contender; a shift-conditional analysis centering it appears missing for segmentation foundation models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Residual architectures can absorb low-level corrections anywhere, so attention LoRA may match patch-embed LoRA even on sensor shifts.
default_community_belief: First-layer adaptation is trivial preprocessing territory; real adaptation capacity belongs in attention blocks.
falsifiable_prediction: A shift-type x placement interaction study will show patch-embed adaptation winning on synthetic and real sensor shifts at 10-100x parameter efficiency, with the advantage inverting on semantic/layout shifts.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three sensor shifts and three semantic shifts; patch-embed-only vs attention-only LoRA at matched parameters; interaction analysis.
fastest_falsification: One synthetic noise-spectrum shift, both placements: under a GPU-day.
main_risk: The patch-embed layer may be too low-capacity to absorb realistic compound shifts, relegating wins to synthetic cases.

one_line: Linear adapters provably cannot express contrast inversion: a class of domain shifts where LoRA must fail and tiny gated (nonlinear) adapters must win
problem: LoRA's additive linear updates are treated as universally sufficient; identifying a natural shift class outside their expressivity would give the field its first principled negative result and a targeted alternative.
core_hypothesis: Shifts that require input-conditional sign flips of feature responses (contrast inversion between domains, e.g., structures bright in one modality and dark in another) cannot be represented by input-independent linear weight deltas at any rank; small nonlinear adapters (gated MLPs conditioned on local features) handle them with few parameters.
why_important: A clean expressivity boundary for the dominant PEFT method informs when practitioners must switch mechanisms, and inversion-like shifts are common between imaging modalities.
why_possibly_novel: LoRA limitations are discussed empirically; a constructed natural shift class with a theoretical inexpressibility argument plus experimental confirmation for segmentation appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: MAE-pretrained features may already be contrast-sign-invariant in relevant channels, making inversion an easy shift for any method and destroying the testbed.
default_community_belief: With enough rank, LoRA approximates any needed update; expressivity is never the binding constraint in practice.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic inversion tasks, LoRA performance will plateau far below full fine-tuning regardless of rank (an expressivity gap, not an optimization one, verified by rank sweeps and training-length controls), while gated adapters with fewer parameters close the gap.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build paired datasets differing only by intensity inversion; sweep LoRA ranks {1..64} and training budgets; compare against gated adapters and full FT; verify the plateau structure.
fastest_falsification: Frozen-model check: measure zero-shot performance drop under inversion; if small, the testbed premise fails — one hour.
main_risk: The network may implement inversion-robustness via existing nonlinearities (absolute-value-like features), letting linear deltas exploit them and voiding the impossibility argument.

one_line: A scanline state-space sidecar gives frozen SAM long-range thin-structure continuity: connectivity metrics improve with zero change to region IoU, targeting the exact failure everyone reports
problem: SAM fragments long thin structures (wires, cracks, vessels-like curves) because attention at patch resolution does not enforce continuity; standard PEFT improves local contrast handling but leaves fragmentation — the topology of the error is untouched by the mechanism.
core_hypothesis: Continuity is a sequential property best captured by linear-time recurrent/state-space scans along image rows, columns, and diagonals; a tiny sidecar performing such scans over neck features, added to decoder inputs and trained alone, will specifically improve connectivity statistics (fewer components, longer traced paths) while leaving areal metrics unchanged — a signature proving the mechanism works as intended.
why_important: It attacks the most-cited SAM failure mode with a mechanism matched to the failure's structure (sequential continuity), demonstrating failure-driven adapter design over generic capacity addition.
why_possibly_novel: State-space modules are used in new backbones; retrofitting one as a frozen-model sidecar with connectivity-specific evaluation appears untried.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If frozen features do carry faint continuity evidence, generic LoRA might also learn to use it, erasing the dissociation.
default_community_belief: Thin-structure failure is a resolution problem; only higher-resolution inputs or heavy architecture change can address it.
falsifiable_prediction: On thin-structure datasets, the sidecar will reduce fragmentation counts substantially with near-zero region-IoU change, while a parameter-matched extra LoRA rank improves neither; the double dissociation is the test.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two thin-structure datasets; sidecar vs matched-parameter LoRA; report connectivity metrics (component counts, path completeness) alongside IoU and boundary-F.
fastest_falsification: Probe first: train a linear connectivity predictor on frozen neck features along known thin structures; no signal means the sidecar has nothing to scan — one day.
main_risk: Continuity errors may originate in the encoder losing the structure entirely (sub-patch width), in which case no decoder-side sequential module can recover what is not represented.

judge_flags.reason: SAM + scanline state-space sidecar is the SAM+Mamba pairing pattern.

one_line: The embarrassing baseline: a static per-deployment spatial logit prior (one bias map) captures most of the 'adaptation' gain in fixed-camera settings — PEFT papers may be re-learning where things are
problem: Many applied SAM adaptations target fixed or near-fixed viewpoints (industrial stations, surveillance, fixed microscopy protocols) where object locations are highly predictable; adaptation methods are never compared against simply learning the spatial prior.
core_hypothesis: In fixed-viewpoint deployments, a learned static bias field added to mask logits (plus a threshold recalibration) captures a large fraction of reported PEFT gains, because much of what adapters learn there is spatial regularity rather than appearance understanding.
why_important: Every applied paper on such domains should have to beat this baseline; introducing it recalibrates claimed contributions and gives practitioners a zero-risk first step.
why_possibly_novel: Positional priors are ancient in classic segmentation; their absence as a controlled baseline in the SAM-PEFT literature is the gap this fills.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prompt-conditioned decoding already localizes via the prompt, so spatial priors may be redundant with prompt information and capture little.
default_community_belief: PEFT gains on applied tasks reflect learned appearance/domain knowledge, not spatial memorization.
falsifiable_prediction: On fixed-viewpoint tasks, the bias-map baseline will reach a substantial fraction (hypothesized >50%) of LoRA gains at ~10^5x fewer effective parameters, while on viewpoint-diverse tasks it will capture almost nothing — quantifying how much 'adaptation' is spatial memorization.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three fixed-viewpoint and two diverse-viewpoint adaptation tasks; fit the bias map on the training labels; compare against LoRA and report gain fractions per setting.
fastest_falsification: One fixed-camera dataset, fit bias map, evaluate: a few hours.
main_risk: The baseline may work embarrassingly well, which is a finding, or embarrassingly poorly, which still calibrates — the risk is mainly that fixed-viewpoint public datasets are scarce.

judge_flags.title: Static spatial-prior baseline may explain fixed-camera adaptation gains

one_line: Conformal prompt sets: distribution-free per-mask coverage guarantees for SAM by calibrating over prompt perturbations instead of model internals
problem: Safety-critical users need statements like 'the true mask is inside this envelope with 90% probability', which no confidence score of SAM provides, and classic conformal methods for segmentation require pixelwise scores that promptable models complicate.
core_hypothesis: The ensemble of masks generated by a calibrated family of prompt perturbations forms a natural nested envelope structure; conformal calibration on a small labeled set can select the perturbation radius achieving target coverage, yielding distribution-free guarantees that inherit validity regardless of SAM's internal miscalibration.
why_important: It provides the first practical guarantee layer for interactive segmentation in regulated settings, using only black-box access — no retraining, no internal scores trusted.
why_possibly_novel: Conformal prediction for segmentation exists via pixel scores; using the prompt channel as the randomization device for envelope construction appears specific to promptable models and unexplored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Coverage guarantees hold marginally, not per-instance, and users may find marginal guarantees insufficient for the intended safety cases.
default_community_belief: Uncertainty for SAM means its IoU head or ensembles; formal coverage guarantees are out of reach for interactive models.
falsifiable_prediction: On held-out data from the calibration distribution, prompt-set envelopes will achieve nominal coverage within statistical tolerance across domains, with envelope sizes tracking true difficulty; coverage will degrade gracefully (and detectably) under distribution drift.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement envelope construction from jittered prompts; calibrate radius on 200 labeled masks; verify empirical coverage on 500 held-out masks across 2 domains; stress-test under mild drift.
fastest_falsification: Nestedness check of jittered-prompt mask families on 100 images: hours; heavy multimodality kills the construction.
main_risk: Prompt perturbations may produce non-nested, multimodal mask families (granularity switching), breaking the envelope construction.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Quality estimation transfers better than segmentation: SAM's IoU head may remain reliable on domains where its masks fail, enabling self-supervised adaptation with the model as its own judge
problem: Label-free adaptation needs a trustworthy error signal on the target domain; the assumption that all of SAM degrades together under shift forecloses using one part of the model to supervise another, without evidence either way.
core_hypothesis: Judging mask quality is an easier, more domain-invariant function than producing masks (analogous to verification vs generation); the IoU head's rank correlation with true quality will decay much more slowly under domain shift than mask quality itself, opening a usable teacher-student gap within one model.
why_important: A validated generation-verification gap inside SAM would give a principled foundation for a whole family of self-adaptation methods, replacing heuristic pseudo-label filtering.
why_possibly_novel: Verification-generation gaps are discussed for language models; measuring the analogous internal gap in a segmentation foundation model, and exploiting it for adaptation, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The IoU head reads the same shifted features, so its judgments may collapse in lockstep with mask quality, closing the gap before it opens.
default_community_belief: All heads of a model degrade together under shift; internal confidence is the first casualty of OOD, not the last.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a domain-shift severity ladder, plotted decay curves will show mask IoU dropping steeply while IoU-head rank correlation stays high until much larger shifts, and adaptation that optimizes predicted-IoU on unlabeled target data will yield true-IoU gains precisely in the window where the gap exists.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a 5-step shift ladder (progressive corruptions plus real domains); measure both decay curves; run predicted-IoU-maximization adaptation in the identified window on one real domain.
fastest_falsification: Rank-correlation vs mask-quality decay on a corruption ladder: pure inference, one day.
main_risk: Optimizing against the internal judge invites reward hacking: masks that fool the IoU head without improving true quality.

one_line: Pixelwise disagreement across SAM's three mask hypotheses approximates epistemic uncertainty at zero cost — validate it against deep ensembles once, use it everywhere
problem: Pixelwise uncertainty for SAM currently requires ensembles or MC-dropout (expensive, and dropout-free architectures complicate the latter); the multimask output is a free ensemble-like signal whose calibration nobody has validated.
core_hypothesis: Variance across the three mask logit maps captures a useful share of epistemic uncertainty (hypothesis-level disagreement), correlating with error locations nearly as well as small deep ensembles at three orders of magnitude lower cost, and the correlation persists under domain shift.
why_important: Free, always-available uncertainty maps enable error-aware downstream use (review triage, active learning, fusion) for every SAM deployment without infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: The multimask outputs are used for selection, not as an uncertainty ensemble; a rigorous calibration study against ensembles, including the failure-envelope characterization, appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correlated heads systematically agree on exactly the confident mistakes where uncertainty is most needed, potentially making the proxy dangerous rather than merely imperfect.
default_community_belief: Real uncertainty requires independent ensemble members; single-forward-pass signals are toy proxies.
falsifiable_prediction: Pixelwise multimask variance will achieve error-localization AUROC within a small margin of a 5-member ensemble in-domain and OOD, and its failure cases will be systematic (unanimous-but-wrong regions) rather than random, enabling a documented validity envelope.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 datasets (1 in-domain, 2 OOD), compute multimask-variance maps and 5-ensemble variance maps; compare error-localization AUROC and calibration; catalog unanimous-error cases.
fastest_falsification: Variance-vs-error AUROC on one OOD dataset: pure inference, hours.
main_risk: The three hypotheses share almost all computation, so their disagreement may capture only granularity ambiguity, missing the feature-level uncertainty that matters OOD.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

one_line: Router-free adapter zoos: selecting the right domain adapter by nearest-centroid on pooled SAM embeddings works >95% of the time — serving infrastructure nobody needs to train
problem: Serving many domain adapters requires deciding per request which to apply; learned routers add training, drift, and failure modes, discouraging adapter-zoo architectures despite their efficiency.
core_hypothesis: SAM's pooled encoder embeddings separate deployment domains so cleanly that a centroid classifier (fit from a handful of unlabeled images per domain) routes requests with negligible error, and residual misroutes are benign because embedding-adjacent domains have functionally similar adapters.
why_important: Removing the router as a trained component makes multi-domain SAM serving a configuration problem instead of an ML problem, directly enabling practical adapter marketplaces.
why_possibly_novel: Feature-based domain classification is old; the specific claims about SAM-embedding separability of realistic adapter domains and the benign-misroute property appear unmeasured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The benign-misroute assumption may fail: nearby domains can need opposite corrections (e.g., mirrored annotation conventions).
default_community_belief: Reliable routing requires trained gating networks or metadata; embedding heuristics are too brittle for production.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a 10-domain adapter zoo, centroid routing will exceed 95% accuracy with 20 reference images per domain, and end-to-end IoU under routing will be within 1 point of oracle assignment, with misroute costs correlating inversely with embedding distance.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a 10-domain zoo from public datasets, fit centroids, measure routing accuracy and end-to-end IoU vs oracle and vs a trained router baseline.
fastest_falsification: Routing-accuracy measurement over public datasets needs no adapter training at all: one day.
main_risk: Fine-grained domain distinctions that matter for adapters (same modality, different annotation conventions) may be invisible in image embeddings, exactly where routing matters most.

one_line: A computable merge-compatibility score: Fisher-information overlap between adapters predicts whether merging them will hurt, before you merge
problem: Adapter merging outcomes are currently discovered empirically per pair; without a predictive compatibility measure, building merged multi-domain models is trial-and-error that scales quadratically in the zoo size.
core_hypothesis: Interference under merging is driven by both adapters needing to move the same sensitive directions differently; the overlap of their (diagonal) Fisher information masks, weighted by update disagreement, predicts post-merge degradation accurately enough to triage merge decisions without evaluation runs.
why_important: It converts merge planning from experiment-bound to computation-bound, enabling automated construction of merged serving models from large adapter collections.
why_possibly_novel: Fisher-weighted merging exists as a method; using Fisher overlap as a pre-merge predictive diagnostic, validated against realized degradation for segmentation adapters, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interference may be dominated by a few outlier parameters or data-dependent effects invisible to aggregate overlap statistics.
default_community_belief: Merge quality is only knowable by merging and evaluating; cheap statistics cannot anticipate functional interference.
falsifiable_prediction: Across many adapter pairs, the compatibility score computed from training-time statistics will correlate strongly (rank correlation >0.7) with measured post-merge minimum-task degradation, outperforming parameter-space cosine similarity and subspace-angle baselines.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 8 adapters, form all 28 pairs, compute scores and actual merge outcomes, fit and cross-validate the predictor against baselines.
fastest_falsification: Reuse any existing set of trained adapters: compute scores, merge pairs, correlate — two days without new adapter training.
main_risk: Diagonal Fisher approximations may be too crude for attention layers, capping predictive power below usefulness.

one_line: Constructive interference exists: adapting to domain B sometimes improves already-deployed domain A, and the direction is predictable from label-style similarity, not image similarity
problem: Sequential adaptation is managed defensively (freeze, isolate, replay) under the assumption that new tasks can only harm old ones; positive backward transfer is treated as noise rather than a resource to be engineered.
core_hypothesis: Backward transfer sign is governed by annotation-convention alignment between tasks (boundary tightness, occlusion policy) more than by visual similarity; convention-aligned task pairs show systematic positive backward transfer because the second task refines shared decoding conventions, and a label-statistics comparison predicts the sign in advance.
why_important: If positive transfer is predictable, continual deployment can be scheduled to strengthen old domains for free, inverting the field's defensive posture toward sequential adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: Backward transfer is studied in continual learning generically; identifying annotation convention as the controlling variable for segmentation adapters appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Positive backward transfer may be a small-sample artifact that vanishes with proper evaluation variance controls.
default_community_belief: New-task training degrades old tasks; the only question is how much and how to prevent it.
falsifiable_prediction: In an NxN sequential-adaptation matrix, backward-transfer sign will be predicted by a label-convention similarity metric with accuracy well above chance and above image-embedding similarity, and convention-aligned curricula will beat isolation strategies on average across old tasks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Six tasks with characterized label conventions; run sequential pairs in both orders; regress backward-transfer sign/magnitude on convention similarity vs embedding similarity.
fastest_falsification: Two convention-aligned and two misaligned pairs, sequential runs with seed replication: three GPU-days for a sign check.
main_risk: Convention similarity is hard to quantify independently of the models being studied, risking circular metrics.

one_line: SAM2's memory bank multiplies first-frame errors: quantify the error-compounding rate and show video adaptation should target memory attention, not the image encoder
problem: Video segmentation adaptation ports image-model recipes (tune the encoder), but SAM2's distinguishing component is its streaming memory; if initial-frame errors compound through memory retrieval, encoder-centric adaptation misallocates all its budget.
core_hypothesis: Corrupted early-frame masks enter the memory bank and bias subsequent retrievals toward repeating the error (a positive feedback loop); the compounding rate (error growth per frame attributable to memory rather than appearance) is measurable by intervention (injecting controlled first-frame errors), and memory-attention adaptation reduces compounding where encoder adaptation cannot.
why_important: It redirects the emerging SAM2-adaptation literature toward the architecturally-correct target and introduces compounding-rate as the metric video adaptation should optimize.
why_possibly_novel: Error propagation is studied in tracking classically; an interventional decomposition of memory-driven vs appearance-driven error for promptable video segmenters, tied to PEFT placement, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On real OOD video, per-frame appearance failure may dominate so heavily that memory effects are second-order noise.
default_community_belief: Video domain adaptation is appearance adaptation; the memory mechanism is domain-neutral machinery.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled first-frame corruptions will produce error growth curves significantly steeper than frame-independent baselines predict, and PEFT on memory-attention projections will flatten these curves more per parameter than encoder LoRA, especially on OOD video.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On video datasets, inject calibrated first-frame mask errors, measure downstream error growth vs a memory-ablated control; then compare memory-attention PEFT vs encoder PEFT on OOD videos at matched parameters.
fastest_falsification: First-frame error injection on 20 videos with growth-curve measurement: inference-only, one day.
main_risk: SAM2's design may already gate low-confidence memories effectively, making compounding rare outside adversarial injections.

one_line: Video domain gap lives in temporal association, not appearance: tuning only SAM2's memory/object-pointer projections beats encoder LoRA for OOD video at a fraction of the parameters
problem: OOD video failures (losing the object, identity switches) are treated as appearance problems, but SAM2 separates appearance (image encoder) from association (memory attention and object pointers), and nobody has decomposed which subsystem the domain gap occupies.
core_hypothesis: For many OOD video domains the per-frame appearance features remain adequate (single-frame prompted accuracy stays high) while cross-frame association degrades (tracking metrics collapse); this dissociation is measurable per-domain and predicts that memory-pathway PEFT dominates encoder PEFT exactly where the association gap exceeds the appearance gap.
why_important: A two-number diagnostic that tells video practitioners which subsystem to adapt saves large amounts of misdirected tuning and maps how domain shift decomposes in modern streaming architectures.
why_possibly_novel: Appearance-vs-association decomposition for promptable streaming segmenters, used prescriptively for PEFT placement, appears unexplored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Association machinery may be so appearance-dependent that no clean association-gapped domain exists in practice.
default_community_belief: Better features fix video: encoder adaptation is the default lever for any video domain gap.
falsifiable_prediction: A per-domain decomposition (single-frame prompted IoU vs tracking consistency) will identify association-gapped domains, on which memory-projection tuning will outperform parameter-matched encoder LoRA, with the reverse holding on appearance-gapped domains.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 4 OOD video domains, measure the two gap components; run memory-only vs encoder-only PEFT per domain; test the predicted crossover.
fastest_falsification: The gap decomposition itself (single-frame vs tracking metrics on 2 domains) is inference-only: one day.
main_risk: The two components interact (bad features corrupt memories), potentially blurring the decomposition on real domains.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

one_line: OOD track loss in SAM2 is largely an occlusion-head calibration failure: one temperature scalar per domain restores tracking without touching segmentation
problem: When SAM2 loses objects on out-of-domain video, teams retrain broadly; but the decision to declare an object absent flows through a small occlusion/visibility prediction whose calibration under domain shift has never been isolated as the failure point.
core_hypothesis: Domain shift moves the operating point of the occlusion score (systematically over-predicting absence on unfamiliar appearance), so a large share of track losses are threshold failures, fixable by per-domain temperature/threshold recalibration on a handful of labeled clips.
why_important: A two-parameter fix for the most user-visible video failure mode would be the cheapest adaptation result in the video segmentation literature, and the audit methodology transfers to any streaming segmenter with an absence head.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration-under-shift is studied for classifiers; isolating the absence-decision head as the dominant OOD failure channel in promptable video segmentation appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Score miscalibration and mask degradation may be so correlated OOD that thresholding fixes little in practice.
default_community_belief: Track loss means the model no longer recognizes the object; the remedy is feature adaptation or more video fine-tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: Auditing OOD track-loss events will attribute a majority to occlusion-score misfires (object visibly present, score says absent) rather than mask-quality collapse, and a single recalibrated threshold will recover a large fraction of lost tracks with no weight changes.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 OOD video sets, log occlusion scores at every track-loss event with human labels of true visibility; attribute causes; sweep the threshold/temperature and measure track-recovery vs new-error trade-off.
fastest_falsification: Score-vs-visibility audit on 50 track-loss events: a day of inference plus annotation.
main_risk: Attribution requires careful causality (bad masks may precede bad scores), demanding frame-level audit protocols to avoid mislabeling the failure source.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

one_line: Process-defined regions (wetness, rust, burn marks) sit outside SAM's prompt-expressible space: no click can mean 'the affected area' — an empirical expressivity boundary study
problem: Industrial and scientific users constantly want regions defined by a process or condition rather than by objecthood (the wet part of the floor, corroded metal); SAM returns object-like masks, and it is unknown whether any prompting strategy can express such intents at all.
core_hypothesis: SAM's prompt-to-mask mapping is constrained to a learned space of 'plausible object extents'; condition-defined regions whose boundaries cross object boundaries are outside this space, so no sequence of point/box prompts reaches them (bounded best-achievable IoU), which defines a measurable expressivity frontier of the prompt language.
why_important: Documenting what promptable segmentation cannot express — with a search-based upper-bound methodology — tells the field where new prompt types or output heads are genuinely required rather than more adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: SAM failure reports list examples; an oracle-prompt-search methodology establishing per-category expressivity upper bounds appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Condition regions often have photometric signatures (specular wetness, rust color) that SAM's features may actually delineate once a couple of clicks anchor them.
default_community_belief: With clever prompting or light tuning SAM segments anything spatially coherent.
falsifiable_prediction: Exhaustive prompt search (many clicks, boxes, combinations, all three mask outputs) on condition-region benchmarks will plateau at a low best-achievable IoU compared to matched object-region controls, and the plateau will persist after moderate PEFT, indicating an output-space rather than knowledge deficit.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a small condition-region set (wet/dry, rust/clean boundaries crossing objects); run large-budget prompt search on frozen SAM for best-achievable IoU vs object controls; repeat after LoRA adaptation.
fastest_falsification: 50 condition-region images with a 100-prompt search budget each: two days; near-control-level achievable IoU refutes the frontier claim.
main_risk: Prompt search is combinatorial; practical budgets may under-estimate the true upper bound, making the plateau an artifact of search rather than expressivity.

one_line: SAM's logits secretly contain alpha mattes: soft transparency information survives binarization training and can be extracted without retraining
problem: Translucent and wispy boundaries (glass, veils, fine hair-like structure) need soft mattes, and the assumption that SAM (trained on binary masks) contains no such information forces users to separate matting models.
core_hypothesis: To minimize loss on inconsistent boundary supervision, SAM learned to output intermediate logit values that correlate with true mixing coefficients; an affine or monotone remapping of pre-threshold logits therefore approximates an alpha matte in boundary bands, recoverable with zero training.
why_important: Free approximate matting from an already-deployed model unlocks soft-edge use cases (composition, occlusion-aware editing, uncertainty-aware measurement) without new infrastructure, and reveals what supervision noise taught the model.
why_possibly_novel: Logit-softness has been used as confidence; its interpretation and calibration as physical mixing coefficients for promptable models appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The upsampling path may sharpen logits toward saturation, leaving too little dynamic range in exactly the bands that matter.
default_community_belief: Binary-mask training destroys sub-pixel/transparency information; matting requires purpose-built models and losses.
falsifiable_prediction: On matting benchmarks with GT alpha, remapped SAM logits in boundary bands will correlate with true alpha substantially above the binary-mask baseline, and a tiny calibration head (trained on 10 images) will approach dedicated-matting quality in the band while failing gracefully in wide-gradient regions.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On public matting data, extract SAM boundary-band logits, fit monotone calibration on 10 images, evaluate alpha correlation and composition quality vs binary baseline and a matting model.
fastest_falsification: Logit-vs-alpha correlation on 20 matting images: hours.
main_risk: Logit softness may encode model uncertainty rather than mixing fraction, correlating with alpha only accidentally on easy cases.

judge_flags.title: SAM logits secretly contain alpha mattes

one_line: Does SAM think shadows belong to objects? A systematic attached-shadow inclusion bias exists and can be toggled by steering a single direction in prompt-embedding space
problem: Attached shadows are included in masks inconsistently, corrupting measurement applications (sizing, counting area); the phenomenon is treated as random noise rather than a structured, steerable model behavior.
core_hypothesis: SA-1B annotation practice induced a probabilistic shadow-inclusion policy conditioned on shadow contrast and geometry; the decision is encoded compactly enough that a single learned direction added to prompt embeddings shifts the inclusion probability smoothly — a steerable convention rather than a fixed error.
why_important: Convention steering without weight changes would let one frozen model serve both 'with shadow' and 'without shadow' users, and demonstrates a general technique: extracting annotation-policy dimensions as controllable directions.
why_possibly_novel: Activation steering is explored in language models; convention-level steering of a segmentation model's output policy through the prompt channel appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The behavior may be bimodal and context-locked (always include at high contrast), leaving no smooth dimension to steer.
default_community_belief: Shadow handling is stochastic annotation noise inherited by the model; changing it requires retraining on relabeled data.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled shadow benchmark (objects photographed/rendered with and without attached shadows) will show consistent inclusion statistics as functions of shadow properties, and optimizing one steering vector on 20 examples will move inclusion rates strongly in both directions with negligible effect on non-shadow boundaries.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble/render 200 shadow-controlled scenes; measure baseline inclusion statistics; train the steering vector on 20 examples; evaluate toggling on the rest plus a non-shadow control suite.
fastest_falsification: Baseline inclusion statistics on 50 shadow scenes: half a day; incoherent statistics (no systematic policy) kill the steering premise.
main_risk: Shadow inclusion may be decided by local image evidence deep in the decoder, not compactly represented in any prompt-space direction.

one_line: Prompt teleportation in periodic textures: clicks on one instance of a repeating pattern select a different instance, revealing position-appearance binding failure in the decoder
problem: In repetitive scenes (tiles, windows, fabric patterns, arrays of parts) SAM sometimes segments an identical-looking neighbor instead of the clicked instance; this bizarre failure is anecdotal, unquantified, and mechanistically unexplained.
core_hypothesis: Decoder cross-attention matches prompt positional encodings against appearance-dominated keys; when many tokens share appearance, attention resolves to the wrong instance because positional precision is under-weighted relative to appearance similarity — predicting teleportation rate rises with pattern periodicity and falls with positional distinctiveness.
why_important: Industrial inspection and counting tasks are full of periodic structures; understanding and mitigating instance-binding failure matters practically, and the phenomenon is a clean probe of how promptable decoders bind position to content.
why_possibly_novel: The failure is known as anecdote; a parametric characterization plus an inference-time re-weighting mitigation appears absent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The rate may be negligible outside adversarially perfect periodicity, making it a non-problem in real imagery.
default_community_belief: Clicks reliably bind to the clicked location; instance confusion is a rare curiosity not worth modeling.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic periodic arrays, teleportation rate (mask centered off the clicked instance) will increase with the number of identical instances and decrease with spacing irregularity, and upweighting positional components of prompt embeddings at inference will reduce teleportation without retraining.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic grids with controlled instance count, spacing jitter, and appearance noise; measure teleportation rates; test the positional-upweighting knob and a one-negative-click-on-neighbor protocol.
fastest_falsification: Synthetic-grid teleportation measurement: a few hours to know whether the effect is common enough to study.
main_risk: Teleportation may actually originate in encoder feature aliasing (identical tokens), in which case decoder-side reweighting cannot fix it.

one_line: Masks leak into mirrors: SAM merges objects with their reflections, and a rank-1 surgical decoder edit might suppress reflection-binding as a model-editing case study
problem: Reflective surfaces (mirrors, water, glossy floors, glass) cause masks to bleed into reflections; beyond cataloging, nobody has asked whether such a specific relational failure can be surgically removed from a frozen model without broad retraining.
core_hypothesis: Reflection-binding is mediated by a low-dimensional feature pattern (symmetric appearance match across a boundary of reversed geometry); a targeted rank-1 or few-parameter edit in decoder attention, fit on a small curated reflection set, can suppress the binding with minimal collateral damage — establishing 'surgical editing' as a PEFT category for relational failure modes.
why_important: If specific relational failures are surgically editable, model maintenance can shift from retraining cycles to a library of validated micro-edits — a different economics of foundation-model upkeep.
why_possibly_novel: Model editing is developed for factual knowledge in language models; porting the surgical-edit paradigm to relational segmentation failures appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even in language models, edits generalize poorly and cause drift; the segmentation analogue may inherit exactly those weaknesses.
default_community_belief: Failure modes are fixed by data: collect examples, fine-tune broadly; surgical parameter-level fixes are a language-model curiosity.
falsifiable_prediction: The reflection-leak rate on a curated benchmark will drop by a large factor after a rank-1 edit trained on <=50 examples, while a matched-size generic LoRA achieves less suppression and more collateral drift on a broad control suite.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate 150 reflection scenes; fit rank-1 decoder edits vs matched LoRA; evaluate leak suppression, in-domain controls, and broad zero-shot drift.
fastest_falsification: Fit the rank-1 edit on 30 examples and test on 50 held-out scenes: two GPU-days including curation.
main_risk: Reflection-binding may be distributed across encoder features rather than localized in decoder attention, making low-rank edits ineffective.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

one_line: SAM has an upright-photo orientation prior: 45-degree rotations hurt more than 90-degree ones, and test-time canonicalization beats weight tuning for orientation-free domains (aerial, microscopy)
problem: Domains without a gravity-defined 'up' (satellite, microscopy, PCB inspection) adapt SAM with rotation-augmented fine-tuning by default, without knowing the structure of the orientation bias they are trying to erase or whether erasing it is the right move.
core_hypothesis: SA-1B's photographic upright bias plus axis-aligned window partitioning produce an anisotropic performance profile over rotation angle (worst at odd angles like 45 degrees, partially recovered at 90-degree multiples due to grid alignment); given this structure, inference-time canonicalization (predict-and-rotate or symmetrize) preserves the strong upright operating point and beats rotation-augmented PEFT which averages performance down across angles.
why_important: It replaces a costly default (rotation-augmented tuning) with a cheaper, better inference strategy for a whole class of scientific domains, and documents an architecture-data interaction (grid alignment) in the bias structure.
why_possibly_novel: Rotation sensitivity is known generically; the scalloped-profile prediction tied to window-grid alignment, and the canonicalize-vs-average-down comparison for promptable models, appear new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The bias may be small for typical object scales, or augmented tuning may not lower the peak measurably, removing canonicalization's advantage.
default_community_belief: Rotation augmentation during fine-tuning is the correct fix for orientation-diverse domains.
falsifiable_prediction: The IoU-vs-rotation curve will show the predicted scalloped anisotropy (local maxima at 90-degree multiples); rotation-averaged fine-tuning will flatten the curve by lowering the peak; canonicalization will match peak performance at all input orientations on orientation-free domains.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure IoU over rotations at 15-degree steps on natural and aerial data; compare rotation-augmented LoRA vs canonicalization (ensemble or learned orientation predictor) on 2 orientation-free domains.
fastest_falsification: The rotation-sweep profile on frozen SAM: inference-only, hours; a flat or unstructured curve deflates the hypothesis.
main_risk: Canonicalization needs a reliable orientation estimator on domains that may lack orientation cues entirely, potentially reintroducing errors.

one_line: JPEG blocks resonate with SAM's patch grid: compression artifacts aligned to the 16-pixel lattice cause a performance cliff that half-patch-shift ensembling removes for free
problem: Deployed imagery is mostly compressed, and SAM robustness studies treat JPEG as generic noise; but JPEG's 8x8 block lattice divides SAM's 16x16 patch lattice exactly, creating a structured alignment that may produce non-generic failure.
core_hypothesis: Block-boundary artifacts injected at fixed positions within each patch produce correlated perturbations across all tokens (a coherent attack on patch statistics), so quality degradation vs JPEG level has a cliff once artifacts dominate intra-patch variance; shifting the image by 8 pixels (half-lattice) decorrelates artifact-to-patch alignment, so a two-inference shift ensemble recovers most of the cliff.
why_important: A free robustness trick for the compressed-imagery reality of production systems, plus a demonstration that architecture-lattice interactions (not just noise magnitude) drive robustness — informative for all patch-based models.
why_possibly_novel: JPEG robustness is measured as a corruption benchmark; the lattice-alignment mechanism and the shift-ensemble remedy for promptable segmenters appear unexamined.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The 8-vs-16 alignment may be irrelevant because JPEG artifacts concentrate at low frequencies that patch statistics absorb smoothly.
default_community_belief: Compression robustness is a scalar property measured per quality level; remedy is augmentation with compressed images during training.
falsifiable_prediction: IoU-vs-JPEG-quality curves will drop non-linearly with a knee, the knee will move when images are pre-shifted by non-multiples of 8, and the two-shift ensemble will recover a large fraction of the loss at low quality levels — none of which generic-noise models predict.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep JPEG quality on 2 datasets, with and without sub-lattice pre-shifts, measure IoU curves and the ensemble recovery; verify artifact-alignment statistics in patch space.
fastest_falsification: Quality sweep with and without an 8-pixel shift on 100 images: inference-only, hours.
main_risk: Modern encoders' deblocking and the encoder's learned robustness may smooth the cliff into an ordinary slope, leaving only a marginal ensemble gain.

one_line: A sampling theorem for prompt grids: derive and validate the minimal automatic-mask-generation grid density guaranteeing coverage of all objects above a given scale
problem: Automatic mask generation prompts SAM on a uniform point grid with folklore densities; users discover missed objects empirically and compensate by oversampling everything, multiplying compute without guarantees.
core_hypothesis: The probability that a grid point 'hits' an object well enough to recover it is a measurable function of object scale, shape convexity, and grid spacing; from this hit function, a coverage guarantee (all objects above scale s recovered with probability p) follows analytically, giving a principled density-vs-scale trade-off with measurable blind-spot structure at specific scale-offset combinations.
why_important: Everything-mode is the workhorse of dataset bootstrapping and pseudo-labeling; replacing folklore densities with guarantees reduces cost and, more importantly, documents what everything-mode systematically misses (a bias inherited by every dataset it generates).
why_possibly_novel: Grid density is treated as an engineering knob; a formal coverage analysis with validated predictions and adaptive-grid consequences appears absent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Multimask outputs and post-filtering interact with grid hits in messy ways that may defeat clean analytical treatment.
default_community_belief: Denser grids are simply better; 32x32 or 64x64 are safe defaults and coverage is not formally analyzable.
falsifiable_prediction: The empirically fitted hit function will predict measured coverage curves across datasets within tight error, revealing systematic blind spots (objects at ~1.5x grid spacing with concave shapes), and theorem-guided adaptive grids will match uniform-grid coverage at a fraction of the prompts.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit the hit function on one dataset (hit/miss vs scale, convexity, offset), predict coverage on 2 unseen datasets across grid densities, verify blind-spot predictions, and test the adaptive grid.
fastest_falsification: Coverage-vs-density curves on one dataset against the fitted prediction: one day of inference.
main_risk: The hit function may depend heavily on domain-specific appearance (not just geometry), limiting cross-dataset prediction accuracy.

one_line: Test-time prompt optimization: gradient-descend the prompt embedding (not the weights) against the IoU head to find 'virtual clicks' better than any human click
problem: For a frozen SAM, the only optimizable quantities at deployment are the prompts themselves; human clicks explore a tiny discrete subset of the continuous prompt-embedding space, and nobody treats prompt embeddings as an optimization variable at inference.
core_hypothesis: The prompt-embedding space contains points (unreachable by any physical click) that decode to better masks; ascending the model's own predicted-IoU (or stability) surface over prompt embeddings finds them, improving masks with zero weight changes and zero labels — an alternative to PEFT for frozen deployments.
why_important: It reframes adaptation as inference-time search in prompt space — cacheable, reversible, per-image — and probes how much performance frozen SAM leaves on the table due to prompt-interface discreteness.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt tuning trains persistent embeddings on labeled data; per-image, label-free, test-time prompt-embedding search against internal quality signals appears new for segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Off-manifold prompt embeddings may decode to garbage because the decoder never saw anything outside the discrete prompt vocabulary's span.
default_community_belief: Prompts are user inputs, not optimization variables; improving a frozen model at test time means TTA on weights or ensembling.
falsifiable_prediction: Starting from a user click, 10-30 steps of embedding-space ascent will improve true IoU on a majority of hard cases (where initial IoU<0.7), with gains persisting when the objective is stability rather than the (hackable) IoU head, and failure concentrated where both objectives are miscalibrated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 300 hard cases from 2 domains, run embedding ascent with both internal objectives, measure true-IoU deltas and reward-hacking rate (predicted up, true down); compare against extra simulated human clicks at matched inference cost.
fastest_falsification: Ascent on 30 hard cases with true-IoU tracking: a few hours; dominant reward-hacking kills it.
main_risk: The IoU head's gradients may lead into adversarial regions of prompt space (predicted quality up, true quality down) often enough to make the method untrustworthy without labels.

one_line: A constant half-pixel boundary offset from bilinear logit upsampling: every SAM mask is systematically shifted, and a one-parameter correction improves all results universally but invisibly
problem: Sub-pixel systematic biases are invisible in IoU but matter for measurement applications (areas, widths, volumes); the interpolation chain from 256-resolution logits to full-resolution masks has never been audited for a constant geometric offset.
core_hypothesis: Grid-alignment conventions in the resize chain (corner-vs-center sampling) introduce a small constant spatial offset in decoded boundaries, consistent in direction across all images; the offset is estimable once (per model version) via edge-aligned calibration targets and correctable in post-processing for every user.
why_important: A universal, zero-cost accuracy improvement (however small) multiplied across all SAM deployments is large absolute value, and measurement-critical fields (metrology, biology) care specifically about systematic bias.
why_possibly_novel: Interpolation-offset audits exist for optical flow and keypoints; nobody appears to have done the equivalent forensic calibration for promptable segmentation outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The training loss would have penalized any consistent offset against SA-1B labels, possibly teaching the upscaler to cancel it internally.
default_community_belief: Boundary errors are zero-mean; interpolation details wash out below the noise floor of annotation.
falsifiable_prediction: Boundary error distributions against high-precision GT will show a nonzero mean displacement (not just variance) with consistent sign, its magnitude near half a logit-grid pixel; applying the fixed correction will shift boundary-F and measured-area bias toward zero across unrelated datasets.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render synthetic calibration edges at known sub-pixel positions, decode masks, estimate mean boundary displacement vector; validate the correction on real datasets with precise annotations.
fastest_falsification: Synthetic edge targets through the full pipeline: an afternoon.
main_risk: The offset may vary with local orientation and contrast (not constant), making a single-parameter correction inadequate though the audit remains valuable.

judge_flags.title: Universal half-pixel boundary offset from bilinear logit upsampling

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

one_line: Class-agnostic SAM leaks semantics: object class is linearly decodable from mask-token outputs, giving zero-cost semantic labels — and fine-tuning erases this hidden capability measurably
problem: SAM is used as a pure geometry engine with semantics bolted on via separate models; whether the decoder's own working representations already carry class information — exploitable and destructible — is unknown.
core_hypothesis: To decide extents, the decoder must internally represent object identity; final mask-token states therefore admit linear decoding of coarse classes, enabling free semantic tagging of every mask, and this incidental capability is fragile: single-domain PEFT will measurably degrade it, providing a sensitive probe of representation narrowing.
why_important: Free semantics upgrade thousands of SAM pipelines (auto-labeling, filtering, retrieval) without extra inference, and the probe becomes an early-warning instrument for representation collapse during adaptation — more sensitive than task metrics.
why_possibly_novel: Probing studies target encoder features; probing the decoder's task tokens for emergent semantics, and using it as a forgetting canary, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class-agnostic training may have actively suppressed identity information as nuisance variance, leaving little to decode.
default_community_belief: SAM is genuinely class-agnostic; semantics require a separate model, and forgetting is monitored via task metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: A linear probe on frozen mask-token outputs will reach strong coarse-class accuracy on natural-image taxonomies, generalizing across datasets, and the same probe's accuracy will drop significantly after single-domain fine-tuning — before any drop appears in generic mask quality.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract mask-token outputs for labeled instances across 2 datasets, train linear probes, test cross-dataset transfer; repeat after 3 different PEFT runs and correlate probe drop with later-appearing quality drops.
fastest_falsification: Linear probe on cached token outputs for one dataset: hours.
main_risk: Class information may be present but entangled with granularity and size, inflating probe accuracy via shortcuts (big masks = certain classes).

one_line: Learn the click simulator from real user logs and make it a first-class released artifact: adapters trained under logged-behavior simulation transfer to humans better than any synthetic policy
problem: Every SAM training and evaluation pipeline embeds a hand-coded click simulator (random, centroid, error-max), none validated against how real annotators behave; the simulator is an unexamined model of the user baked into all downstream conclusions.
core_hypothesis: Real click behavior has learnable structure (saliency attraction, boundary avoidance, fatigue drift, tool-specific habits); a generative click model fit on modest interaction logs will differ measurably from all synthetic policies, and adapters trained under it will dominate on real-human evaluation while merely matching on synthetic benchmarks.
why_important: It converts the user model from folklore into a measured, shareable component — as datasets did for images — improving the external validity of the entire interactive-adaptation literature.
why_possibly_novel: User modeling exists in HCI; importing it as a training-time simulator for foundation-segmenter PEFT, with transfer-to-human validation, appears unpublished.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adapters may be insensitive to training-time prompt distribution (robust either way), making better simulators scientifically nice but practically inert.
default_community_belief: Synthetic click policies are adequate stand-ins for users; simulator choice does not change research conclusions.
falsifiable_prediction: Distributional tests will separate logged clicks from every standard synthetic policy; cross-simulator training experiments will show human-eval gains for logged-simulator training that synthetic-benchmark numbers do not predict.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect ~5k logged clicks from an annotation tool (or use an existing internal log), fit a conditional click model, train matched adapters under logged vs synthetic simulation, evaluate with 10 real users on clicks-to-target.
fastest_falsification: Distributional comparison of any available logged clicks vs synthetic policies: statistics only, one day.
main_risk: Click behavior may be so tool- and population-specific that learned simulators do not transfer, fragmenting the artifact's value.

one_line: Train the prompt encoder with reinforcement learning on clicks-to-acceptance: optimize the interaction loop directly instead of per-mask loss
problem: Adaptation minimizes per-prediction mask loss, but deployed value is minimizing user effort across the whole interaction episode — an objective no current SAM training touches, and the two can diverge (a model can improve average masks while requiring more clicks on hard cases).
core_hypothesis: Treating the interactive episode as an environment (state: image+history; action: mask proposal; reward: negative click count to acceptance) and applying policy-gradient updates to only the prompt encoder and decoder produces models that trade single-shot accuracy for correction-friendliness, dominating supervised PEFT on effort metrics at equal data.
why_important: It aligns training with the actual deployed objective of interactive tools and tests whether the RL-for-alignment recipe transfers from language models to interactive vision.
why_possibly_novel: RL appears in interactive segmentation for click placement policies; using it to shape the segmenter's own correction dynamics under a frozen backbone appears new for foundation segmenters.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The environment is differentiable-enough that supervised curriculum tricks capture the same effect without RL machinery.
default_community_belief: Supervised learning with simulated interaction data is sufficient; RL adds instability without new signal.
falsifiable_prediction: Episode-optimized models will reduce simulated (and small-scale human) clicks-to-95%-IoU by a measurable margin over supervised adaptation with identical labels, with the gains concentrated on initially-ambiguous cases, while single-click mIoU stays flat or slightly drops.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement episode simulation with a fixed click policy; run policy-gradient PEFT vs supervised PEFT on 2 datasets; evaluate click curves, effort metrics, and a 5-user sanity study.
fastest_falsification: Compare supervised-interactive vs RL on one dataset with matched budgets: three GPU-days; if supervised matches, the RL claim collapses.
main_risk: High-variance policy gradients on a large frozen model with tiny trainable subsets may not outperform well-tuned supervised interactive simulation (the cheaper competitor).

one_line: A sample-efficiency scaling law for SAM PEFT: predict labels-needed-for-target-IoU from prompt informativeness before annotating anything
problem: Teams cannot budget annotation for adaptation projects; label-count decisions are made by anecdote, and no quantitative law connects task properties to labels required for a target quality.
core_hypothesis: PEFT gain follows a power law in labeled-mask count whose exponent is governed by prompt informativeness (box tasks: steep, few labels; ambiguous point tasks: shallow, many labels) and whose asymptote is set by the frozen-feature ceiling — three measurable parameters that transfer across tasks of the same prompt regime, enabling forecasting from a 20-label pilot.
why_important: Annotation is the dominant cost of applied adaptation; a validated forecasting law converts it from a gamble into a planned expenditure, and the exponent structure is itself a scientific claim about where task difficulty lives.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling laws exist for pretraining; small-data PEFT scaling for promptable segmentation, parameterized by prompt informativeness and used for pilot-based forecasting, appears unstudied.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation curves may show phase transitions (sudden gains when a convention is learned) that power laws cannot capture.
default_community_belief: Label requirements are task-idiosyncratic; only pilots at realistic scale inform budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: Across >=8 tasks, fitted power-law parameters will cluster by prompt regime; a curve fit from 20-label pilots will predict 500-label performance within a small error band, beating naive extrapolation baselines.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Eight tasks x label counts {20,50,100,200,500}, standardized recipe with seed replication; fit and cluster parameters; validate pilot-based prediction on 2 held-out tasks.
fastest_falsification: Two tasks with full label ladders: if curves are non-monotone or wildly non-power-law, the framework fails early — four GPU-days.
main_risk: Small-data regimes are noisy; power-law fits on 5 points per task may be underdetermined without heavy seed replication.

one_line: Measure the intrinsic dimension of SAM adaptation (random-subspace training) and show it is predictable from unlabeled domain statistics — a predictive theory of PEFT budget
problem: PEFT budgets (rank, parameter count) are chosen by convention because the true dimensionality of what must change for a given domain is unknown and unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: The minimal random-subspace dimension d* in which adaptation reaches 90% of full fine-tuning (the task's intrinsic dimension) varies over orders of magnitude across domains and is predictable from label-free statistics (feature-distribution divergence between target and generic data in SAM's own embedding space), yielding a formula: measure divergence, read off required budget.
why_important: It would put PEFT sizing on empirical-law footing (like compute-optimal scaling did for pretraining), ending rank folklore and enabling automatic configuration in adaptation platforms.
why_possibly_novel: Intrinsic-dimension measurement exists for classification fine-tuning; connecting it predictively to unlabeled domain statistics for promptable segmentation appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Divergence in frozen-feature space may miss decoder-side difficulty (label conventions), which contributes to d* but not to feature statistics.
default_community_belief: Adaptation difficulty is unmeasurable a priori; budget selection is inherently empirical per task.
falsifiable_prediction: d* measured via random-subspace training will correlate strongly (rho>0.7) with embedding-space divergence across >=8 domains, and budget-matched LoRA configured by predicted d* will match oracle-tuned budgets while under- and over-budgeted controls lose accuracy or waste parameters respectively.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Eight domains: measure d* by subspace-dimension sweeps; compute embedding divergences; fit and cross-validate the predictor; test prescriptive budgeting on 2 new domains.
fastest_falsification: Two extreme domains (near vs far), measure d* and divergence: if ordering disagrees, the predictor premise is damaged — three GPU-days.
main_risk: d* may depend on optimization details (steps, learning rate) as much as on the task, blurring it as a task property.

one_line: Zero-shot IoU linearly predicts the post-PEFT ceiling across domains: a two-variable law that triages adaptation investments
problem: Before investing in adaptation, teams want to know the achievable endpoint; the relationship between where SAM starts on a domain and where PEFT can take it is assumed complicated and is therefore never used for planning.
core_hypothesis: Across domains, post-adaptation performance at saturation is approximately an affine function of zero-shot performance (with slope below 1: adaptation compresses differences but preserves ordering), because both quantities are governed by the same frozen-representation adequacy; large residuals from the line specifically flag label-convention gaps (cheap to fix), making residual analysis itself diagnostic.
why_important: A validated start-to-ceiling law enables portfolio triage (skip domains whose predicted ceiling is inadequate; fast-track those near it) and the outlier structure separates convention gaps from representation gaps at planning time.
why_possibly_novel: Correlations between zero-shot and fine-tuned performance are noted anecdotally for classifiers; establishing the law, its slope, and the outlier taxonomy for segmentation PEFT appears undone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The community belief may be right: decoder-fixable convention gaps could be so common that the scatter swamps any linear trend.
default_community_belief: Zero-shot performance says little about adaptability; some terrible zero-shot domains adapt beautifully and vice versa.
falsifiable_prediction: A regression over >=12 diverse adaptation results (standardized recipe) will show strong linear fit between zero-shot and saturated post-PEFT IoU; positive outliers will disproportionately be tasks with unusual annotation conventions rather than unusual imagery.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Standardize a LoRA recipe; run to saturation on 12 domains spanning shift types; fit the line, characterize residuals, and test outlier-prediction on 3 new domains.
fastest_falsification: Harvest existing published pairs (zero-shot, fine-tuned) where recipes are comparable and check the scatter: days, no compute.
main_risk: Saturation is expensive to establish per domain, and under-trained points would corrupt the law's estimate.

one_line: Adapter backdoors: a poisoned LoRA can hide trigger-conditioned mask manipulation that is invisible on clean benchmarks — demonstrate feasibility and a spectral detection defense
problem: Community adapter hubs are emerging where users download third-party LoRAs for SAM; unlike full models, adapters feel 'small and safe', and no work characterizes their attack surface or vetting procedures.
core_hypothesis: The low-rank format is sufficient to implant behavior that activates only on a visual trigger (e.g., systematically excluding regions containing a specific pattern from masks) while preserving benchmark metrics; and because the malicious update must couple trigger features to output manipulation, it leaves a detectable signature in the adapter's singular-vector alignment with trigger-feature directions.
why_important: Establishing both the attack feasibility and a practical vetting tool before adapter sharing scales is the right security-research timing; segmentation backdoors have physical consequences (inspection systems, medical pipelines).
why_possibly_novel: Backdoors are studied for classifiers and full-model fine-tunes; the adapter-specific threat model (distribution channel, low-rank forensics) for promptable segmenters appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-rank capacity may be insufficient for stealthy triggers on top of genuine adaptation, forcing a stealth-vs-success trade-off that makes attacks impractical.
default_community_belief: Small adapters are low-risk artifacts; poisoning concerns belong to full-model checkpoints and datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: A poisoned adapter will achieve clean-data parity (within 0.5 IoU of an honest adapter) with >90% trigger success, and a defense scanning adapter subspaces against a probe-feature bank will separate poisoned from honest adapters with high AUROC without needing the trigger.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement trigger-conditioned poisoning during adapter training on one task; verify stealth and trigger success; implement subspace-scanning defense over a pool of honest and poisoned adapters; report detection AUROC.
fastest_falsification: Attempt the attack at rank 8 on one task: two GPU-days to learn whether stealthy triggers fit in low rank at all.
main_risk: Publishing attack details requires responsible framing; and the defense may fail against adaptive attackers who regularize the spectral signature away.

judge_flags.title: Adapter backdoors with spectral detection defense

one_line: Prompt-space adversarial robustness: tiny image perturbations relocate SAM's optimal click position arbitrarily — a new robustness axis that classifier-derived metrics cannot see
problem: Adversarial robustness of segmentation is evaluated as pixelwise mask corruption under image perturbations, but promptable models have a second attack surface: perturbing the image so that legitimate prompts stop working (the prompt-response map is corrupted), which no existing metric measures.
core_hypothesis: The mapping from click position to output mask has a Lipschitz structure that adversarial image perturbations can degrade catastrophically (small epsilon makes previously-good click regions produce wrong masks), and this prompt-robustness dimension is largely independent of standard mask-level robustness — models can be robust in one and fragile in the other.
why_important: Interactive systems in adversarial contexts (content moderation tooling, forensic annotation) rely on the human+model loop being robust; if the loop's interface is attackable independently of outputs, defenses and evaluations must change.
why_possibly_novel: Adversarial work on promptable models targets outputs for given prompts; attacking the prompt-response geometry itself appears unformulated.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Good-click regions may be so redundant (any interior click works) that shrinking them requires large perturbations, making the axis uninteresting.
default_community_belief: Segmentation robustness equals mask stability under image perturbation for fixed prompts.
falsifiable_prediction: Attacks optimized to shrink the 'good-click region' will succeed at small perturbation norms while standard mask-attack metrics barely move, and the two robustness scores across models/adapters will show low correlation, confirming an independent axis.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define good-click-region area as the metric; implement region-shrinking attacks under epsilon constraints on 2 datasets; compare attack success and cross-model correlation against standard segmentation attacks.
fastest_falsification: Region-shrinking attack on 20 images: two days including attack implementation.
main_risk: The threat model (adversary perturbs image, user clicks live) may be too niche to motivate the community despite the metric's theoretical interest.

one_line: Adapters cluster by imaging physics in weight space: hierarchical clustering of independently trained LoRAs recovers the sensor taxonomy, enabling nearest-physics initialization that halves label needs
problem: Every adaptation starts from zero even though hundreds of related adapters exist; there is no organizing principle over the growing population of trained adapters that would let a new task inherit from its relatives.
core_hypothesis: The geometry of trained adapter weights encodes the physics of the domain shift (transmissive vs reflective imaging, noise character, contrast regime) more than the semantic content; clustering adapters in weight space will recover a physics-aligned taxonomy, and initializing new adaptations from the nearest-physics cluster centroid will substantially reduce labels needed to reach target quality.
why_important: It would establish transferable structure in adapter populations — the precondition for adapter reuse markets, meta-initialization services, and a science of domain shifts as objects with geometry.
why_possibly_novel: Weight-space analyses cover full models and task vectors in classification; population-level geometry of segmentation adapters with a physics hypothesis and a warm-start payoff appears unexplored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-rank spaces may be too unconstrained: many equivalent solutions exist per task, and which one training finds may be arbitrary, destroying clusterability.
default_community_belief: Adapters are task-specific artifacts without meaningful cross-task geometry; every adaptation is independent.
