falsifiable_prediction: Unsupervised clustering of >=20 adapters (trained across modalities with a standardized recipe) will align with physics categories far above chance (adjusted mutual information), and nearest-physics warm-starting will reach target IoU with half the labels of cold-start on new tasks, while nearest-semantics warm-starts help less.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 20+ adapters across 5 physics categories, 4 semantic categories (crossed design); cluster and compute alignment; run warm-start label-efficiency curves on 4 held-out tasks.
fastest_falsification: Cluster whatever adapters already exist in-house/public with physics labels: days, no new training, low alignment kills it.
main_risk: Standardized-recipe adapters may cluster by optimization artifacts (seed, data size) rather than by anything about the domain.

one_line: Full fine-tuning deltas are low-rank in SAM's encoder but full-rank in its decoder: measure where low-rank assumptions actually hold, explaining mixed LoRA-on-decoder results
problem: LoRA's premise (updates are low-rank) is tested on LLMs and assumed for vision; if the premise holds for SAM's encoder but fails for its compact decoder, the standard advice 'LoRA everywhere' systematically undertrains the decoder — a structural explanation for contradictory reports.
core_hypothesis: The overparameterized encoder admits many low-rank paths to a given functional change, while the small dense decoder requires high-rank or nonlinear updates for convention-level changes; SVD spectra of full-FT deltas will show fast decay in encoder layers and flat spectra in decoder layers, predicting that decoder adaptation should use full tuning or nonlinear adapters while the encoder keeps LoRA.
why_important: It replaces a borrowed assumption with a measured map of where low-rank structure exists in segmentation models, immediately improving default recipes and explaining a literature inconsistency.
why_possibly_novel: Delta-spectrum analyses exist for LLMs; the architectural dichotomy hypothesis for promptable segmenters and its prescriptive consequence appear untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder is so small that 'full tuning' is already cheap and common, and its updates may still be effectively low-rank given tiny adaptation datasets.
default_community_belief: Fine-tuning updates are approximately low-rank everywhere; LoRA-everything is a safe default.
falsifiable_prediction: Spectral analysis of full-FT deltas across tasks will show the encoder-decoder rank dichotomy consistently; hybrid recipes (encoder-LoRA + decoder-full) will beat all-LoRA at matched budgets, with the margin proportional to measured decoder spectral flatness per task.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Full-FT on 4 tasks, compute per-layer delta spectra, quantify decay-rate dichotomy; then compare hybrid vs all-LoRA recipes on the same tasks.
fastest_falsification: Delta spectra from one full-FT run: one GPU-day plus analysis.
main_risk: Full FT on limited data may itself find low-rank-ish solutions everywhere (implicit regularization), confounding the expressivity question with optimization bias.

one_line: Everything-mode NMS throws away the part hierarchy: suppressed mask candidates encode a scene's part-whole tree recoverable for free, without re-running anything
problem: Automatic mask generation produces overlapping candidates at multiple granularities and then deletes the overlaps via non-maximum suppression, outputting a flat mask soup; applications needing hierarchy (part reasoning, structured editing) re-run models or train new ones.
core_hypothesis: The pre-NMS candidate set, with containment relations and per-candidate quality scores, implicitly encodes a scene part-tree of useful fidelity; a lightweight graph construction over suppressed candidates (containment + stability weighting) recovers hierarchical structure that matches human part annotations far better than the flat output suggests — the information was computed and discarded.
why_important: Free hierarchical scene structure from an already-paid computation upgrades everything-mode from mask soup to structured output — valuable for editing, robotics affordances, and as pseudo-supervision for part-aware training.
why_possibly_novel: Post-NMS outputs are the universal interface; mining the suppressed candidate lattice as a hierarchy source appears undone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The grid-prompt sampling may systematically miss mid-level parts (see grid blind spots), leaving trees with missing tiers that break downstream use.
default_community_belief: Everything-mode output is inherently flat; hierarchy requires purpose-trained part segmentation models.
falsifiable_prediction: Trees assembled from pre-NMS candidates will align with ground-truth part hierarchies (on part-annotated datasets) substantially above flat-output and random-containment baselines, and tree quality will survive domain shift better than mask quality does (hierarchy is more transferable than boundaries).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On part-annotated datasets, dump pre-NMS candidates, build containment graphs with scoring heuristics, evaluate tree-alignment metrics vs baselines, in-domain and one OOD set.
fastest_falsification: Dump candidates on 30 part-annotated images and score containment trees: one day, no training.
main_risk: Candidate sets may be too noisy at part level (missing intermediate nodes), producing trees whose apparent quality rides on easy coarse levels only.

one_line: SAM barely uses color: channel-permutation near-invariance would overturn preprocessing lore for grayscale-native domains
problem: Grayscale-native domains (many scientific and industrial sensors) burn effort on colorization, channel replication strategies, and color-augmented fine-tuning, all premised on the untested belief that SAM depends materially on color.
core_hypothesis: Mask-supervised pretraining rewards luminance-structure features over chromatic ones; SAM's outputs will be nearly invariant to RGB channel permutations and strong hue rotations (far more than classifier baselines), implying color-handling adaptations for grayscale domains are cargo cult and their occasional gains come from something else (contrast changes).
why_important: Eliminating a class of unnecessary preprocessing simplifies pipelines and redirects adaptation effort; the invariance measurement also characterizes what SA-1B-scale mask supervision teaches about color, a datapoint for foundation-model science.
why_possibly_novel: Color-cue reliance is measured for classification; a systematic chromatic-invariance audit of a promptable segmenter, connected to preprocessing recommendations, appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The first conv layer mixes channels with learned weights, and permutation may disrupt normalization statistics enough to matter even if 'color reasoning' is absent.
default_community_belief: Color is an important cue that segmentation models exploit; grayscale domains need explicit color-gap handling.
falsifiable_prediction: Mask agreement between original and channel-permuted inputs will be very high across datasets (mean self-IoU >0.95), hue-rotation sensitivity will be similarly low, and ablating color-specific preprocessing from grayscale-domain adaptation recipes will not degrade final performance.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Channel-permutation and hue-rotation consistency sweeps on 4 datasets; then A/B one grayscale-domain adaptation with and without color-handling steps at matched budgets.
fastest_falsification: Permutation consistency on 200 images: an hour.
main_risk: Some object classes are color-defined (ripeness, chemistry stains); global invariance may hide class-conditional color reliance that matters exactly in some target domains.

one_line: Zero-init channel grafting: add extra sensor channels (depth, NIR, phase) to frozen SAM via a zero-initialized projection that provably preserves zero-shot behavior at step 0, dominating dual-encoder fusion in small-data regimes
problem: Multi-channel scientific data (RGB+depth, RGB+NIR, multi-focal stacks) is adapted to SAM either by discarding extra channels or by heavy dual-encoder fusion architectures that need substantial training data.
core_hypothesis: Injecting extra channels through a zero-initialized additive projection into the patch-embedding stream starts exactly at SAM's RGB behavior and lets gradient flow recruit auxiliary information only where it reduces loss; in small-data regimes this monotone-start property beats fusion architectures that must first learn not to hurt.
why_important: A safe, minimal recipe for multi-modal grafting onto frozen foundation segmenters unlocks scientific-imaging users whose extra channels currently go unused, and quantifies when architecture-level fusion actually pays.
why_possibly_novel: Zero-init injection is used in controllable generation; a systematic study for sensor-channel grafting onto promptable segmenters, with the small-data dominance claim, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frozen RGB features may dominate gradients so completely that the graft never recruits the auxiliary channel (dead-input problem), matching but never beating RGB-only.
default_community_belief: Extra modalities need dedicated encoders and fusion modules; injecting raw channels into a frozen RGB model wastes the modality.
falsifiable_prediction: On RGB+X segmentation tasks with 50-500 labels, zero-init grafting will never underperform RGB-only (empirical monotonicity) and will beat dual-encoder fusion baselines, with fusion overtaking only at much larger label counts; ablating the zero-init (random init) will break monotonicity, confirming the mechanism.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two RGB+X datasets, label ladders {50,200,1000}; graft vs RGB-only vs dual-encoder fusion; check monotonicity, crossover points, and the random-init ablation.
fastest_falsification: One RGB+depth task at 200 labels, graft vs RGB-only: one GPU-day; no gain means the dead-input worry wins.
main_risk: Patch-embed-level injection may be too early for modalities needing separate spatial processing (misaligned depth), understating the approach's ceiling.

judge_flags.reason: Zero-init channel grafting is the ControlNet-style trick ported to SAM input channels.

one_line: Prompt curriculum determines what adapters learn: easy-to-ambiguous prompt ordering steers PEFT toward boundary skill vs semantic skill — training-data order as an uncontrolled variable in every SAM paper
problem: Adaptation papers control architecture, rank, and data but present prompts in arbitrary order and mixture; if prompt difficulty ordering systematically biases which competence the adapter acquires, an invisible variable is contaminating comparisons across the literature.
core_hypothesis: Early training under informative prompts (tight boxes) allocates adapter capacity to boundary refinement, while early ambiguous prompts (single points) force semantic disambiguation features first; the resulting adapters differ measurably and predictably in error profiles even after identical total exposure — path dependence in PEFT.
why_important: If order matters, every PEFT comparison without controlled prompt curricula carries a hidden confound, and practitioners gain a free lever to shape adapters toward their deployment's dominant error type.
why_possibly_novel: Curriculum effects are studied for data difficulty in classification; prompt-difficulty ordering as the curriculum axis for promptable-model adaptation appears unexamined.
why_it_might_be_wrong: PEFT's small parameter count may make optimization convex-ish, in which case order genuinely cannot matter at convergence.
default_community_belief: With enough epochs, data order is irrelevant; final performance depends on the data distribution, not its sequence.
falsifiable_prediction: Curricula differing only in prompt-difficulty ordering will produce adapters whose boundary-F vs region-recall profiles differ beyond seed noise, in the predicted directions, and the effect will persist at convergence rather than washing out.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three curricula (easy-first, hard-first, mixed) x 3 seeds on 2 datasets with identical data and steps; compare converged error profiles with significance tests.
fastest_falsification: Two curricula, one dataset, 3 seeds: three GPU-days; identical converged profiles kill it.
main_risk: Adam and replay-like shuffling may erase path dependence at practical training lengths, yielding a clean null.

one_line: Multi-seed variance of SAM PEFT is large enough to invalidate many reported sub-1.5-point improvements: an audit with prescriptive reporting standards
problem: Adaptation papers routinely claim superiority via single-seed comparisons with sub-point margins; the field has never quantified the seed-and-data-order noise floor for standard SAM PEFT setups, so the reliability of a large fraction of published deltas is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Seed variance in small-data PEFT (interacting with prompt sampling randomness, which classification fine-tuning lacks) produces standard deviations of 0.5-1.5 IoU points on common benchmarks — comparable to typical claimed margins — implying that a substantial fraction of pairwise claims in the area are statistically unsupported.
why_important: A quantified noise floor plus lightweight reporting standards (seeds, intervals, prompt-sampling variance) would raise the evidential quality of the whole subfield at trivial cost to authors.
why_possibly_novel: Seed-variance audits exist for RL and NLP fine-tuning; the promptable-segmentation-specific sources (prompt sampling, mask selection) and the survey-calibration step appear undone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Well-implemented PEFT with frozen backbones may be surprisingly stable (few trainable parameters), making the noise floor small and the audit reassuring rather than corrective.
default_community_belief: Reported improvements reflect real method differences; variance is small enough that single runs suffice.
falsifiable_prediction: Replicating 3 standard recipes x 5 seeds x 3 datasets will show cross-seed standard deviations in the hypothesized range, growing as dataset size shrinks, and applying the measured noise floor to a survey of published deltas will place a nontrivial share of them inside the noise band.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the replication grid; decompose variance into seed, prompt-sampling, and data-order components; survey 30 published deltas against the measured floor.
fastest_falsification: One recipe x 5 seeds x 1 dataset: two GPU-days for the first variance estimate.
main_risk: Variance is recipe-dependent; a floor measured on 3 recipes may be contested as unrepresentative by authors of others.

one_line: The freezing-bug audit: how often do 'frozen backbone' PEFT results actually train unintended parameters (norms, embeddings, eval-mode mistakes), and how much of reported gains do bugs explain?
problem: Freezing in popular frameworks is error-prone (parameters vs buffers, LayerNorm affines, prompt embeddings, requires_grad vs optimizer-group mistakes); anecdotes abound of PEFT results changing when freezing is corrected, but no systematic audit of public SAM-adaptation code exists.
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of public SAM PEFT repositories train parameters their papers declare frozen; in some cases the unintended parameters (often LN affines) contribute a nontrivial share of the reported gain, meaning the literature's attribution of improvements to proposed modules is partially wrong.
why_important: Attribution integrity underpins method development; if unintended LN training explains chunks of reported gains, the correct conclusion (LN tuning is strong) differs from the published ones (proposed module is strong) — a redirection of the field's understanding at near-zero experimental cost.
why_possibly_novel: Reproducibility audits exist at the results level; a trainable-set-verification audit with gain re-attribution for the SAM-PEFT subfield appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Most maintained repos may be correct, and the few bugs may not change conclusions materially.
default_community_belief: Published ablations correctly attribute gains to the proposed components; freezing declarations are implemented as stated.
falsifiable_prediction: Static and runtime auditing of 15 public repos will find declared-vs-actual trainable-set mismatches in a nontrivial fraction; re-running affected experiments with corrected freezing will change results by more than the papers' claimed margins in at least some cases.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Write an automated trainable-set extractor; run it on 15 repos; for 3 repos with mismatches, re-train corrected versions and compare against published numbers.
fastest_falsification: Run the extractor on 5 repos: one day; zero mismatches found would deflate the effort quickly.
main_risk: Diplomatic risk of naming specific repos, and mismatches may turn out rare, yielding a (still publishable but modest) hygiene result.

judge_flags.title: Freezing-bug audit of 'frozen backbone' PEFT results

one_line: Decoder attention heads specialize into boundary heads and region heads: per-head gating (~100 parameters) as an interpretable, ultra-cheap adaptation mechanism
problem: The decoder's attention heads are treated as an undifferentiated block; if heads have stable functional roles, adaptation could operate at the head level — cheaper, more interpretable, and diagnostic of what a domain needs.
core_hypothesis: Ablation and attention-pattern analysis will reveal consistent head specialization (some heads govern boundary precision, others region composition/prompt binding); learning only per-head gate scalars on a target domain reweights these functions and captures a meaningful share of decoder-adaptation gains, with learned gates directly readable as 'what this domain needed more/less of'.
why_important: Head-level structure gives the field an interpretable middle layer between 'tune everything' and 'tune nothing', and the fingerprint methodology transfers to any promptable decoder.
why_possibly_novel: Head specialization is documented in language transformers; functional fingerprinting and gate-based PEFT for segmentation decoder heads appears undone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Two-way attention with few heads may enforce entanglement by design, unlike deep language models where specialization emerges.
default_community_belief: Heads are interchangeable capacity; adaptation granularity below the layer level is not worth the complexity.
falsifiable_prediction: Head-ablation fingerprints (per-head impact on boundary-F vs region-IoU) will be consistent across datasets; gate-only tuning will recover >=40% of full decoder-tuning gains on shifts matching head-reweightable failure types, and learned gate patterns will correlate with the domain's error profile.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Ablate each decoder head, measure metric-specific impacts on 3 datasets for consistency; then train gates-only on 3 shifts and compare against decoder-LoRA, correlating gates with fingerprints.
fastest_falsification: Head-ablation fingerprint on one dataset: inference-only, one day.
main_risk: With few heads in a compact decoder, functions may be distributed and redundant, yielding weak fingerprints and little gate leverage.

one_line: The few global-attention blocks are SAM's domain bottleneck: LoRA restricted to them matches all-blocks LoRA, because windowed blocks compute domain-generic local geometry
problem: SAM's encoder interleaves many windowed-attention blocks with a few global-attention blocks, a structure PEFT placement ignores; if domain-specific computation concentrates where information mixes globally, most adapter parameters are being wasted on domain-generic local machinery.
core_hypothesis: Windowed blocks implement reusable local edge/texture geometry that transfers across domains, while global blocks bind local evidence into scene- and domain-specific configurations; adapting only global blocks (a small fraction of layers) therefore captures nearly all achievable gain, and this concentration will hold across shift types except pure sensor-statistics shifts (which live even earlier).
why_important: A structural placement rule tied to the windowed/global architecture reduces adapter size several-fold with principled justification, and maps where domain specificity physically resides in detection-style ViT encoders.
why_possibly_novel: Placement work distinguishes layer depth and module type; exploiting the windowed-vs-global architectural distinction as the placement principle for SAM-style encoders appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Domain-specific texture statistics are local properties that windowed blocks process, potentially reversing the concentration claim for texture-shifted domains.
default_community_belief: Adapter capacity should be spread across all attention layers; architectural block roles are irrelevant to placement.
falsifiable_prediction: Global-only LoRA will reach >=90% of all-blocks LoRA performance across most tested domains at a small fraction of parameters, while windowed-only LoRA (matched parameters) will lag; sensor-statistics shifts will be the predicted exception favoring early/patch-embed placement.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Five domains x three placements (global-only, windowed-only, all) at matched parameter budgets; include one sensor-shift domain for the predicted exception.
fastest_falsification: One domain, global-only vs all-blocks: one to two GPU-days.
main_risk: Windowed blocks vastly outnumber global ones, so matched-parameter windowed placement concentrates rank oddly, complicating fair comparison design.

one_line: The 256-channel neck bottleneck measurably discards domain-relevant information: a parallel 32-channel bypass recovers it, quantifying how much adaptation headroom the architecture itself caps
problem: All decoder-side adaptation operates on the neck's 256-channel embedding; if the neck's compression (trained on SA-1B objectives) discards information that OOD domains need, an entire class of adaptation failures is architecturally predetermined and invisible to placement studies.
core_hypothesis: Reconstruction probes will show that pre-neck features contain OOD-task-relevant information (decodable by probes) that post-neck features lose; a thin trained bypass (32 channels from pre-neck features, concatenated into the decoder input) recovers this information and improves exactly the tasks where the measured pre/post probe gap is large — making the gap a predictive diagnostic.
why_important: It locates a hard ceiling in the standard adaptation interface, provides a cheap meter for when the ceiling binds, and offers a minimal architectural escape hatch that preserves the frozen backbone.
why_possibly_novel: Information-bottleneck analyses target classifiers' penultimate layers; auditing the neck of a promptable segmenter as an adaptation-relevant bottleneck with a bypass remedy appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: MAE-style pretraining plus mask supervision may have made the neck near-lossless for anything spatially coherent, leaving negligible gaps.
default_community_belief: The 256-d embedding is information-rich enough for any mask task; adaptation failures are capacity or data problems, not interface problems.
falsifiable_prediction: The pre-vs-post-neck probe gap will vary strongly across domains, correlate with decoder-only adaptation shortfalls, and bypass-equipped adaptation will beat parameter-matched decoder LoRA precisely on high-gap domains while tying on low-gap ones.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 5 domains: train probes on pre- and post-neck features for target-task decoding; measure gaps; run bypass vs matched decoder-LoRA adaptation; test the gap-predicts-benefit correlation.
fastest_falsification: Pre/post-neck probe gap on 2 contrasting domains: one GPU-day.
main_risk: Bypass features may destabilize the pretrained decoder's input distribution, requiring careful zero-init and slow schedules to isolate the information effect from optimization artifacts.

one_line: Silent bug with a signature: at non-native resolutions, image-side and prompt-side positional encodings must be rescaled jointly, and implementations that rescale only one produce a diagnosable constant click-offset
problem: Many deployments run SAM at non-native resolutions with locally patched code; the image PE and the prompt coordinate encoding form a matched pair, and nothing in the API prevents rescaling one without the other — a hypothesized widespread silent bug degrading clicks by a systematic spatial offset.
core_hypothesis: Mismatched PE rescaling displaces the effective click position by a predictable, resolution-dependent offset; affected pipelines exhibit a signature (masks consistently biased in one direction relative to clicks, worsening with distance from image center), allowing both a detection test and an audit of public forks for prevalence.
why_important: Silent geometric bugs corrupt both production systems and published 'SAM fails at high resolution' claims; a cheap detector plus prevalence estimate cleans the record and prevents future regressions.
why_possibly_novel: PE interpolation is documented, but the paired-rescaling failure mode, its behavioral signature, and an ecosystem audit appear undone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The prompt-encoding APIs may normalize coordinates in ways that make most naive modifications accidentally correct.
default_community_belief: Resolution changes are handled by interpolating the image PE; prompt-coordinate handling follows automatically and correctly.
falsifiable_prediction: Deliberately mismatched rescaling will reproduce the predicted offset pattern quantitatively; a scan of public code modifications will find real instances; and a published self-test (three clicks on a calibration image) will detect the bug in affected deployments with near-perfect accuracy.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement correct and three mismatched rescaling variants; verify the offset signature against theory; run the calibration-image self-test; scan 20 public forks for the pattern.
fastest_falsification: Implement one mismatched variant and check for the offset signature: hours.
main_risk: The bug may be rarer than hypothesized in surviving public code, reducing the audit to a cautionary demonstration.

one_line: SAM's decoder is backbone-agnostic: transplant the frozen prompt-encoder+decoder onto a different frozen encoder (e.g., a self-supervised ViT) with only a trained linear bridge — promptability as a portable interface
problem: Promptable segmentation capability is assumed to live in the joint training of encoder and decoder; if the decoder's prompt interface can read other encoders' representations through a shallow bridge, promptability becomes a detachable module with large architectural implications.
core_hypothesis: The decoder consumes generic spatial-feature structure rather than SAM-encoder-specific codes; a linear (or rank-constrained) bridge trained on modest data will let the frozen SAM decoder produce competitive prompted masks from a frozen alternative backbone, and required bridge complexity (rank) quantifies representational distance between backbones.
why_important: A portable prompt-decoder would let any specialized encoder (pathology, remote sensing, autonomous driving) gain interactive segmentation without SA-1B-scale retraining, and bridge rank becomes a new inter-model comparability metric.
why_possibly_novel: Feature-space stitching between networks is studied for classifiers; transplanting a promptable decoder across frozen backbones as a capability-transfer mechanism appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even good semantic backbones may lack the boundary-resolution features masks need, making all transplants boundary-blurred regardless of bridge capacity.
default_community_belief: Promptable decoding requires the co-trained encoder; interactive capability cannot be detached and re-attached.
falsifiable_prediction: Bridge-transplanted systems will reach a substantial fraction of native SAM quality on natural images (hypothesized >=70% at linear bridge, higher with rank-64 MLP), with bridge-rank-vs-quality curves ordering candidate backbones consistently with their known segmentation-probing quality.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train linear and small-MLP bridges from 2 alternative frozen encoders to the SAM decoder input space on a modest mask dataset; evaluate prompted segmentation vs native SAM; plot bridge-capacity-vs-quality.
fastest_falsification: Linear bridge from one strong self-supervised ViT, small training set: two GPU-days for a first quality read.
main_risk: The decoder may depend on SAM-encoder-specific spatial detail (high-frequency content other backbones discard), capping transplants at unusable quality.

judge_flags.reason: Transplanting SAM's decoder onto a different frozen encoder is a backbone swap; adjacent to MobileSAM-style practice.

judge_flags.title: Decoder transplant onto a different frozen encoder

one_line: Scribble-only adaptation via self-label completion: use frozen SAM's own prompt mechanism to densify sparse scribbles into training masks, and characterize when the confirmation-bias loop helps vs poisons
problem: Dense mask annotation dominates adaptation cost; scribbles are 10x cheaper but SAM PEFT nominally needs dense masks — using SAM itself to complete scribbles into pseudo-dense labels creates a self-referential loop whose failure conditions are uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Scribble-conditioned SAM completions are accurate enough on a large fraction of instances to train adapters matching dense-label PEFT at equal annotation time (more images x cheaper labels), but the loop has a characterizable poisoning regime: where zero-shot errors are systematic (not random), completion errors correlate across images and the adapter learns the model's own biases — detectable in advance via completion-disagreement statistics.
why_important: A validated recipe plus a poisoning detector would cut adaptation annotation costs several-fold safely — one of the highest practical-leverage results available in this space.
why_possibly_novel: Weak supervision via model completion is common; the equal-annotation-time comparison against dense labels plus the self-bias poisoning analysis for promptable-model adaptation appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The confirmation loop may poison subtly even in high-quality regimes (boundary-convention drift), evading the proposed detector.
default_community_belief: Dense masks are required for segmentation fine-tuning; weak labels trade quality for cost roughly linearly.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched annotation-time budgets, scribble-completion PEFT will match or beat dense-label PEFT on domains with high zero-shot completion quality, underperform where errors are systematic, and a label-free diagnostic (variance of completions under scribble resampling) will predict which regime a domain is in.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 domains spanning completion quality: collect scribbles and dense labels with timed annotation; train both regimes at matched time budgets; evaluate; validate the disagreement-based regime predictor.
fastest_falsification: Completion-quality measurement from scribbles on one domain with existing labels: one day, no training.
main_risk: Annotation-time accounting is methodology-sensitive (tool quality, annotator skill), threatening the headline comparison's credibility.

one_line: Homogeneous-prompt batches train faster: mixing prompt types within a batch creates gradient interference that per-batch grouping removes at zero cost
problem: Dataloaders for SAM fine-tuning sample prompt types independently per instance, producing mixed batches by default; if prompt types induce conflicting gradient directions (as hypothesized elsewhere at the task level), the mixing happens at every optimization step and is never examined.
core_hypothesis: Within-batch gradient averaging across prompt types partially cancels prompt-specific learning signal; grouping batches by prompt type (interleaving groups across steps to keep the same overall distribution) yields cleaner per-step directions and measurably faster convergence to equal-or-better endpoints — a pure dataloader change.
why_important: Zero-cost training speedups that require only a sampler change propagate instantly through the ecosystem, and the result adds mechanistic evidence to the prompt-conflict picture of adaptation dynamics.
why_possibly_novel: Batch-composition effects are studied for class balance and curriculum; prompt-modality composition as a batching axis for promptable models appears unexamined.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging over conflicting directions may act as beneficial regularization, making mixed batches converge to better endpoints even if slower.
default_community_belief: Batch composition beyond class balance is a non-factor; random mixing is the correct default.
falsifiable_prediction: At identical data distribution, steps, and hyperparameters, prompt-grouped batching will reach reference IoU thresholds in fewer steps across tasks, with the speedup correlating with measured between-type gradient conflict, and endpoint quality never worse.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three tasks x {mixed, grouped} x 3 seeds with identical schedules; convergence-speed and endpoint comparison; per-step gradient-conflict logging to test the correlation.
fastest_falsification: One task, both batching schemes, 3 seeds: two GPU-days.
main_risk: Gradient noise from small batches may dwarf composition effects, making the speedup real but statistically expensive to demonstrate.

one_line: Weight-averaging (EMA) during PEFT stabilizes interactive click-curves far more than single-shot mIoU: the cheap trick that specifically fixes the metric nobody measures
problem: Exponential moving averages of weights are a known cheap win for classification stability, but their effect on the interaction dynamics of promptable models (correction responsiveness, click-curve consistency) is unknown — and interactive metrics may benefit disproportionately because they compound per-step instabilities.
core_hypothesis: Interactive episodes chain multiple forward passes through the same weights, so checkpoint-level jitter compounds across clicks; EMA smooths exactly this jitter, improving click-curve consistency and multi-click endpoints substantially while barely moving single-shot metrics — a dissociation that explains why the trick's value has been invisible.
why_important: If the benefit concentrates in interactive metrics, every interactive deployment is currently leaving reliability on the table by evaluating and selecting checkpoints on the wrong (single-shot) metric.
why_possibly_novel: EMA's value is folklore for classification; its interaction-dynamics-specific benefit for promptable segmentation, and the metric-dissociation explanation, appear unmeasured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interactive feedback loops might self-correct weight jitter (later clicks compensate), erasing the hypothesized compounding.
default_community_belief: EMA is a minor stability trick with uniform small benefits; metric choice for checkpoint selection is inconsequential.
falsifiable_prediction: EMA-averaged adapters will show markedly lower across-checkpoint and across-prompt variance in click curves and better 5-click endpoints, with single-click mIoU differences near zero — the dissociation pattern, replicated across tasks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three tasks, PEFT with and without EMA, evaluate single-click mIoU and full click curves across 3 seeds and multiple late checkpoints; test the dissociation.
fastest_falsification: One task with and without EMA, click-curve variance comparison: one GPU-day.
main_risk: The effect may be a general variance reduction visible in all metrics, making the interactive-specific framing an overclaim.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Pixelwise logit fusion of zero-shot and adapted SAM, gated by the IoU head: output-space ensembling that beats weight-space interpolation on the robustness-accuracy front
problem: Deployments want in-domain gains without OOD regressions; weight-space solutions (adapter scaling) apply one global trade-off to every pixel of every image, but the right mixture plausibly varies per input and per region.
core_hypothesis: The zero-shot and adapted models fail in complementary regions (adapted wins in-domain structures, zero-shot wins on generic structures the adapter distorted); a per-mask gating using both models' quality self-estimates approximates oracle selection, and output-space fusion therefore Pareto-dominates the weight-interpolation family derived from the same adapter.
why_important: A deployment recipe achieving specialization without regression using two forward passes and no training would be widely adopted, and the complementarity measurement quantifies what adaptation actually breaks.
why_possibly_novel: Model ensembling is ancient; the specific zero-shot/adapted complementarity structure and self-estimate gating for promptable segmenters, benchmarked against weight interpolation, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The adapted model's IoU head is itself decalibrated by adaptation (per the calibration-forgetting hypothesis), potentially corrupting the gate exactly when it matters.
default_community_belief: Managing the specialization-generalization trade-off is a training-time or weight-space problem.
falsifiable_prediction: On mixed evaluation suites (target domain + generic probes), gated logit fusion will dominate the alpha-scaling curve (better generic retention at equal in-domain gain), and the gating signal's accuracy at picking the better model per instance will exceed 70%.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 3 adapted models: build fusion with IoU-head-based gating; evaluate against alpha-sweeps on mixed suites; measure per-instance gating accuracy against oracle.
fastest_falsification: Oracle-selection upper bound first (choose better model per instance using GT): hours; if even oracle fusion barely beats alpha-scaling, the idea is bounded uninteresting.
main_risk: Double inference cost may exclude latency-sensitive deployments, restricting impact to offline and quality-critical uses.

one_line: Mine hard negatives from everything-mode: AMG's false-positive masks on target-domain images are the highest-value supervision for PEFT, worth more per label than random ground-truth masks
problem: Adaptation datasets are built by labeling random or representative images, ignoring the information structure of where the frozen model already fails; everything-mode provides a free, exhaustive catalog of the model's false beliefs on unlabeled target data that nobody exploits for data selection.
core_hypothesis: Masks that AMG confidently produces but that are wrong for the target domain (spurious structures, merged objects, convention violations) identify precisely the decision-boundary regions where supervision moves the adapter most; annotating and training against these hard negatives yields more IoU per annotation than matched quantities of standard labels.
why_important: Data selection is the cheapest lever in adaptation; a mining recipe using computation the pipeline already runs (AMG) would improve the label-efficiency of nearly every applied SAM project.
why_possibly_novel: Active learning by model uncertainty is standard; mining confident-but-wrong AMG outputs as the selection signal (confidence-error mining rather than uncertainty sampling) for promptable-segmenter PEFT appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confident errors may be exactly the unlearnable cases (annotation-ambiguous or resolution-limited), wasting budget where no adapter can improve.
default_community_belief: Representative sampling or uncertainty-based active learning are the principled data-selection approaches for fine-tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: At equal annotation budgets, hard-negative-mined training sets will outperform random-selection and diversity-selection baselines on target-domain IoU across multiple domains, with the advantage largest at small budgets and shrinking as budgets grow.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 domains: run AMG over unlabeled pools, have annotators mark false positives among high-confidence masks, build matched-budget training sets (mined vs random vs diversity), train and compare.
fastest_falsification: Small pilot: 100 mined vs 100 random labels on one domain, one training run each: two GPU-days.
main_risk: Hard negatives may concentrate on a few pathological patterns, yielding adapters that fix those but underperform broadly (selection-induced distribution skew).

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: A domain-gap decomposition protocol: swap oracle components (embeddings, prompts, decoder) between in-domain and OOD pipelines to attribute the gap — the missing diagnostic standard for adaptation papers
problem: Every adaptation paper reports a gap and a fix, but never a decomposition of where the gap lives (encoder features vs prompt interpretation vs decoding conventions); without attribution, methods are matched to domains by luck rather than mechanism.
core_hypothesis: Controlled component swaps — evaluating OOD images with in-domain-adapted decoders, oracle prompts, oracle embeddings (from a fine-tuned encoder), and combinations — yield an additive-enough decomposition of the zero-shot gap into three interpretable components, and the resulting per-domain gap profiles predict which PEFT family (encoder LoRA, prompt-side, decoder-side) works best.
why_important: A standardized diagnostic that tells you which adaptation family to use before running them all would reduce wasted experiments field-wide, and gap profiles become comparable objects across papers.
why_possibly_novel: Component-swap attribution is used in ML debugging informally; a formalized, validated protocol for promptable-segmentation domain gaps appears absent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong interactions between components (feature quality changes what prompts mean) may break additivity badly enough to make profiles misleading.
default_community_belief: Domain gap is a scalar; method choice is empirical trial-and-error or follows fashion.
falsifiable_prediction: The decomposition components will sum to within 20% of the total gap on most domains (approximate additivity), profiles will vary qualitatively across domains, and the profile-predicted best PEFT family will match empirical winners in a majority of test domains.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 6 domains with enough labels to build oracle components: run the full swap matrix, test additivity, then run the three PEFT families and validate profile-based prediction.
fastest_falsification: Two-component swap (oracle prompts vs oracle decoder) on one domain: two GPU-days including building the oracles.
main_risk: Oracle components require per-domain fine-tuning to construct, making the protocol expensive to validate (though cheap to apply approximately afterward).

one_line: The frozen-prompt-encoder convention is unjustified: click-semantics gaps (what a click means in this domain) are cheaply fixable by prompt-encoder tuning and unfixable by encoder LoRA — test the convention everyone inherits
problem: Virtually all SAM PEFT recipes freeze the prompt encoder by convention (it is small and 'just encodes coordinates'), yet domains differ in what a click should mean (select the lesion vs the organ, the defect vs the part); this intent-mapping plausibly lives exactly in the frozen component.
core_hypothesis: For domains with prompt-intent mismatch, tuning the prompt encoder (embeddings and coordinate MLPs) fixes the mismatch with tiny data, while encoder/decoder LoRA fixes it only expensively and indirectly; conversely, for feature-gap domains prompt-encoder tuning does nothing — a clean double dissociation that indicts the blanket freezing convention.
why_important: Overturning (or validating) a universal recipe default with a mechanism-mapped dissociation directly improves practice, and cleanly separates two failure classes that are currently conflated as 'domain gap'.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-encoder tuning appears in isolated recipes without analysis; the intent-vs-feature dissociation study that would justify or kill the freezing convention appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Intent may be resolved in decoder cross-attention rather than prompt encoding, making the decoder the true home of click semantics.
default_community_belief: The prompt encoder is a fixed coordinate codec; freezing it is obviously correct and not worth revisiting.
falsifiable_prediction: On intent-mismatch tasks (same imagery, different granularity conventions), prompt-encoder tuning will match full-LoRA performance at a small fraction of parameters and data, while on modality-shift tasks it will produce near-zero gain; recipes unfreezing it will never lose versus the convention.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct intent-mismatch tasks (relabel one dataset at two granularities) and modality-shift tasks; compare prompt-encoder-only, LoRA-only, and combined tuning at matched budgets.
fastest_falsification: One dual-granularity relabeled dataset, prompt-encoder-only vs decoder-only tuning: one to two GPU-days.
main_risk: The prompt encoder's parameter count is so small that 'tuning it' may under-determine intent changes, pushing the fix into the decoder anyway.

judge_flags.title: Frozen-prompt-encoder convention is unjustified

one_line: Camouflage as the universal hardness axis: performance on camouflaged-object benchmarks predicts a domain's PEFT ceiling for low-contrast targets — a transferable hardness ruler
problem: Low-contrast target domains (many industrial and scientific cases) cannot predict their adaptation ceilings without running adaptations; if a public hardness axis (camouflaged-object segmentation difficulty) transfers, it becomes a free calibration instrument for private domains.
core_hypothesis: The feature property limiting SAM on camouflaged objects (foreground-background statistical similarity) is the same property limiting low-contrast domain adaptation; a domain's position on a contrast-similarity spectrum (measurable without labels) maps to a predictable post-PEFT ceiling via a curve fit once on public camouflage-graded data.
why_important: A public, reusable hardness ruler lets any team place their domain on a curve and read off an expected ceiling before annotation — portfolio planning powered by an existing benchmark's gradient of difficulty.
why_possibly_novel: Camouflage benchmarks are used to rank models; using their difficulty gradient as a transferable measurement instrument for adaptation forecasting appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The single-axis assumption may be too strong: hardness may be multi-dimensional in ways one statistic cannot summarize.
default_community_belief: Cross-domain difficulty comparison is apples-to-oranges; each domain's adaptability must be measured directly.
falsifiable_prediction: Ranking targets by a foreground-background feature-similarity statistic will predict post-PEFT IoU across both public camouflage-graded subsets and unrelated low-contrast domains with high rank correlation, and the fitted hardness-to-ceiling curve will transfer between the two families within a modest error band.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute the similarity statistic and run standardized PEFT across camouflage-difficulty strata and 4 private-style low-contrast domains; fit on the former, predict the latter.
fastest_falsification: Similarity-statistic vs zero-shot-IoU correlation across camouflage strata and 2 low-contrast domains: inference plus statistics, two days.
main_risk: Camouflage difficulty involves shape-disruption factors beyond contrast similarity, potentially breaking transfer to domains whose hardness is purely photometric.

one_line: Prompt dropout during PEFT: randomly hiding clicks at training time buys robustness to under-specified prompts at deployment — a deliberate, quantified trade against fully-specified accuracy
problem: Deployed prompts are sparser and worse than training prompts (users click once, detectors emit one box), but adaptation trains with fully-specified prompt sets, optimizing a regime deployment rarely sees.
core_hypothesis: Randomly dropping a fraction of prompts during training forces the adapter to extract more information per prompt and to hedge appropriately under under-specification, improving few-prompt performance at a small, controllable cost to many-prompt performance — with the trade-off curve stable enough to be tuned per deployment.
why_important: It aligns training with deployment prompt sparsity using a one-line change, and the quantified trade-off lets teams pick operating points instead of inheriting an accidental one.
why_possibly_novel: Dropout on input tokens is generic; treating prompt-set sparsification as a deployment-alignment regularizer for promptable segmenters, with the explicit trade-off characterization, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Few-prompt failures may be information-theoretic (genuinely ambiguous), in which case no training scheme improves them and dropout only hurts the specified regime.
default_community_belief: Train with the richest available prompts; robustness to sparse prompting comes from the pretrained model.
falsifiable_prediction: Prompt-dropout-trained adapters will improve 1-click and single-box metrics consistently across tasks while losing bounded amounts at 5+ prompts, tracing a smooth controllable trade-off as dropout rate varies, and the improvement will exceed what test-time tricks (prompt duplication) achieve.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three tasks x dropout rates {0, 0.25, 0.5} x 3 seeds; evaluate across prompt-count ladder (1 to 8); map the trade-off surfaces.
fastest_falsification: One task, two dropout rates, prompt-count ladder evaluation: one GPU-day.
main_risk: Interaction with iterative-refinement training (which also varies prompt counts) may already provide the benefit, making explicit dropout redundant.

one_line: Reweight training loss by prompt information content instead of resampling by instance size: size-balancing corrects the wrong variable in promptable-model adaptation
problem: Class/size imbalance handling is imported unchanged from semantic segmentation (resample rare/small instances), but in promptable training each example's effective difficulty depends on the prompt-mask pair's information geometry, not on instance frequency — the imported fix may target a proxy.
core_hypothesis: The correct importance weight for a promptable training example is the residual uncertainty of the mask given the prompt (low for tight boxes on isolated objects, high for points in clutter); weighting by this quantity yields better-calibrated capacity allocation than size- or frequency-based schemes, improving overall IoU without the overfitting-to-small-objects pathologies resampling causes.
why_important: It replaces an inherited heuristic with a principle native to promptable models, likely improving most adaptation recipes and clarifying what 'hard example' means when supervision is prompt-conditional.
why_possibly_novel: Loss weighting by difficulty is classic; deriving the weight from prompt-conditional mask uncertainty (estimable from SAM's own multimask spread) appears specific and new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Size and prompt-information may correlate so strongly in practice that the schemes are indistinguishable, making the refinement academic.
default_community_belief: Size/frequency rebalancing is the appropriate imbalance treatment for segmentation fine-tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: Information-weighted training will beat size-resampled and uniform baselines on overall and per-stratum metrics across tasks, and its advantage will correlate with the diversity of prompt-information levels in the dataset — vanishing on datasets where prompts are uniformly informative.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement weights from multimask-spread estimates; three tasks x {uniform, size-resampled, information-weighted} x 3 seeds; per-stratum analysis.
fastest_falsification: Measure the size-vs-information correlation on 3 datasets: statistics over cached inference, hours; near-perfect correlation kills the motivation.
main_risk: The uncertainty estimate (from the frozen model) may be miscalibrated exactly on the domains being adapted, corrupting the weights.

one_line: In-context segmentation through embedding correspondence: use a reference image+mask as a 'visual prompt' via frozen-feature matching, and measure the true capacity limits of training-free one-shot transfer
problem: One-shot class transfer (segment what I marked in this reference image, in all future images) is served today by trained personalization or fine-tuning; the training-free alternative — matching target-image features to reference-mask features and converting matches into prompts — lacks a rigorous capacity characterization: when does it work, when does it break, and what governs the boundary?
core_hypothesis: Frozen SAM embeddings support correspondence-based prompt generation well for texture-distinct, spatially-compact classes and fail predictably as intra-class appearance variance grows relative to inter-class distance in embedding space; this variance-ratio statistic (computable from a handful of references) predicts one-shot transfer quality before deployment.
why_important: One-shot visual prompting without training is the cheapest possible personalization; a validated predictor of when it suffices would route users between training-free and PEFT paths automatically.
why_possibly_novel: Correspondence-based personalization exists as method papers claiming successes; the calibrated capacity boundary and pre-hoc applicability predictor appear missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM's class-agnostic embeddings may lack the instance-discriminative structure correspondence needs, capping the method at texture-trivial classes regardless of statistics.
default_community_belief: One-shot personalization either needs training or works as a neat demo; its applicability boundary is unknowable a priori.
falsifiable_prediction: Across many classes, training-free correspondence prompting will span near-supervised to near-chance performance, with the embedding variance-ratio statistic predicting per-class quality with high rank correlation — turning anecdotal 'sometimes works' into a calibrated applicability test.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement reference-to-target correspondence prompting over 30 classes spanning distinctiveness; measure quality; compute variance-ratio statistics from 5 references per class; validate the predictor on held-out classes.
fastest_falsification: Ten classes spanning distinctiveness with a simple matcher: two days for the spread and a first predictor check.
main_risk: Correspondence quality depends on implementation details (feature layer, matching method), making the capacity boundary partially method-specific rather than model-intrinsic.

one_line: The negative-transfer boundary: map the (label-count, domain-gap) plane where PEFT hurts versus helps, producing the field's missing go/no-go chart
problem: PEFT is assumed beneficial whenever labels exist, but small-data adaptation on large-gap domains can underperform the zero-shot baseline (overfitting to unrepresentative labels while breaking pretrained competence); the boundary of this regime has never been mapped, so practitioners walk into it blind.
core_hypothesis: Negative transfer occupies a contiguous region of the (label-count, gap-severity) plane — small n, large gap — whose boundary follows a predictable form (required n grows with gap); the boundary is estimable from cheap proxies (zero-shot IoU as the gap axis) and standard-recipe pilots, yielding a reusable decision chart with confidence bands.
why_important: 'When NOT to fine-tune' is the most common unanswered practitioner question; an empirical chart with transfer validation would be cited constantly and prevent silent quality regressions in deployed systems.
why_possibly_novel: Negative transfer is documented in transfer learning broadly; a quantitative regime map for promptable-segmenter PEFT with boundary-transfer validation appears absent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With frozen backbones and small adapters, catastrophic overfitting may be rare enough that the negative region is practically empty.
default_community_belief: Fine-tuning with any labeled data is at worst neutral; more adaptation is monotonically safer as labels grow.
falsifiable_prediction: A grid of adaptations (6 gap levels x 6 label counts x 3 seeds) will show a coherent negative-transfer region rather than scattered failures, the fitted boundary will transfer to held-out domains within stated uncertainty, and recipe changes (stronger regularization) will shift the boundary predictably rather than eliminating it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct the grid using progressive corruptions plus real domains for gap levels; run the standardized recipe; fit and cross-validate the boundary; test on 2 unseen domains.
fastest_falsification: Two extreme grid cells (20 labels x large gap; 500 labels x small gap) x 3 seeds: three GPU-days to confirm the phenomenon exists.
main_risk: The boundary may be recipe-sensitive enough that the chart needs qualification per recipe family, reducing its universality.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

one_line: Foundation models place medical boundaries at intensity gradients even when clinical ground truth is defined functionally, producing a measurable systematic offset.
problem: Many clinical boundaries (tumor margins with microscopic infiltration, edema halos) are defined by treatment convention rather than by a visible edge, yet promptable foundation models were pretrained on natural images where object boundaries coincide with photometric edges.
core_hypothesis: Foundation-model boundary placement in medical images is an edge-snapping process: predicted contours are attracted to the locally strongest intensity gradient regardless of the task definition of the target boundary.
why_important: If boundary error is a systematic edge-snapping bias rather than random noise, averaging, ensembling, and more data will not fix it; margin-critical applications like radiotherapy planning would need a structurally different decoding objective.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary error is usually reported as an aggregate surface distance; decomposing it into gradient-attraction bias versus residual noise as an explicit, testable mechanism appears less explored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuned models may learn convention offsets easily because the offset is locally constant, making the bias disappear after even modest adaptation.
default_community_belief: Boundary errors of foundation models are treated as generic imprecision that scales down with more medical fine-tuning data.
falsifiable_prediction: Across structures whose ground-truth contour is deliberately offset from the strongest gradient (e.g., clinical target volumes with fixed margins), the signed distance from predicted contour to the nearest strong gradient will be significantly smaller than the signed distance to the ground-truth contour, and this bias will persist after fine-tuning with limited data.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one public dataset where the labeled boundary is convention-defined rather than edge-defined, compute for each boundary point the offset between prediction, label, and nearest strong gradient, and test whether the prediction-to-gradient distance distribution is tighter than prediction-to-label.
fastest_falsification: A one-day analysis on an existing model's predictions: histogram of contour-to-gradient versus contour-to-label distances on any margin-convention dataset.
main_risk: Suitable public datasets with convention-defined boundaries and reliable labels may be scarce, and gradient strength must be defined carefully to avoid a circular measure.

one_line: Where human raters disagree most, single-mask foundation models are most confidently wrong rather than uncertain.
problem: Inter-rater variability defines an irreducible ambiguity zone in medical segmentation, but foundation models output a single deterministic mask with high confidence everywhere.
core_hypothesis: Foundation-model confidence is anti-correlated with rater consensus in ambiguity zones: the model commits to one plausible contour mode with high logit confidence exactly where raters spread out.
why_important: Clinical deployment plans often use model confidence for triage; if confidence is blind to genuine ambiguity, triage will systematically miss the cases that most need human review.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration studies usually compare confidence to a single ground truth; conditioning the analysis on rater-disagreement maps as the ambiguity reference is a different question.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary-adjacent confidence dips may already capture most rater disagreement because raters mostly disagree near boundaries anyway.
default_community_belief: Softmax or mask-logit confidence of large pretrained models is assumed to be a usable proxy for ambiguity after simple recalibration.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-rater datasets, voxelwise model confidence inside the inter-rater disagreement band will not be significantly lower than confidence in consensus regions at matched distance-to-boundary, contradicting the assumption that confidence tracks ambiguity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use any public multi-rater segmentation dataset, compute rater-disagreement maps, stratify model confidence by disagreement level while controlling for distance to the mean contour, and test for the predicted flat or inverted relationship.
fastest_falsification: Correlation analysis between existing model entropy maps and published rater-variance maps on one dataset; requires no training.
main_risk: Distance-to-boundary is a strong confounder; without careful matching the analysis can rediscover the trivial fact that boundaries are uncertain.

one_line: Single-mask decoders collapse multimodal contour distributions to one rater style rather than an average, and which mode wins is dataset-order dependent.
problem: When training labels mix several annotation conventions, a deterministic segmentation head must resolve the conflict somehow, and how foundation models resolve it is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Fine-tuned foundation models do not average conflicting conventions; they lock onto the convention of whichever subset dominates early training batches, making the learned boundary style an artifact of data ordering.
why_important: Multi-institutional training is the default path to scale; if convention capture is order-dependent, reported model behavior is unreproducible in a clinically meaningful way.
why_possibly_novel: Run-to-run variance is usually measured as Dice noise; attributing it to discrete convention capture with a designed two-convention corpus is a sharper claim.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SGD may genuinely interpolate conventions at the voxel level because the loss is convex in the output probabilities for fixed features.
default_community_belief: Training on mixed conventions yields a stable averaged boundary, and seed variance is negligible noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Two fine-tuning runs differing only in data order, on a corpus with two labeled conventions, will produce models whose contours match different conventions, with between-run contour disagreement concentrated in the inter-convention band.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a mixed corpus by relabeling one structure under two explicit rules (e.g., include versus exclude a visible capsule), fine-tune twice with different seeds and orders, and measure which rule each model reproduces.
fastest_falsification: Two small fine-tuning runs on a synthetically bi-conventional dataset and a paired contour comparison.
main_risk: The effect may require label conflicts larger than those in realistic corpora, making the demonstration artificial.

one_line: Predicted contour curvature statistics of foundation models match natural-image object statistics, not anatomical shape statistics.
problem: Anatomy has characteristic curvature spectra (smooth organ capsules, high-curvature folds); pretraining on natural images may impose a wrong prior on contour geometry.
core_hypothesis: Foundation-model masks carry a transferable curvature prior from pretraining: their contour curvature spectrum deviates from ground-truth anatomy toward the curvature spectrum of natural-image objects, especially in low-contrast regions where the prior dominates the likelihood.
why_important: A geometric prior mismatch predicts where models fail without needing labels, enabling targeted review; it also suggests that shape-aware decoding, not more data, is the fix.
why_possibly_novel: Failure analyses focus on overlap metrics; treating curvature spectra as a fingerprint of the pretraining prior is an unusual measurement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decoder upsampling and post-processing may dominate contour geometry, erasing any pretraining shape prior.
default_community_belief: Pretraining priors are assumed to transfer only as generic edge and texture features, not as measurable shape-statistics biases in outputs.
falsifiable_prediction: The distribution of local contour curvature of zero-shot predictions will differ from ground truth in a consistent direction across organs, and the deviation will grow as local image contrast decreases.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute curvature histograms for predicted versus ground-truth contours on one CT and one MR dataset, stratified by local contrast, and test for a consistent directional shift.
fastest_falsification: Curvature-spectrum comparison on existing zero-shot predictions; purely analytical, no training.
main_risk: Curvature estimation on voxelized masks is noisy and resolution-dependent; the effect could be an artifact of mask discretization.

one_line: Prompt-perturbation instability is a label-free probe that localizes clinically ambiguous boundary regions.
problem: Identifying which boundary segments are ambiguous normally requires multiple raters, which is expensive; a cheap intrinsic probe would be valuable.
core_hypothesis: For promptable models, the local flip rate of mask boundaries under small prompt perturbations is causally linked to image-intrinsic ambiguity and therefore predicts inter-rater disagreement zones without any labels.
why_important: A validated label-free ambiguity probe would let institutions target their scarce multi-rater annotation budget and would give deployment-time review maps.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is usually treated as a robustness defect to minimize; reinterpreting it as an ambiguity sensor with quantitative validation against raters inverts the framing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rater disagreement includes protocol and style components invisible to any image-based probe, capping the achievable correlation at a low value.
default_community_belief: Prompt sensitivity is noise to be engineered away, and ambiguity estimation requires ensembles or explicit probabilistic heads.
falsifiable_prediction: Voxelwise prompt-jitter flip maps will correlate with multi-rater disagreement maps substantially better than image-gradient baselines and better than model entropy at matched compute.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-rater dataset, generate flip maps from N jittered prompts per case, compute correlation with rater disagreement, and compare against entropy and gradient baselines.
fastest_falsification: One inference-only experiment on an existing multi-rater dataset with an off-the-shelf promptable model.
main_risk: Flip maps may mostly reflect model-specific artifacts (patch grid, prompt encoding) rather than image ambiguity.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Foundation models systematically truncate structures at partial-volume ends, and the truncation length is predictable from the point spread function.
problem: Thin structure tips and organ poles fade gradually due to partial-volume averaging; how learned models decide where a structure ends in fading signal is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Foundation models apply an implicit intensity threshold learned from pretraining statistics, so they truncate fading structures at a fixed fraction of peak contrast, making the missed length a deterministic function of local PSF and contrast rather than random error.
why_important: Tip truncation drives clinically important errors (vessel length, lesion extent); a predictable law would allow analytic correction instead of retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Connecting dense-prediction failure quantitatively to acquisition PSF via phantoms, and validating the same constant on real data, treats the model as a measurable instrument.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may use contextual continuation cues rather than local intensity, breaking any local threshold law.
default_community_belief: Errors at thin ends are attributed to class imbalance and resolution limits, assumed reducible only by higher resolution or more data.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic phantoms with controlled PSF blur, the length of missed structure tip will scale linearly with blur width at fixed contrast, with a slope stable across structure types, and real-data tip errors will match the phantom-derived slope.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate blurred synthetic tubes and cones spanning blur and contrast levels, measure predicted-versus-true endpoint offsets, fit the scaling law, then test the fitted law on one real dataset with thin structures.
fastest_falsification: Phantom-only version of the experiment runs in hours with an existing checkpoint.
main_risk: Real anatomy confounds (branching, neighboring tissue) may swamp the clean phantom law.

one_line: Fine-tuned foundation models transfer an institution's contouring style to new anatomy more readily than they transfer anatomical accuracy.
problem: Institutions differ in systematic contouring style (tight versus generous margins); it is unknown whether adaptation learns anatomy or style.
core_hypothesis: Style is a low-dimensional, easily learnable bias, so a model fine-tuned on institution A applied at institution B will show a global signed volume bias matching A's style, even for organs absent from the fine-tuning set.
why_important: If style transfers globally, cross-site validation numbers conflate style mismatch with capability, and simple per-site bias correction could recover substantial performance.
why_possibly_novel: Site effects are usually modeled as image-domain shift; modeling them as annotation-style shift that generalizes across organs within a model is a distinct mechanism.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Style may be organ-specific rather than global, in which case unseen organs would show no bias.
default_community_belief: Cross-site performance drops are attributed to scanner and population shift in the images, not to transferable annotation style in the labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-institution evaluation will show a signed boundary offset that (a) has consistent sign across organs, (b) matches the sign of the source institution's style relative to the target, and (c) appears even on organs never seen during fine-tuning.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune on one institution's labels, evaluate signed surface distance per organ on another institution with different documented style, including held-out organ classes, and test for the consistent sign pattern.
fastest_falsification: Signed-distance audit of existing cross-site evaluation outputs, if paired-style datasets are already available.
main_risk: Requires two datasets with genuinely different, documented contouring conventions and overlapping organ sets.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Foundation-model confidence peaks on smooth intensity ramps, exactly where clinical boundary uncertainty is greatest, an inversion with measurable structure.
problem: Smooth transitions (edema, infiltration) are hard for clinicians but may be easy for edge-based models to commit to, creating a dangerous confidence inversion.
core_hypothesis: Model confidence is driven by local decision-margin in feature space, which is high on smooth monotonic ramps because any threshold yields a stable mask, so confidence and clinical uncertainty become inversely related on ramp-type boundaries specifically.
why_important: This would identify a specific, screenable boundary class where confidence-based review queues actively fail, with a concrete mitigation (profile-type detection).
why_possibly_novel: Boundary-type-conditional calibration analysis (step versus ramp) is a finer-grained question than global calibration studies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ramp regions may produce genuinely diffuse logits in modern architectures with strong augmentation, keeping confidence low there.
default_community_belief: Confidence errors are assumed uniform along boundaries, fixable by global temperature scaling.
falsifiable_prediction: Partitioning boundary segments into step-type and ramp-type by intensity profile, ramp-type segments will show higher model confidence but higher inter-rater variance, yielding a negative confidence-to-ambiguity correlation restricted to ramps.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Classify boundary voxels by fitted intensity-profile type on a multi-rater dataset and compare confidence and rater variance across types.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only stratified calibration analysis on one existing multi-rater dataset.
main_risk: Profile-type classification is itself noisy and may not cleanly separate the two regimes.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Models trained under two contouring conventions cannot interpolate to an intermediate instruction, revealing that convention is memorized, not parameterized.
problem: Ideally a model could be told how aggressive a margin to draw; whether current architectures represent convention as a controllable variable is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Convention is entangled in weights rather than represented as a latent control axis, so a model trained on two discrete conventions with condition codes will fail to produce sensible intermediate contours when given interpolated codes.
why_important: Controllable margin aggressiveness would let one model serve multiple clinical protocols; demonstrating the failure motivates explicit convention-conditioning research.
why_possibly_novel: Treating annotation convention as an explicit conditioning axis and testing interpolation behavior is a designed probe rather than an observational study.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Distance-to-boundary is nearly linear in margin width, which is an easy function; the model may interpolate perfectly.
default_community_belief: Conditioning inputs are assumed to give smooth control over output properties as they often do in generative models.
falsifiable_prediction: Given condition-code interpolation between tight and generous margin conventions, output contours will jump discontinuously between the two learned styles rather than move smoothly, as measured by mean signed distance versus code value.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Relabel one organ under two margin rules, train with a scalar condition input, sweep the condition at test time, and plot signed distance versus condition value for smoothness.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale training on a single organ with synthetic margin relabeling; one short training run.
main_risk: Failure to interpolate might be fixable trivially with more condition values, making the negative result weak.

one_line: Weighting training loss by rater-disagreement maps changes where models place boundaries but not aggregate Dice, exposing metric blindness to ambiguity handling.
problem: It is unclear whether incorporating known ambiguity into the loss changes model behavior in a way standard metrics can even detect.
core_hypothesis: Disagreement-weighted losses shift boundary placement toward consensus regions and soften commitments in ambiguity zones, but because ambiguous voxels are few, Dice and surface metrics remain statistically unchanged, hiding a real behavioral difference.
why_important: If true, the field's standard metrics cannot see the property that matters for ambiguity-aware deployment, and ambiguity-zone metrics need to become standard.
why_possibly_novel: The claim is about metric detectability of a training intervention, not about the intervention improving a headline number.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Surface-distance metrics may be sensitive enough near boundaries to capture the change after all.
default_community_belief: If a training change matters clinically, it should show up in Dice or surface distance; metric sufficiency is assumed.
falsifiable_prediction: Two models trained with and without disagreement weighting will be indistinguishable in Dice yet significantly different in ambiguity-zone-restricted metrics and in agreement with held-out raters.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models on a multi-rater dataset with and without disagreement weighting, evaluate with global metrics and ambiguity-zone-restricted metrics, and test the dissociation.
fastest_falsification: One paired training run on an existing multi-rater dataset with a pre-registered ambiguity-zone metric.
main_risk: The intervention might change nothing at all, which is a publishable null but weaker.

one_line: Logit iso-contours of dense predictors carry recoverable sub-voxel boundary information that discrete masks discard.
problem: Clinical margins are specified in millimeters, often below voxel size; whether learned dense predictors encode sub-voxel boundary position in their continuous outputs is untested.
core_hypothesis: The pre-threshold logit field varies smoothly across the true boundary, so interpolated iso-contours estimate boundary position with sub-voxel accuracy relative to higher-resolution ground truth, beating the discrete mask by a measurable margin.
why_important: Free sub-voxel accuracy from existing models would matter for volumetry of small structures and margin verification without any retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Sub-voxel evaluation of learned dense predictors against genuinely higher-resolution ground truth is rarely set up explicitly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Logit slopes near boundaries may be governed by training-label voxelization noise rather than image evidence, containing no true sub-voxel signal.
default_community_belief: Voxel resolution is treated as the hard floor of boundary accuracy; outputs are binarized before any geometric analysis.
