why_possibly_novel: The oversampling-resistance test separates representational limits from data limits, a distinction usually left as speculation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Angle may proxy for radius and contrast so tightly that no independent angle effect survives proper controls.
default_community_belief: Missed branches are attributed to class imbalance and resolution, fixable with more data and higher resolution.
falsifiable_prediction: Angle-stratified recall will decline with acuity across two architectures and two organ systems after covariate control, and targeted oversampling of acute bifurcations will yield significantly less improvement than equivalent oversampling yields for size-driven misses.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Angle-stratified recall analysis with covariate control on one vascular dataset, then a paired oversampling intervention comparing angle-targeted versus size-targeted gains.
fastest_falsification: Angle-stratified recall on existing predictions of one vessel benchmark.
main_risk: Accurate branch-angle ground truth requires careful centerline processing that can inject its own bias.

one_line: Foundation models hallucinate surgically removed organs at high rates, and the hallucination is driven by contextual expectation rather than local evidence, demonstrable by context-ablation.
problem: Post-resection patients are common in clinical populations, but standard corpora contain mostly intact anatomy; model behavior when an expected organ is absent tests whether predictions are evidence-driven or expectation-driven.
core_hypothesis: Models synthesize expected-organ predictions from contextual cues (neighboring anatomy, body habitus) when local evidence is absent, so hallucination rates on post-resection cases will be high, and ablating the surrounding context (masking neighbors) will reduce hallucination more than ablating the local region itself, proving expectation-driven generation.
why_important: Expectation-driven hallucination in absence cases produces exactly the errors automated volumetry pipelines cannot catch, and defines a necessary absence-detection benchmark for clinical certification.
why_possibly_novel: The context-ablation dissociation identifies the causal information source of hallucination, going beyond documenting that absence cases fail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fluid-filled or reorganized post-surgical fossae may provide misleading local evidence, making hallucination evidence-driven after all.
default_community_belief: Models are assumed to segment what is present; systematic generation of absent anatomy is not part of standard failure analysis.
falsifiable_prediction: On nephrectomy or splenectomy cases, organ hallucination will occur at substantial rates with confident predictions in the empty fossa; context-masking interventions will reduce hallucination while local-evidence perturbations will not, dissociating the two information sources.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect post-resection cases from public sources, measure hallucination rates, run context-masking versus local-perturbation arms on hallucinating cases.
fastest_falsification: Hallucination-rate count on a few dozen post-resection scans with an existing multi-organ model.
main_risk: Public post-resection cases with labels are limited; a modest curated set is required.

judge_flags.title: Hallucinating surgically removed organs

one_line: Anatomical ordering constraints along body axes are learnable by sequence models over organ tokens but are demonstrably absent from dense decoders, explaining a class of gross mislabelings.
problem: Gross mislabeling errors (labeling an organ far from its possible axial range) persist in dense models; whether the missing knowledge is representable and learnable in an alternative factorization is a designable question.
core_hypothesis: Dense per-voxel decoding lacks a mechanism for global ordering constraints (organ A cannot appear caudal to organ B), while a sequence model over slice-level organ tokens learns these constraints from the same data; hybridizing the two will eliminate ordering violations at negligible accuracy cost, proving the failure is architectural, not informational.
why_important: Gross mislabelings destroy clinical trust disproportionately; attributing them to a specific missing architectural mechanism with a working fix would be both explanatory and practical.
why_possibly_novel: The factorization argument (same data, different constraint expressibility) isolates architecture as the causal variable for a specific clinical error class.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large-context transformers may already encode ordering implicitly, making violations negligible at current scale.
default_community_belief: Gross errors are expected to vanish with scale, without needing explicit structural mechanisms.
falsifiable_prediction: Ordering-violation rates will be substantial for dense decoders and near zero for the sequence-hybrid at matched training data, and the hybrid's corrections will be concentrated on gross mislabelings without degrading boundary accuracy.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure ordering violations for a dense model on one whole-body dataset, train a slice-token sequence layer on the same labels, compare violation rates and boundary metrics of the hybrid.
fastest_falsification: Ordering-violation census on existing whole-body predictions.
main_risk: Ordering violations may be too rare in modern large models to justify the mechanism, which the census will reveal cheaply.

judge_flags.reason: Dense decoder + sequence-model hybrid is a Module A+B pairing as stated.

one_line: Registration-free label propagation via foundation-model correspondence beats classical deformable registration only above a deformation-magnitude threshold, giving a measurable regime map for when learned correspondence pays.
problem: Learned correspondence and classical registration compete for atlas-based label propagation, with conflicting reports; a regime variable (deformation magnitude) may govern which wins where.
core_hypothesis: Classical registration excels under small smooth deformations due to explicit regularization, while learned correspondence tolerates large or discontinuous deformations where optimization fails; propagation accuracy versus deformation magnitude will show a crossover at a measurable threshold that transfers across anatomies once normalized by structure scale.
why_important: A validated regime map converts an unresolved methods debate into a per-case routing rule and clarifies what each paradigm actually contributes.
why_possibly_novel: The normalized-crossover claim with cross-anatomy transfer is a quantitative regime theory, not another head-to-head average comparison.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The governing variable may be appearance shift rather than deformation magnitude, in which case the crossover will not organize the data.
default_community_belief: One paradigm is assumed generally superior depending on community, with disagreements attributed to implementation quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying atlas-target pairs by independently estimated deformation magnitude, classical methods will dominate below a threshold and learned correspondence above it, with the normalized crossover consistent across two anatomical regions.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run both propagation methods across deformation-stratified pairs on one dataset, locate the crossover, replicate on a second anatomy.
fastest_falsification: Deformation-stratified accuracy comparison on one existing registration benchmark.
main_risk: Deformation magnitude estimation requires a reference method, risking circularity that must be handled with independent estimators.

one_line: The spatial autocorrelation structure of segmentation errors differs qualitatively between foundation models and task-specific models, and this signature identifies error provenance without ground truth.
problem: Errors are studied through magnitudes, not spatial statistics; if different model families produce characteristically different error textures, the texture itself carries diagnostic information usable in unlabeled deployment.
core_hypothesis: Foundation models produce long-range correlated errors (semantic misreadings spanning regions) while task-specific models produce short-range boundary-noise errors, so error-field autocorrelation lengths will separate model families, and the signature will persist in prediction-disagreement fields computable without labels.
why_important: Error-texture signatures would let deployment monitors infer failure type (semantic versus boundary) from unlabeled disagreement, enabling type-appropriate mitigation such as review routing.
why_possibly_novel: Treating the error field as a spatial stochastic process with family-specific signatures imports spatial statistics into model diagnostics in a way overlap metrics cannot express.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning may homogenize error textures across families, erasing the signature.
default_community_belief: Error spatial structure is not treated as an object of study; metrics aggregate it away.
falsifiable_prediction: Error autocorrelation lengths will cluster by model family across datasets, and unlabeled disagreement-field statistics between two models will predict which family each belongs to with high accuracy, validating a label-free provenance diagnostic.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute error autocorrelation for two model families on two datasets, test family separation, then verify the unlabeled disagreement-field version.
fastest_falsification: Autocorrelation comparison on existing predictions from one foundation and one task-specific model.
main_risk: Autocorrelation may be dominated by structure size and dataset properties rather than model family.

one_line: Web-scale pretrained models show membership-inference signals for public medical benchmark images, implying zero-shot medical results are partially contaminated evaluations.
problem: Public medical benchmarks circulate on the open web and may enter web-scale pretraining corpora, so zero-shot medical evaluations of such models may measure memorization rather than generalization, but no dense-prediction contamination audit exists.
core_hypothesis: Pretraining exposure leaves detectable traces: feature-space membership-inference statistics will separate long-public benchmark images from acquisition-matched private images, and zero-shot segmentation quality will be systematically higher on the exposed subset, quantifying contamination inflation.
why_important: If zero-shot medical claims are contamination-inflated, the field's assessment of foundation-model medical readiness is systematically optimistic, affecting research priorities and clinical expectations.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination auditing methodology exists for language models; a dense-prediction, medical-specific audit combining membership inference with performance stratification appears underdeveloped.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Medical images may be too rare or deduplicated in web corpora to leave detectable membership traces.
default_community_belief: Zero-shot medical evaluations are read as clean measurements of transfer capability.
falsifiable_prediction: Membership scores will discriminate public-benchmark from matched-private images above chance for web-scale models but not for models with controlled pretraining corpora, and the public-private zero-shot performance gap will exceed the gap measured for uncontaminated models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute membership statistics for one web-scale model over a public benchmark and a matched private set, compare zero-shot performance between the two under matched difficulty.
fastest_falsification: Membership-score separation test on one benchmark against any available private comparison set.
main_risk: Access to genuinely unexposed matched private data is the hard requirement; difficulty matching between sets is delicate.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Fine-tuned medical models reproduce near-duplicate training contours for anatomically similar patients, revealing template memorization masquerading as segmentation skill.
problem: Whether medical segmentation models interpolate learned templates versus compute evidence-driven boundaries matters for their trustworthiness on novel anatomy, and is testable through output-similarity forensics.
core_hypothesis: For patients anatomically close to training cases, models emit contours whose agreement with the nearest training mask exceeds what image evidence similarity justifies, indicating retrieval-like behavior; the effect will strengthen with model capacity and training repetition.
why_important: Template retrieval fails precisely on atypical patients where evidence-driven boundaries matter most, and constitutes an unmeasured privacy channel exposing training contours.
why_possibly_novel: Mask-space memorization forensics for dense medical prediction, distinct from image-space memorization studies, targets what the model actually leaks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense prediction losses may penalize verbatim retrieval enough that outputs never exceed evidence-justified similarity.
default_community_belief: Segmentation models are assumed to generalize by construction, with memorization treated as a classification and generation problem.
falsifiable_prediction: Prediction-to-nearest-training-mask similarity will exceed prediction-to-ground-truth similarity on a measurable subset of test cases, the excess will correlate with training-case proximity, and capacity or epoch increases will amplify it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Index training masks, compute per-test-case nearest-training-mask agreement versus ground-truth agreement for one fine-tuned model, analyze the excess-agreement subset.
fastest_falsification: Nearest-mask agreement audit on one small fine-tuned model where training data is available.
main_risk: Anatomical regularity produces genuine similarity; the null model of justified similarity must be constructed carefully.

one_line: Foundation-model embeddings re-identify patients across scans and modalities at rates constituting a quantifiable privacy failure of feature-sharing pipelines.
problem: Sharing frozen features instead of images is treated as privacy-preserving in federated and research settings, but the linkage risk of foundation-model features across a patient's scans is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Foundation features encode patient-individuating anatomy (bone geometry, vascular patterns) stably enough that embedding matching will link same-patient scans across time and even across modalities far above chance, making feature sharing a re-identification channel.
why_important: Regulatory treatment of derived features hinges on identifiability; a quantified linkage rate directly informs whether feature sharing needs image-grade protection.
why_possibly_novel: Re-identification is studied for raw images and generative outputs; a systematic audit of task-model features as the leaking object, with utility-privacy trade-off curves, addresses the pipeline people actually share.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggressive pooling in feature extraction may destroy individuating detail, keeping linkage near chance.
default_community_belief: Frozen features are informally regarded as anonymized derivatives safe to share.
falsifiable_prediction: Same-patient linkage from pooled embeddings will vastly exceed chance on longitudinal datasets, will survive feature-dimension reduction and noising at levels that preserve segmentation utility, and cross-modality linkage will remain above chance.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Embed a longitudinal dataset, measure linkage precision-recall versus feature perturbation strength, plot against downstream segmentation utility.
fastest_falsification: Linkage test on embeddings of one public longitudinal dataset.
main_risk: Findings depend on population size; small cohorts overestimate practical linkage risk and scaling analysis is needed.

one_line: Cross-dataset patient duplication silently inflates medical generalization claims: deduplication at the patient level measurably shrinks reported cross-dataset transfer performance.
problem: Public medical datasets are assembled from overlapping institutional sources, so the same patients may appear in nominally independent train and test sets, but patient-level cross-dataset dedup audits are not standard practice.
core_hypothesis: Patient overlap across public dataset pairs is nonzero and concentrated among datasets drawing from the same registries; removing detected duplicates will reduce cross-dataset evaluation scores by a measurable margin, revising generalization narratives for affected benchmark pairs.
why_important: Cross-dataset evaluation is the field's main generalization evidence; quantifying its contamination determines how much of that evidence stands.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic patient-level (not image-level) duplication auditing across medical benchmark pairs, with re-evaluation consequences, has the character of necessary metascience not yet routinized.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Major benchmark curators may already deduplicate against each other, making true overlap negligible.
default_community_belief: Distinct dataset names are treated as implying disjoint patients.
falsifiable_prediction: Image-fingerprint matching across popular dataset pairs will find duplicate patients above negligible rates in at least some pairs, and dedup-then-reeval will lower transfer scores specifically for models trained on the overlapping source.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run perceptual and anatomical fingerprint matching across two commonly paired datasets, verify candidate duplicates, re-evaluate one published-style transfer setup after removal.
fastest_falsification: Fingerprint matching between one suspected dataset pair.
main_risk: Verification of duplicates without metadata access relies on imaging evidence alone, risking false positives that must be conservatively handled.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Brief narrow fine-tuning catastrophically erases the robustness benefits of medical foundation models while preserving in-distribution accuracy, making the erosion invisible to standard validation.
problem: Foundation models are adopted for robustness, then routinely fine-tuned on narrow local data; whether the robustness that motivated adoption survives fine-tuning is rarely verified because validation only covers the narrow distribution.
core_hypothesis: Fine-tuning reshapes features toward local shortcuts, so robustness to corruptions and site shift will degrade steeply within early fine-tuning epochs while in-distribution metrics improve, creating a hidden robustness-accuracy divergence with a measurable time course.
why_important: Institutions believe they deploy robust foundation models when they may deploy narrowly overfit derivatives; the divergence time course defines what monitoring fine-tuning pipelines need.
why_possibly_novel: Robustness-forgetting dynamics during medical fine-tuning, measured as a trajectory rather than an endpoint comparison, characterizes a process the field treats as a black box.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong regularization and small learning rates in common recipes may preserve robustness far better than hypothesized.
default_community_belief: Fine-tuning is assumed to add local competence while retaining pretrained robustness, especially with parameter-efficient methods.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking both in-distribution accuracy and out-of-distribution robustness across fine-tuning steps will show robustness loss beginning within the first epochs and reaching a substantial fraction of the pretrained-to-scratch robustness gap, while validation metrics show only improvement; parameter-efficient variants will show a slower but qualitatively similar erosion.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one foundation model on single-site data, checkpoint frequently, evaluate each checkpoint on in-distribution and shifted suites, plot the divergence.
fastest_falsification: Checkpoint-trajectory robustness evaluation on one fine-tuning run.
main_risk: Robustness suites must be genuinely independent of fine-tuning data or the erosion will be underestimated.

one_line: Training segmentation models on generatively synthesized medical images reintroduces memorized real-patient content, laundering privacy leakage through the synthetic label.
problem: Synthetic images from generative models trained on real patient data are shared as privacy-safe training material, but generative memorization means the synthetic corpus may embed real-patient content that downstream models then absorb.
core_hypothesis: Memorized fragments in synthetic corpora are frequent enough that segmentation models trained purely on synthetic data will exhibit membership-inference signals for the original real patients, demonstrating leakage transitivity through the synthetic intermediary.
why_important: Synthetic-data-sharing frameworks rest on the assumption that generation breaks the privacy chain; demonstrating transitivity would invalidate a widely used compliance argument.
why_possibly_novel: Two-hop privacy analysis (real to generative to downstream task model) with attenuation controls extends memorization auditing beyond the generative model itself.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Task-model training may compress away instance-specific content, breaking the leakage chain at the second hop.
default_community_belief: Synthetic data is treated as severing the link to source patients for privacy purposes.
falsifiable_prediction: Membership inference against the synthetic-trained segmentation model will discriminate original-training patients from matched controls above chance, the signal will track duplication levels in the generative corpus, and pruning near-duplicate synthetic images will attenuate it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a generator on a known cohort, synthesize a corpus, train a segmentation model on it, run membership inference on the original cohort versus controls.
fastest_falsification: Membership inference on an existing public synthetic-trained model where the generative source cohort is documented.
main_risk: End-to-end pipeline is compute-heavy, and weak generators may under-represent the risk modern generators pose.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Lesion-centered cropping conventions in benchmark construction teach models a center-prior shortcut that inflates benchmark scores and collapses under whole-image deployment.
problem: Many lesion segmentation datasets are distributed as crops centered on the pathology, embedding the curator's knowledge of lesion location into the data geometry itself.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on centered crops internalize a spatial prior that the target is central, so their benchmark performance contains a location-prior component that vanishes on uncentered whole images, and the gap measures the shortcut's contribution.
why_important: Benchmark-to-clinic performance drops are usually blamed on distribution shift; quantifying the curation-geometry shortcut isolates a fixable, curation-level cause.
why_possibly_novel: Auditing dataset construction geometry as a shortcut source, with the randomized-crop counterfactual benchmark, targets the data pipeline rather than the model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong augmentation with random cropping during training may already erase the center prior.
default_community_belief: Cropping is viewed as a neutral standardization step in dataset preparation.
falsifiable_prediction: Center-prior probes (performance versus target offset from crop center) will show strong positional dependence for crop-trained models; evaluation on randomized-crop versions of the same cases will drop performance by a margin that predicts the whole-image deployment gap.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on a centered-crop dataset, evaluate at systematically varied target offsets and on randomized re-crops, quantify the positional performance profile.
fastest_falsification: Offset-sweep evaluation of any crop-trained public model.
main_risk: Some datasets provide whole images making the issue dataset-specific; the audit must survey which benchmarks are affected.

one_line: Adapter weights from federated medical fine-tuning are invertible enough to reconstruct site-identifying data statistics, undermining the privacy rationale for sharing adapters instead of data.
problem: Parameter-efficient adapters are exchanged in federated medical setups under the assumption that small weight sets cannot leak site data, an assumption without quantified adversarial testing for dense prediction.
core_hypothesis: Adapter deltas encode site-specific distribution statistics (intensity profiles, prevalence, protocol signatures) recoverable by an adversary with the base model, enabling site identification and partial reconstruction of training-distribution properties from adapters alone.
why_important: Federated medical learning's regulatory case leans on parameter sharing being non-identifying; quantifying adapter leakage informs whether adapter exchange requires the same protection as gradients, whose leakage is known.
why_possibly_novel: Adversarial analysis of adapters as the leakage object, specific to dense medical prediction and site-level (not patient-level) privacy, addresses the currently preferred federation currency.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adapter compression may genuinely bottleneck site information below recoverable levels.
default_community_belief: Small adapter weight sets are assumed to be practically anonymous relative to gradients or full models.
falsifiable_prediction: A classifier over adapter weights will identify the contributing site far above chance; optimization-based inversion will recover distributional properties (mean intensity profiles, lesion prevalence estimates) matching the true site statistics within tight error.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune adapters per site on a multi-site dataset, train site classifiers on adapter weights, attempt statistical inversion, compare against ground-truth site statistics.
fastest_falsification: Site-classification test over adapters from a simulated multi-site split.
main_risk: Site-level leakage may be considered acceptable by some frameworks, requiring careful positioning of what harm is demonstrated.

judge_flags.title: Federated adapter weights invert to site statistics

one_line: Public leaderboard iteration produces measurable test-set adaptation in medical segmentation: late submissions outperform early ones on the public split but not on a sequestered refresh.
problem: Long-lived public benchmarks accumulate community-wide adaptive overfitting through repeated evaluation, but medical segmentation lacks the refresh experiments that quantified this in other fields.
core_hypothesis: Iterative leaderboard optimization fits the specific test split's idiosyncrasies (case mix, annotation style), so the public-split improvement trajectory over benchmark lifetime will substantially exceed the improvement measured when the same methods are re-evaluated on a fresh, protocol-identical sequestered set.
why_important: Benchmark-driven progress narratives steer research investment; quantifying how much medical leaderboard progress is split-specific adaptation calibrates trust in reported gains.
why_possibly_novel: The refresh-set methodology is established elsewhere but executing it for medical dense prediction, where annotation style is a live confound, answers a domain-specific open question.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Medical leaderboards with hidden test sets and submission limits may have prevented meaningful adaptive overfitting.
default_community_belief: Leaderboard gains are read as genuine methodological progress.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating a chronological sample of leaderboard methods on a newly annotated refresh set will show a flatter progress curve than the public split shows, with the divergence growing with submission date and concentrating in structures with ambiguous annotation conventions.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate a small refresh set under the original protocol for one long-lived benchmark, re-evaluate publicly available historical methods, compare trajectories.
fastest_falsification: Trajectory comparison using any benchmark that already possesses an unused sequestered split.
main_risk: Refresh annotation must faithfully replicate the original protocol or style drift will masquerade as overfitting.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Contamination inflates lesion segmentation scores more than organ segmentation scores because idiosyncratic lesion masks are memorizable while regular organ shapes are learnable, an asymmetry that fingerprints contamination.
problem: Contamination effects are discussed monolithically, but structures differ in how much memorization can help: regular anatomy is predictable from generalization alone, while irregular lesions are not, suggesting a diagnostic asymmetry.
core_hypothesis: Memorization contributes performance in proportion to target idiosyncrasy, so exposure-related performance gaps (exposed versus unexposed cases) will be significantly larger for lesion targets than for organ targets within the same images, and this asymmetry itself can serve as a contamination detector requiring no private baseline.
why_important: A contamination signature computable from within-model comparisons would give the community a practical audit tool that does not depend on scarce guaranteed-private data.
why_possibly_novel: Using the differential memorability of structure types as an internal control for contamination detection is a designed inference trick rather than a direct audit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Lesion memorization may not survive pretraining compression, making both gaps equally small even under exposure.
default_community_belief: Contamination is assumed to inflate all results uniformly, and detection is assumed to require clean holdout data.
falsifiable_prediction: In models with suspected exposure, the exposed-unexposed gap will be several times larger for lesions than organs; in verified-clean models both gaps will be near zero, validating the asymmetry as a contamination fingerprint.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one suspected-exposure model, compare exposure-related gaps across lesion and organ targets on the same cases, calibrate the null on a model with documented clean pretraining.
fastest_falsification: Gap-asymmetry computation on one model with plausible exposure and one clean-trained control.
main_risk: Lesion versus organ difficulty differences must be normalized carefully or the asymmetry could reflect difficulty, not memorization.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Above a quality threshold, Dice ranking of models is uncorrelated with ranking by margin-critical clinical error, so leaderboard order stops carrying clinical meaning exactly where models now operate.
problem: Modern models cluster in a high-Dice regime where residual differences may be dominated by clinically irrelevant voxels, but leaderboards still use Dice order to declare progress.
core_hypothesis: In the saturated regime, Dice differences reflect interior and easy-boundary voxels while clinically decisive errors (margin breaches near critical structures) vary independently, so rank correlation between Dice and clinically weighted error across top models will be near zero even as both metrics remain individually reliable.
why_important: If leaderboard order is clinically meaningless at the frontier, method selection for deployment needs different instruments, and reported state-of-the-art claims need reinterpretation.
why_possibly_novel: The regime-dependence claim (correlation collapses only above a threshold) is sharper than generic metric criticism and directly measurable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Margin-critical errors may in fact co-vary with Dice tightly even at the frontier, since both track boundary quality.
default_community_belief: Higher Dice is treated as better clinical quality throughout the performance range.
falsifiable_prediction: Across the top tier of models on one benchmark, Spearman correlation between Dice rank and margin-breach rank will be statistically indistinguishable from zero, while in the low-Dice tier the same correlation will be strongly positive, demonstrating regime dependence.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a spread of public models on one dataset with both Dice and a margin-breach metric near critical structures, compute tier-stratified rank correlations.
fastest_falsification: Tier-stratified rank-correlation computation on any benchmark's public predictions.
main_risk: Defining the clinically weighted metric requires clinical input to be credible.

judge_flags.title: Dice ranking decouples from margin-critical clinical error

one_line: Boundary metrics and volumetric metrics disagree most on precisely the structures where clinical stakes are highest, making metric choice a hidden clinical judgment.
problem: Metric families (overlap, boundary distance, volume agreement) are used interchangeably, but their disagreement structure across anatomy types is undocumented, so metric choice may silently determine which models look best for critical structures.
core_hypothesis: Metric disagreement grows with structure elongation, thinness, and boundary ambiguity, which are also markers of clinical criticality (vessels near targets, thin organ walls), so the anatomy where metrics disagree most overlaps heavily with the anatomy where errors matter most, and cross-metric model rankings will flip exactly there.
why_important: Demonstrating that metric choice matters most where clinical stakes are highest would force explicit metric justification in medical segmentation papers, changing reporting norms.
why_possibly_novel: Mapping the anatomy-conditional disagreement structure between metric families, and overlaying clinical criticality, is a systematic study of a question usually addressed with single anecdotes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With modern models, metric disagreement may be too small anywhere to flip rankings meaningfully.
default_community_belief: Metric families are seen as roughly interchangeable summaries differing in sensitivity, not in verdicts.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-structure cross-metric rank correlations will decrease with elongation and ambiguity statistics, and the set of structures with ranking flips will overlap significantly with an independently defined clinical-criticality list.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-structure model rankings under three metric families on one multi-structure benchmark, correlate disagreement with shape statistics and a criticality list.
fastest_falsification: Cross-metric ranking comparison on existing benchmark predictions.
main_risk: The clinical-criticality list must come from external clinical sources to avoid circularity.

one_line: Reported average improvements of foundation models over specialists come from redistributing errors across cases (fixing easy, breaking hard), detectable as increased per-case variance at improved means.
problem: Mean metric improvements are reported without distributional analysis, hiding whether new models improve uniformly or trade improvements on many cases against regressions on a vulnerable minority.
core_hypothesis: Foundation-model adaptation shifts the error distribution asymmetrically: means improve but the hard-case tail worsens or stagnates, so paired per-case analysis will reveal a significant regression subset with identifiable characteristics (atypical anatomy, rare protocols), contradicting the uniform-improvement narrative.
why_important: Case-level regressions are what clinical safety cares about; if means hide systematic regressions, model-update decisions need distributional gates, not mean gates.
why_possibly_novel: Treating model comparison as a paired distributional test with regression-subset characterization imports clinical-trial thinking into benchmark practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Foundation adaptation may genuinely dominate per-case, with regression subsets within noise bounds.
default_community_belief: Mean improvements are interpreted as broad improvements benefiting cases roughly uniformly.
falsifiable_prediction: Paired case-level comparisons between a foundation-adapted model and a strong specialist will show a regression subset exceeding seed-noise expectations, concentrated in identifiable strata, with tail quantiles improving less than means or worsening.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paired evaluation of one foundation-adapted model versus one specialist on one benchmark with seed-replicated baselines, regression-subset analysis.
fastest_falsification: Paired per-case delta histogram on one public comparison.
main_risk: Distinguishing systematic regressions from seed noise requires multiple training seeds, adding compute.

one_line: At equal Dice, foundation models and specialists make categorically different kinds of errors (semantic confusions versus boundary noise), so error taxonomy, not magnitude, is what changed with the paradigm shift.
problem: Model families are compared by magnitude metrics that cannot express qualitative differences in what goes wrong, leaving the clinical character of the foundation-model shift undocumented.
core_hypothesis: Pretraining changes the error-generating process: at matched aggregate scores, foundation models will show relatively more semantic errors (wrong-structure assignments, hallucinated regions) and fewer boundary-noise errors than specialists, a taxonomy shift with distinct clinical risk profiles.
why_important: Clinical risk depends on error type (a hallucinated structure misleads differently than a noisy edge); paradigm adoption decisions should weigh taxonomy, which current evaluation never surfaces.
why_possibly_novel: Dice-matched taxonomy comparison isolates qualitative error character from quantity, a controlled design that magnitude-based comparisons cannot emulate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning may homogenize error taxonomies, leaving only magnitude differences between families.
default_community_belief: Equal scores are read as equivalent behavior; error character is assumed similar at similar performance.
falsifiable_prediction: Classifying errors into a fixed taxonomy for Dice-matched model pairs, the taxonomy distribution will differ significantly between families with the predicted direction, and the difference will replicate across two datasets.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select Dice-matched model pairs, apply an automated error-taxonomy classifier to their error components on one dataset, test distribution differences.
fastest_falsification: Taxonomy classification of errors for one Dice-matched pair on one dataset.
main_risk: Automated taxonomy classification must be validated against expert judgment on a sample.

one_line: Typical medical segmentation test sets are statistically underpowered to detect the between-model differences the field routinely claims, computable by resampling without new data.
problem: Papers declare superiority from small test sets without power analysis, and the case-level variance structure of segmentation metrics (heavy tails, correlated structures) makes intuitive sample-size judgments unreliable.
core_hypothesis: The minimum detectable effect at conventional power for common test-set sizes exceeds the median claimed improvement in recent comparisons, meaning a substantial fraction of published superiority claims are statistically undecidable on their own evidence, and the shortfall is worse for small-structure metrics with heavy-tailed case distributions.
why_important: If typical comparisons are underpowered, the field's empirical record contains substantial noise mistaken for progress, and benchmark design needs power-based sizing standards.
why_possibly_novel: Turning the diffuse concern about small test sets into concrete minimum-detectable-effect curves per benchmark and metric provides a reusable methodological instrument.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Case-level pairing may make comparisons more powerful than naive variance suggests, rescuing many claims.
default_community_belief: Benchmark test sets are implicitly treated as large enough for the comparisons made on them.
falsifiable_prediction: Bootstrap-based power analysis on public benchmarks will show minimum detectable effects larger than typical claimed margins for common sample sizes, and replicated seed runs will produce ranking flips at rates consistent with the computed underpowering.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute bootstrap power curves for two public benchmarks across metrics, compare against a survey of claimed margins in recent literature, validate with multi-seed ranking-stability runs.
fastest_falsification: Power-curve computation on one benchmark via bootstrap, no training required.
main_risk: The literature survey component must avoid cherry-picking; inclusion criteria need pre-registration.

judge_flags.title: Medical test sets statistically underpowered for claimed deltas

one_line: Switching from single-rater to consensus ground truth flips model rankings on medical benchmarks, showing that leaderboard order partly measures agreement with one annotator's style.
problem: Most benchmarks use single-rater labels, implicitly evaluating agreement with one individual, but the sensitivity of model rankings to the ground-truth construction method is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Different models align differently with individual raters versus consensus (depending on their training-label provenance), so re-scoring against consensus labels will change rankings, with rank instability concentrated among models trained on labels from raters with distinctive styles.
why_important: If rankings depend on whose truth is used, benchmark authority requires consensus-grade references, a costly but quantifiable upgrade the field has not justified empirically.
why_possibly_novel: The ranking-stability-under-reference-change experiment measures a foundational validity property of benchmarks that is assumed rather than tested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model differences may dwarf rater-style effects, keeping rankings stable under any reasonable reference.
default_community_belief: Single-rater ground truth is treated as adequate for stable model comparison.
falsifiable_prediction: On a benchmark subset re-annotated by multiple raters, model rankings under single-rater versus consensus references will show significant rank changes beyond bootstrap noise, and each model's rank movement will be predictable from its training-label style similarity to the original rater.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-rater re-annotation of a benchmark subset, re-scoring of existing public predictions under each reference, rank-stability analysis.
fastest_falsification: Re-scoring existing predictions on any benchmark subset that already has multiple annotations.
main_risk: Re-annotation cost limits subset size, requiring careful power planning for rank-change detection.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Metric-targeted mask post-processing can move benchmark rankings by margins comparable to claimed methodological advances, exposing the gameability of current evaluation.
problem: Morphological post-processing tuned to a specific metric can improve that metric without adding information, but the exploitable margin, the cross-metric cost, and the prevalence of such tuning are unquantified.
core_hypothesis: For each standard metric there exists a post-processing policy improving it by margins comparable to typical publication deltas while degrading other metrics, so single-metric leaderboards are gameable, and an adversarial post-processing audit quantifies each metric's exploitability.
why_important: Quantified gameability bounds would justify multi-metric mandatory reporting and inform which metrics can anchor regulatory claims.
why_possibly_novel: An adversarial audit framework treating metrics as attack targets, producing exploitability constants per metric, formalizes an informal suspicion into measurable properties.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Metrics may be tightly coupled enough that inflating one always shows as visible degradation elsewhere, making gaming self-exposing.
default_community_belief: Post-processing is assumed to be innocuous cleanup, and metrics are assumed hard to inflate without genuine improvement.
falsifiable_prediction: Metric-specific post-processing search will find policies improving the target metric by publication-scale margins on held-out cases, with measurable degradation on non-target metrics, and exploitability will vary systematically across metric families (boundary metrics more exploitable than volumetric ones or vice versa).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid or evolutionary search over morphological post-processing per metric on one benchmark's predictions, report target-metric gains and cross-metric costs.
fastest_falsification: Post-processing search targeting one metric on one set of public predictions.
main_risk: Search may overfit the benchmark; held-out validation within the audit is essential.

one_line: Segmentation-derived volumetry errors are dominated by systematic model-specific bias rather than variance, so cross-sectional accuracy metrics mispredict longitudinal utility entirely.
problem: Volumetry is a primary clinical use of segmentation, and longitudinal change detection depends on error structure (bias stability versus variance), which standard cross-sectional evaluation does not decompose.
core_hypothesis: Each model carries stable structure-specific volume biases that cancel in within-model longitudinal differences, so models with worse cross-sectional accuracy can have superior change-detection precision; the bias-variance decomposition, not aggregate accuracy, predicts longitudinal utility.
why_important: Model selection for longitudinal monitoring currently uses cross-sectional benchmarks; demonstrating rank divergence would redirect evaluation for one of the most consequential clinical applications.
why_possibly_novel: Framing volumetry evaluation around the bias-variance-stability decomposition with longitudinal ground truth connects segmentation benchmarks to biomarker qualification standards.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model biases may drift with acquisition differences between timepoints, destroying the bias-cancellation advantage.
default_community_belief: Better cross-sectional segmentation accuracy is assumed to imply better derived-measurement quality including change detection.
falsifiable_prediction: On test-retest and longitudinal data, per-model volume errors will decompose into a dominant stable bias plus small variance for most structures, within-model change estimates will be far more accurate than cross-sectional errors suggest, and cross-sectional accuracy rank will fail to predict change-detection rank.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several models on a test-retest dataset, decompose volume errors, compare cross-sectional versus change-detection rankings.
fastest_falsification: Bias-variance decomposition of volume errors on one test-retest dataset for two models.
main_risk: Requires repeat-scan data with known or negligible true change, which constrains dataset availability.

one_line: Underspecified task definitions (segment the tumor, with or without necrosis?) account for a measurable share of benchmark error, recoverable by instruction-conditioned evaluation.
problem: Benchmark tasks are specified by a label name whose operational definition varies across datasets and annotators, so models are penalized for resolving underspecification differently than the test annotator did.
core_hypothesis: A quantifiable fraction of measured error is definitional disagreement, not capability failure: evaluating models against multiple explicit instruction-variants of the same task (annotated accordingly) will show that per-model best-variant scores substantially exceed default scores, and that models differ mainly in which definition they implicitly adopted.
why_important: If definitional variance rivals model differences, benchmark comparisons partly measure definitional luck, and instruction-explicit evaluation becomes necessary for valid comparison.
why_possibly_novel: Decomposing benchmark error into definitional versus capability components via instruction-variant re-annotation is an evaluation-science experiment the field has not run.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Within a single benchmark the annotator definition may be consistent enough that definitional error is negligible compared to model error.
default_community_belief: Label names are treated as sufficient task specifications, and all measured error is attributed to model capability.
falsifiable_prediction: Multi-definition re-annotation of a benchmark subset will show each model aligning with an identifiable definition variant, with best-variant error significantly below default error, and the definitional share of error will exceed the typical between-model performance gap.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate a subset under two or three explicit definitions of one ambiguous task, score existing models against each, decompose error.
fastest_falsification: Two-definition re-annotation of a small subset with re-scoring of existing predictions.
main_risk: Choosing which definitional variants are legitimate requires clinical consultation to avoid strawman variants.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: No single medical segmentation checkpoint Pareto-dominates across metric families and anatomy strata; claimed universal superiority dissolves under multi-objective evaluation.
problem: State-of-the-art claims rest on averaged single-metric tables, but clinical requirements are multi-objective (boundary quality, semantic correctness, calibration, robustness), and dominance structure under the full objective vector is never analyzed.
core_hypothesis: Model capabilities involve genuine trade-offs (semantic strength versus boundary precision versus calibration), so the top models form a non-degenerate Pareto front rather than a total order, and which model is optimal depends on the clinical weighting, with front membership stable across datasets but ordering unstable.
why_important: If superiority is weighting-dependent, single-champion narratives misdirect both research competition and clinical procurement, which should instead specify requirement weightings.
why_possibly_novel: Dominance-structure analysis over metric families and anatomy strata reframes benchmarking as multi-objective decision support rather than ranking.
why_it_might_be_wrong: One checkpoint may genuinely dominate if capability differences are large enough to swamp trade-offs.
default_community_belief: A best model exists per benchmark and is identified by the primary metric average.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating leading public checkpoints across a metric-family battery and anatomy strata, no checkpoint will weakly dominate all others; the Pareto front will contain multiple models whose relative order flips under different clinically plausible weightings.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-metric, multi-strata evaluation of several leading checkpoints on two benchmarks, formal dominance analysis.
fastest_falsification: Dominance analysis over existing published per-structure results of top methods on one benchmark.
main_risk: The result could be trivially confirmed if metrics are noisy; dominance tests must account for statistical uncertainty.

one_line: Expert-level performance claims depend on the annotation time budget given to the human baseline: time-controlled comparisons will move or erase claimed model-human parity.
problem: Human baselines in medical segmentation studies are collected under unreported and highly variable time budgets, making model-versus-human comparisons unanchored: the human operating point on the time-accuracy curve is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Human segmentation accuracy is a steep function of time budget in the range typical of annotation sessions, so parity claims made against time-pressured humans will fail against humans at clinically realistic budgets, and the model-human gap should be reported as a function of human time, not a scalar.
why_important: Expert-parity claims drive clinical adoption and regulatory narratives; showing they are artifacts of an unreported experimental parameter would impose time-budget reporting standards.
why_possibly_novel: Treating the human baseline as a psychophysical curve rather than a fixed reference imports human-performance methodology into AI evaluation claims.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Expert accuracy may saturate quickly with time, making baselines robust to budget variation.
default_community_belief: Published human baselines are treated as stable references representing expert capability.
falsifiable_prediction: Collecting human contours at three controlled time budgets will show accuracy differences between budgets comparable to or exceeding claimed model-human gaps, and the parity conclusion will reverse between the lowest and highest budget conditions for at least some structures.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Time-controlled annotation study with a small rater pool on one structure set, comparison of model gap across budget conditions.
fastest_falsification: Small pilot with two time budgets on one structure.
main_risk: Requires human raters and protocol design; modest scale keeps it feasible but limits generality.

judge_flags.title: Expert-parity claims depend on human time budget

one_line: Case difficulty is a stable, model-transcending latent variable: a difficulty score fitted on one model generation predicts failures of future generations, bounding what modeling progress alone can fix.
problem: Whether hard cases are hard for model-specific reasons (fixable by better models) or for case-intrinsic reasons (fixable only by better inputs) determines the ceiling of modeling progress, but difficulty is never decomposed this way.
core_hypothesis: A large share of case difficulty is intrinsic (image quality, atypical anatomy, ambiguous boundaries), so per-case difficulty estimated from older model cohorts will strongly predict failure cases of newer models, and the intrinsic component will define a stable difficulty frontier that successive model generations approach but do not cross.
why_important: If the difficulty frontier is input-limited, further modeling investment has a computable ceiling on existing data, and progress requires acquisition or protocol changes, a strategic conclusion for the field.
why_possibly_novel: Longitudinal difficulty analysis across model generations, with decomposition into intrinsic and model-specific components, treats benchmark history as data about the problem rather than about the models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Foundation-model generations may break correlated failure patterns by changing the error-generating process qualitatively.
default_community_belief: Hard cases are expected to yield progressively to better models; difficulty is treated as model-relative.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-generation difficulty correlation will be high across a span of model eras on the same benchmark, the hardest decile will remain substantially overlapping across generations, and difficulty regression on image-quality plus anatomy-atypicality features will explain most of the stable component.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score per-case difficulty using several older public models, evaluate prediction of newer models' failure cases on the same benchmark, regress stable difficulty on case features.
fastest_falsification: Cross-generation failure-overlap computation using archived predictions from benchmark history.
main_risk: Model generations share training data and biases, which inflates cross-generation correlation beyond true intrinsic difficulty.

one_line: Report-derived weak supervision for segmentation plateaus at coarse localization: adding more report-image pairs improves detection but not boundary fidelity, an information-theoretic ceiling.
problem: Radiology reports are abundant and describe findings, motivating report-supervised segmentation, but reports specify location coarsely, and whether scale can substitute for spatial precision is the governing open question.
core_hypothesis: Report text bounds the extractable spatial information per case, so scaling report-supervised training improves finding-level recall and rough localization with diminishing returns, while boundary-level accuracy plateaus at a level set by report language granularity, unreachable from text scale alone.
why_important: Enormous investment flows into report-supervised medical pretraining; characterizing what it fundamentally cannot deliver prevents misallocated expectations and quantifies the pixel-label budget that remains necessary.
why_possibly_novel: Measuring the plateau structure and its information-theoretic origin, rather than demonstrating feasibility, asks the question the feasibility papers skip.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Emergent grounding at scale might extract finer spatial signal from text-image correlation than per-report information suggests.
default_community_belief: Scaling weak text supervision is expected to progressively solve localization, approaching dense-label performance.
falsifiable_prediction: Scaling curves for report-supervised models will show detection metrics improving with data scale while boundary metrics flatten early; injecting a small number of pixel-level labels will lift the boundary plateau by more than any feasible text-scale increase, demonstrating the ceiling's nature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train report-supervised models at multiple data scales on one report-image corpus, fit scaling curves separately for detection and boundary metrics, run the pixel-label injection arm.
fastest_falsification: Two-scale comparison of detection versus boundary metric improvement on one corpus.
main_risk: Public report-image corpora with evaluation-grade pixel labels are limited, constraining the boundary-metric measurement.

one_line: Medical referring segmentation fails on relational descriptions (posterior to X, between Y and Z) while succeeding on attributive ones, localizing the grounding failure to spatial-relation composition.
problem: Text-guided medical segmentation is evaluated on aggregate benchmarks that mix linguistic phenomena, obscuring which language capabilities dense grounding actually possesses.
core_hypothesis: Current vision-language segmentation architectures ground attributes (size, intensity, laterality as lexical cues) through feature matching but lack a mechanism for composing spatial relations between anatomical referents, so a phenomenon-stratified benchmark will show a large attributive-relational performance gap that persists across model scales.
why_important: Clinical language is heavily relational; if relations do not ground, text-guided clinical tools will fail on ordinary radiology phrasing, and architecture work on relation composition becomes the priority.
why_possibly_novel: Phenomenon-stratified evaluation of medical grounding, isolating relational composition as the failure unit, replaces aggregate claims with a linguistic capability map.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Relational phrases may co-occur with strong lexical shortcuts that models exploit, hiding the compositional deficit.
default_community_belief: Grounding quality is discussed as a single scalar capability improving with scale and data.
falsifiable_prediction: On a relation-versus-attribute stratified test built from the same findings, relational prompts will yield significantly lower accuracy than attributive prompts matched for target difficulty, and scale increases will narrow the attributive gap faster than the relational gap.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct matched attributive and relational prompts for the same targets on one dataset, evaluate one or two text-promptable models, compare strata.
fastest_falsification: Matched-strata evaluation on a few hundred constructed prompts with an existing model.
main_risk: Prompt construction must control target difficulty across strata to avoid confounding.

one_line: Text encoders collapse fine-grained medical entity distinctions into overlapping embedding neighborhoods, and this collision structure predicts which text-prompted segmentation confusions occur.
problem: Text-promptable segmentation inherits the text encoder's semantic geometry, but whether embedding-space collisions between medical terms causally produce segmentation confusions has not been established.
core_hypothesis: When clinically distinct terms (lesion subtypes, adjacent anatomical structures) embed too closely, the mask decoder cannot condition differentially, so the confusion matrix of text-prompted segmentation will be predictable from pairwise text-embedding similarity, and vocabulary fine-tuning that separates embeddings will reduce exactly the predicted confusions.
why_important: This locates a specific bottleneck (text geometry, not visual capability) with a cheap targeted fix, redirecting effort from end-to-end retraining to text-tower repair.
why_possibly_novel: The causal chain from embedding collision to dense-prediction confusion, tested by targeted embedding intervention, goes beyond correlational vocabulary analyses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decoders may rely on few discriminative embedding dimensions invisible to cosine similarity, breaking the predicted correlation.
default_community_belief: Segmentation confusions are attributed to visual similarity; the text tower is assumed adequate given large-scale pretraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Pairwise embedding similarity will rank segmentation confusion rates with strong correlation; embedding-separation fine-tuning of the text tower alone will reduce high-collision confusions significantly more than low-collision ones.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute term-pair embedding similarities and confusion rates for one text-promptable model, test correlation, then run the text-tower separation fine-tuning arm.
fastest_falsification: Embedding-similarity versus confusion-rate correlation on existing model outputs.
main_risk: Visual similarity of the referents confounds the correlation; the intervention arm is essential to establish causality.

one_line: Text-guided segmentation models are negation-blind: prompts asserting absence still produce positive masks, a binary failure with direct clinical-safety consequences.
problem: Clinical language is dense with negation and uncertainty (no evidence of X, rule out Y), and dense-prediction models conditioned on such text must handle absence assertions, an ability never verified for medical segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Contrastively trained text-vision models encode negated and affirmed mentions of a finding nearly identically, so segmentation conditioned on negated prompts will produce masks similar to affirmed prompts, and the failure will persist across prompt paraphrases, reflecting representational rather than parsing failure.
why_important: Negation blindness in automated pipelines converts explicitly excluded findings into segmented findings, a failure class with direct downstream harm potential and regulatory relevance.
why_possibly_novel: Negation handling is studied in medical NLP, but its consequences inside dense visual prediction, including the representational diagnosis, form an untested composition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instruction-tuned multimodal architectures may handle negation better than contrastive ones, making the failure architecture-specific.
default_community_belief: Text conditioning is assumed to modulate segmentation according to prompt semantics including polarity.
falsifiable_prediction: Mask outputs under negated prompts will overlap affirmed-prompt outputs far above the empty-mask baseline, embedding distance between negated and affirmed prompt encodings will be small relative to unrelated prompts, and explicit negation-aware fine-tuning will fix behavior only for trained templates, not novel paraphrases.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one text-promptable model with matched affirmed and negated prompt sets, measure mask overlap and embedding geometry.
fastest_falsification: Affirmed-versus-negated prompt comparison on a few hundred cases with an existing checkpoint.
main_risk: Reasonable expected behavior under negated prompts must be defined (empty mask versus refusal), affecting metric design.

judge_flags.reason: Negation blindness is a known CLIP-family finding; as stated this is the known phenomenon ported to medical segmentation.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Left-right confusion in text-guided medical segmentation is systematically induced by mirror-symmetric augmentation heritage, and its rate is predictable from augmentation policy of the visual backbone.
problem: Laterality is clinically critical (wrong-side interventions), yet visual backbones are commonly pretrained with horizontal-flip augmentation that destroys left-right identity, and the downstream laterality competence of text-guided segmentation is unaudited.
core_hypothesis: Flip-augmented backbones represent mirrored anatomy nearly identically, so text prompts specifying laterality will be grounded at chance or with systematic bias on symmetric anatomy, and backbones pretrained without flips (or with flip-aware labels) will show measurably better laterality grounding, tracing the failure to a specific training decision.
why_important: Laterality errors are among the most consequential in medicine; connecting them to an auditable pretraining choice yields both a screening test and a prevention rule for medical grounding systems.
why_possibly_novel: Attributing a clinical failure class to augmentation heritage through the mirror-distance predictor makes an untested causal link between pretraining hygiene and clinical safety.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Global position encoding may preserve laterality despite flip augmentation, keeping errors low across backbones.
default_community_belief: Laterality is assumed handled by positional context, with augmentation choices considered irrelevant to language grounding.
falsifiable_prediction: Laterality-specified prompts on bilateral structures will show error rates far above non-laterality prompts for flip-augmented backbones, feature distance between an image and its mirror will predict per-backbone laterality error, and flip-free pretraining will reduce the error class substantially.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate laterality-prompted segmentation across backbones with documented augmentation policies, correlate error with mirror-feature distance.
fastest_falsification: Laterality-prompt error measurement plus mirror-distance computation on one flip-augmented model.
main_risk: Backbones differ in many ways beyond flip policy; the mirror-distance mediator analysis carries the causal weight.

one_line: The same clinical target described in jargon versus lay register produces measurably different masks from text-guided models, violating a basic invariance clinical deployment requires.
problem: Text prompts for the same target vary in register (formal terminology, abbreviations, lay descriptions), and mask invariance to meaning-preserving register changes is an unexamined robustness dimension of medical grounding.
core_hypothesis: Medical vision-language training corpora bind visual evidence primarily to formal report language, so register shifts move prompt embeddings across binding-density regions, producing mask changes that exceed clinical tolerance even when human readers judge the prompts synonymous.
why_important: Register robustness determines whether text-guided tools work for the range of real users (specialists, trainees, other professions); quantified instability defines the gap to deployable language interfaces.
why_possibly_novel: Register invariance as a formal robustness axis for dense medical grounding, with corpus-frequency correlation analysis, has not been carved out from generic prompt-sensitivity anecdotes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern instruction-tuned encoders may already achieve near-perfect register invariance, leaving only negligible instability.
default_community_belief: Large text encoders are assumed to normalize register, making meaning-equivalent prompts functionally equivalent.
falsifiable_prediction: Across register-paraphrase sets validated as synonymous by clinicians, mask instability (pairwise overlap between register variants) will significantly exceed the stability observed under trivial syntactic paraphrases, and instability will correlate with the register-frequency imbalance in accessible training corpora.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build clinician-validated register-paraphrase sets for common findings, measure mask stability across registers for one model, compare against syntactic-paraphrase baseline stability.
fastest_falsification: Mask-stability measurement over a small register-paraphrase set on one checkpoint.
main_risk: Synonymy validation requires clinical input; paraphrase sets must avoid subtle meaning changes.

one_line: Cross-lingual degradation of medical text-guided segmentation is larger for dense grounding than for image-level tasks, revealing that spatial binding is the most language-fragile layer of multimodal transfer.
problem: Multilingual medical AI is evaluated at the classification and retrieval level, but dense prediction requires finer text-visual binding whose cross-lingual stability is unknown, affecting equitable deployment beyond English-language health systems.
core_hypothesis: Cross-lingual transfer preserves coarse semantic alignment (sufficient for classification) but degrades the fine-grained token-to-region binding needed for segmentation, so the cross-lingual performance drop will be systematically larger for segmentation than for matched classification on the same cases, and the excess drop will localize to boundary precision rather than detection.
why_important: If dense grounding is the weakest cross-lingual link, multilingual medical AI claims based on classification benchmarks overstate readiness for segmentation-dependent workflows, an equity-relevant correction.
why_possibly_novel: The task-stratified (dense versus image-level) analysis of cross-lingual multimodal transfer isolates which representational layer breaks, a decomposition absent from multilingual medical benchmarks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Grounding may rely on language-neutral keyword anchors, making dense binding no more fragile than classification.
default_community_belief: Cross-lingual robustness measured on classification is assumed representative of all downstream multimodal tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating matched prompts in several languages, the segmentation drop will significantly exceed the classification drop per language, the excess will correlate with language distance from the training corpus distribution, and boundary metrics will degrade before detection metrics.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Translate validated prompt sets into three languages, evaluate one model on matched segmentation and classification tasks, compare per-language drops between task types.
fastest_falsification: Two-language segmentation-versus-classification drop comparison on one model.
main_risk: Translation quality is a confound requiring professional or back-translation-validated prompts.

one_line: Hedging language in radiology reports (possible, cannot exclude) spatially predicts model-annotator disagreement regions, making report uncertainty a free supervision signal for segmentation reliability.
problem: Reports encode radiologist uncertainty linguistically, and segmentation models produce spatial errors, but whether the linguistic uncertainty and the spatial unreliability co-locate has never been measured, leaving a free reliability signal unused.
core_hypothesis: Findings described with hedge words are precisely those with weak image evidence, so segmentation error and inter-annotator disagreement will be significantly elevated for hedged findings versus confidently reported ones, and a hedge-conditioned reliability model will predict per-finding segmentation quality without any pixel-level validation data.
why_important: Hospitals hold millions of report-image pairs; if hedging predicts spatial unreliability, deployment systems gain a validation-free triage signal and weak supervision for uncertainty training at archive scale.
why_possibly_novel: Bridging report linguistics to spatial reliability of dense prediction, with matched-confound testing, connects two literatures (medical NLP uncertainty, segmentation QC) that currently do not cite each other.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hedging reflects reporting culture and legal caution as much as image evidence, which may decouple it from spatial error.
default_community_belief: Report text is used for labels and pretraining, while its uncertainty markers are treated as noise to filter out.
falsifiable_prediction: Linking report sentences to finding regions on a report-paired dataset, hedged findings will show higher segmentation error and rater disagreement than unhedged findings at matched size and contrast, and adding hedge features to a reliability predictor will significantly improve per-finding error prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one report-paired segmentation dataset, classify findings by hedging, compare error and disagreement between hedged and unhedged strata with size and contrast matching.
fastest_falsification: Hedged-versus-unhedged error comparison on one report-paired dataset with existing predictions.
main_risk: Hedged findings differ from unhedged ones in size and subtlety; matching quality determines the study's validity.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: SAM point-prompt outputs on smoke are unstable under tiny click jitter, unlike solid objects.
problem: Interactive segmentation of smoke is unreliable, but nobody has quantified how much of the failure is prompt instability rather than mask quality per se.
core_hypothesis: Because smoke has no internal object structure, SAM's mask decoder latches onto whatever background structure lies near the click, so nearby clicks yield wildly different masks.
why_important: If failure is instability, prompt ensembling is a cheap fix; if it is uniform badness, retraining is needed. The diagnosis changes the remedy.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-jitter robustness has been studied for objects; I am not aware of a systematic jitter-instability characterization specifically on amorphous scattering media like smoke.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM may collapse to the same (bad) low-confidence whole-image mask for every click, giving high inter-click IoU and refuting the instability framing.
default_community_belief: SAM is assumed to fail on smoke because smoke is out of distribution; the failure is treated as monolithic low quality rather than prompt-conditional variance.
falsifiable_prediction: Mean pairwise IoU of SAM masks across 10 clicks jittered within a 10px radius inside GT smoke will be below 0.5, while the same protocol on COCO-style solid objects stays above 0.8.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take any public smoke segmentation set with masks, sample 50 images, run SAM with 10 jittered clicks per image, compute pairwise IoU distributions for smoke vs a solid-object control set.
fastest_falsification: One afternoon: 20 smoke images, 10 jittered clicks each, plot the pairwise IoU histogram against a 20-image COCO control.
main_risk: Instability may be dominated by a few degenerate images, making the average misleading; need per-image analysis.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: SAM's predicted-IoU head is anti-informative on smoke: it ranks its own worst mask first.
problem: Pipelines select among SAM's multimask outputs using its self-predicted IoU, which was trained on object-centric data and may be systematically wrong for amorphous targets.
core_hypothesis: The IoU-prediction head learned that crisp compact masks are good, so on smoke it prefers the crisp wrong mask (a background object) over the diffuse right one.
why_important: Every zero-shot SAM pipeline silently inherits this selector; a corrected selector is a drop-in improvement for all amorphous classes.
why_possibly_novel: Multimask selection error as the dominant failure mechanism on amorphous targets appears unexamined; most work reports only final IoU.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The IoU head may generalize better than the mask decoder itself, in which case argmax-vs-oracle gap stays small even on smoke.
default_community_belief: SAM's confidence outputs are treated as reasonably calibrated across domains and are used for ranking without domain-specific checks.
falsifiable_prediction: On smoke, the gap between oracle mask selection and argmax-by-predicted-IoU selection will exceed 15 IoU points, at least 3x the gap measured on solid objects.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run SAM multimask on 100 smoke images, record all three masks plus predicted IoUs, compare argmax selection vs oracle selection vs the same on an object dataset.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: 30 smoke images, scatter-plot predicted vs actual IoU per candidate mask and compute rank correlation.
main_risk: All three candidate masks may be equally bad on smoke, making selection irrelevant and the finding moot.
