territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Box prompts beat point prompts disproportionately on smoke because extent cannot be inferred from texture.
problem: Prompt-type guidance for practitioners is derived from object benchmarks and may be exactly wrong for amorphous targets.
core_hypothesis: For solid objects, a point suffices because texture and contours define extent; for smoke, extent is the missing information, so a box supplies precisely what the model cannot recover.
why_important: Changes best practice for human-in-the-loop labeling of smoke and fire datasets, where annotation cost dominates project budgets.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-type ablations exist broadly, but a class-conditional analysis contrasting amorphous vs solid targets with a controlled protocol seems missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM may fail on smoke inside the box as well (segmenting the background object within the box), erasing the predicted gap.
default_community_belief: Points are considered a cheap near-equivalent to boxes for most SAM use, with prompt choice treated as minor.
falsifiable_prediction: The box-minus-point IoU gap on smoke will be at least 2x the gap on solid objects under matched protocols.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On matched sets of 100 smoke and 100 object instances, compare SAM IoU for center-click vs GT-box prompting.
fastest_falsification: Half a day with any smoke dataset that has masks: derive boxes from masks, run both prompt types, compare gaps.
main_risk: GT-derived boxes leak extent information, making the comparison trivially favorable to boxes; need noisy human-drawn boxes as a third arm.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: SAM sees through thin smoke: its dominant error is returning the occluded background object, not a wrong smoke boundary.
problem: Failure analyses report low IoU on smoke without distinguishing under-segmentation of smoke from capture of the background object visible through it.
core_hypothesis: SAM's pretraining teaches amodal completion of partially visible objects, so a click on translucent smoke is interpreted as a click on the thing behind it.
why_important: Identifies a specific, nameable failure mechanism (see-through capture) that suggests a specific fix: suppressing background-object evidence before prompting.
why_possibly_novel: The see-through failure mode is anecdotally known for glass but I have not seen it isolated and quantified for smoke as a function of opacity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM might instead return large low-confidence blobs unrelated to background objects, meaning the failure is diffuse rather than see-through.
default_community_belief: Low smoke IoU is attributed to fuzzy boundaries; the possibility that the model is correctly segmenting a different (background) thing is rarely separated out.
falsifiable_prediction: For clicks on smoke regions with alpha below roughly 0.5, more than half of SAM's predicted mask pixels will overlap a background object's mask rather than the smoke GT.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite lab-captured smoke with known alpha over scenes with annotated background objects, click smoke at varying alpha, measure predicted-mask overlap with background-object GT vs smoke GT.
fastest_falsification: One day: 30 composites at 3 alpha levels over scenes with object masks; measure where the predicted mask mass lands.
main_risk: Requires alpha ground truth, which pushes toward synthetic composites that may not represent wild smoke.

judge_flags.title: SAM sees through thin smoke and segments the occluded background

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Iterative click refinement is non-monotonic on smoke: added corrective clicks can make SAM masks worse.
problem: Interactive segmentation assumes each corrective click improves the mask; if this breaks on amorphous targets, annotation tooling built on SAM silently wastes labeler effort.
core_hypothesis: Negative clicks in the smoke transition band are ambiguous evidence (the pixel is both smoke and background), driving the decoder to oscillate between incompatible mask hypotheses.
why_important: Quantifies the real cost of SAM-assisted smoke annotation and motivates matting-style tools instead; also a clean falsifiable failure-mining statistic.
why_possibly_novel: Non-monotonicity of interactive refinement has been noted in medical imaging contexts; a systematic measurement on scattering media appears absent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM's prompt encoder may weight later clicks strongly enough to converge anyway, making non-monotonicity rare in practice.
default_community_belief: More clicks monotonically improve SAM masks; interactive refinement is treated as a reliable fallback when zero-shot fails.
falsifiable_prediction: On smoke, at least 25 percent of refinement steps will decrease IoU, vs under 5 percent on solid objects, and clicks-to-0.7-IoU will be more than 3x higher.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate standard click protocols (center of largest error region) for 20 refinement steps on 100 smoke and 100 object instances; plot IoU trajectories.
fastest_falsification: A few hours: scripted 10-step refinement on 30 smoke images, count IoU-decreasing steps.
main_risk: Results depend heavily on the simulated click policy; need at least two policies plus a small human study to be credible.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Grid-clicking every location inside GT smoke reveals large dead zones where no prompt yields an acceptable mask.
problem: We lack a per-image measure of whether an amorphous region is recoverable by any prompt at all, which conflates model limits with prompt-policy limits.
core_hypothesis: For smoke, a substantial fraction of the region admits no point prompt achieving IoU above 0.5, and this dead-zone fraction is an intrinsic ambiguity score of the image.
why_important: Separates cannot-be-prompted failures from bad-prompt-policy failures, and yields an automatic difficulty ranking for dataset curation and active labeling.
why_possibly_novel: Exhaustive prompt-space sweeps have been used for evaluation, but dead-zone fraction as an ambiguity measure for amorphous classes seems new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dead-zone fraction may be near zero because some prompt always recovers a decent mask, showing that policy, not capability, is the bottleneck.
default_community_belief: Failures are usually reported under one canonical prompt (center click), implicitly assuming a better prompt exists for hard cases.
falsifiable_prediction: Median dead-zone fraction (cells where best-of-3 masks all score below 0.5 IoU) will exceed 40 percent on smoke and stay below 10 percent on solid objects.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 50 smoke images, click every cell of a 16x16 grid restricted to GT masks, record best achievable IoU per cell, compute dead-zone fractions.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day: coarse 8x8 grid on 30 images gives the shape of the answer.
main_risk: Compute-heavy (hundreds of forward passes per image); dead zones may just track thin-smoke alpha, adding nothing beyond opacity.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Downsampling images improves SAM smoke segmentation by destroying the background detail it wrongly latches onto.
problem: Resolution is tuned for object benchmarks; the optimal operating resolution for amorphous, low-frequency targets is unknown and possibly opposite to conventional wisdom.
core_hypothesis: High-frequency background texture visible through smoke supplies the see-through evidence that hijacks SAM; blurring removes the distractor while smoke's low-frequency structure survives.
why_important: A zero-training, one-line preprocessing change that could improve deployed smoke pipelines and reframes resolution as a per-class knob.
why_possibly_novel: Resolution ablations are standard, but the specific prediction of an interior optimum for scattering media, with a mechanistic distractor-removal explanation, seems untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Smoke boundaries, however fuzzy, may still need resolution to place, so IoU could be monotone increasing and the hypothesis dies.
default_community_belief: Higher input resolution is assumed to help or at worst saturate; degrading input to improve segmentation sounds wrong.
falsifiable_prediction: SAM smoke IoU will be non-monotonic in input resolution, peaking at a downsampled scale (for example 4x smaller) where solid-object IoU has already dropped noticeably.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate SAM on a smoke set at 6 resolutions from full to one-eighth scale, same prompts, plot IoU vs scale for smoke and an object control.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: 30 images, 4 scales, one plot.
main_risk: SAM's fixed 1024 input pipeline resizes internally anyway, so external downsampling may be confounded with interpolation artifacts.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: SAM's three granularity outputs collapse to one mask on smoke, showing its ambiguity head encodes part-whole structure, not density structure.
problem: The multimask mechanism is SAM's only tool for expressing ambiguity, and the kind of ambiguity smoke has (how far out does it extend) may be unrepresentable by it.
core_hypothesis: The three outputs were trained to capture subpart/part/whole nesting of solid objects; smoke's ambiguity axis is a density threshold, which the heads never learned, so they degenerate.
why_important: Pinpoints a representational gap: ambiguity heads should span a density sweep for amorphous classes, suggesting a concrete retrofit (threshold-conditioned mask head).
why_possibly_novel: Multimask diversity has been examined for objects; using inter-output collapse as a diagnostic of the type of ambiguity a model can express seems new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The heads may actually produce a loose-vs-tight sweep on smoke (an emergent density axis), which would refute collapse and be interesting in the opposite direction.
default_community_belief: Multimask output is assumed to surface whatever ambiguity exists in the prompt; if masks agree, the region is assumed unambiguous.
falsifiable_prediction: Mean pairwise IoU among SAM's three output masks will exceed 0.85 on smoke clicks (near-duplicates) but sit far lower on solid objects where genuine part-whole nesting exists.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 100 smoke and 100 object clicks, compute the pairwise IoU matrix among the three outputs and compare diversity distributions; check whether smoke outputs ever order by density.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: 30 smoke clicks, inspect and quantify the three-mask diversity.
main_risk: Collapse might reflect low decoder confidence generally rather than a missing ambiguity axis, requiring careful controls with equally low-confidence object cases.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Averaging SAM mask logits over many jittered prompts reconstructs a soft smoke density map for free.
problem: Binary masks are a poor output format for smoke, but retraining for matting is expensive; a zero-training route to soft outputs is missing.
core_hypothesis: Each jittered prompt samples a different plausible binarization of the density field, so the ensemble mean of mask probabilities approximates relative opacity.
why_important: Turns an existing frozen model into a soft smoke matting tool with zero training, useful for alarm thresholding and annotation bootstrapping.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt ensembling for robustness exists; interpreting the ensemble mean as a physical density estimate for scattering media appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask-probability averages may encode prompt-distance artifacts (bullseye patterns around clicks) rather than opacity.
default_community_belief: SAM outputs are binary instruments; recovering continuous density is assumed to require matting-style training or dedicated architectures.
falsifiable_prediction: The rank correlation between prompt-ensemble mean masks and human-annotated relative opacity will exceed 0.6, clearly beating any single SAM output's correlation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 30 smoke images with coarse opacity annotations (3-level ordinal labels suffice), compute ensemble means over 25 jittered clicks and measure ordinal correlation.
fastest_falsification: One day including quick 3-level opacity labeling of 20 images by one person.
main_risk: Ensemble members may all collapse to the same wrong mask (see w14p1c-001 failing), leaving no diversity to average.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Fine-tuning SAM on smoke catastrophically degrades its solid-object skill, much more than fine-tuning on a new object class does.
problem: Teams fine-tune SAM per domain assuming mild forgetting; amorphous targets may require unlearning the edge prior that everything else depends on.
core_hypothesis: Smoke supervision pushes the decoder to accept boundary-free masks, directly fighting the crisp-boundary inductive bias, so forgetting is structural rather than incidental.
why_important: Warns against naive smoke fine-tunes in multi-purpose pipelines and motivates adapter routing or output-format separation for amorphous classes.
why_possibly_novel: Catastrophic forgetting in SAM fine-tuning is discussed generically; the asymmetry prediction tied to boundary-prior conflict appears specific and untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: LoRA's limited capacity may firewall the edge prior, keeping object skill intact and refuting the structural-conflict story.
default_community_belief: Small parameter-efficient fine-tunes are assumed to be safely local, with forgetting roughly proportional to tuning-set size, not tuning-set geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched-budget LoRA fine-tunes will show at least 2x larger held-out object-segmentation degradation when the tuning set is smoke than when it is an unseen solid class of equal size.
minimal_falsification_experiment: LoRA-tune SAM on 500 smoke masks vs 500 masks of one held-out object class; evaluate both models on a fixed object suite and compare degradation.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days for both tunes plus evaluation on a small object suite.
main_risk: Result may hinge on tuning hyperparameters (rank, LR) more than on data type, demanding a small sweep to be fair.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Blurring images barely hurts SAM on smoke but devastates it on objects, proving smoke performance never came from edges.
problem: We attribute smoke failure to missing edges, but no controlled frequency-ablation study isolates which spectral bands SAM actually uses per target type.
core_hypothesis: SAM's smoke masks are driven by low-frequency luminance structure, so removing high frequencies is nearly free for smoke while catastrophic for edge-defined objects.
why_important: Gives a causal, band-resolved account of what signal remains for amorphous targets, informing where to inject engineered cues.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency-bias studies exist for classification (texture vs shape); a band-ablation causal analysis for promptable segmentation on scattering media appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM may rely on mid-frequency texture of smoke granularity itself, so blur could hurt smoke as much as objects.
default_community_belief: Degrading image quality is assumed to hurt segmentation across the board, roughly uniformly per class.
falsifiable_prediction: Gaussian blur at sigma equivalent to removing detail above 8 cycles per object will drop object IoU by 20-plus points while smoke IoU changes by under 5 points; low-frequency contrast compression will show the reverse pattern.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate SAM on smoke and object sets under matched high-pass and low-pass filtering ladders; plot IoU vs cutoff per target type.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: 3 blur levels on 30 smoke plus 30 object images.
main_risk: Blur also spreads smoke's own faint gradients; band effects may entangle target and distractor signal, requiring composites with separable layers.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Drawing a fake thin contour around smoke rescues SAM, proving the failure is edge absence rather than semantic ignorance.
problem: It is unknown whether SAM fails on smoke because it cannot find a boundary or because it does not represent smoke as a segmentable thing at all.
core_hypothesis: SAM's decoder is an edge-snapping machine; given any plausible contour, even artificial, it will complete the smoke mask correctly, showing semantics were never the bottleneck.
why_important: If true, a learned edge-hallucination front-end (drawing pseudo-contours from weak cues) becomes a principled architecture for amorphous segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: Contour-injection as a causal probe of what promptable segmenters are missing seems unexplored, versus common saliency-style analyses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM might ignore faint injected contours entirely, or need implausibly high contrast, indicating deeper representational failure.
default_community_belief: Foundation-model failures on unusual categories are read as distribution gaps needing more data, not as a single missing low-level cue.
falsifiable_prediction: Overlaying a 2px low-contrast synthetic contour along the GT smoke boundary will raise click-prompted IoU by at least 25 points, far more than the same manipulation helps objects.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 50 smoke images, render GT-boundary contours at 3 contrast levels into the image, rerun identical prompts, measure IoU deltas against unmodified baselines.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 20 images, one contrast level, before-after IoU.
main_risk: GT-contour injection is oracle information; the follow-up (hallucinating contours without GT) may be the actually hard problem.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Grayscale conversion cripples fire segmentation but barely touches smoke, splitting the two tasks by their dominant cue.
problem: Fire and smoke are bundled into one task family, yet their failure modes under channel ablations have never been contrasted, hiding that they may need different front-ends.
core_hypothesis: Fire recognition in VFMs is primarily chromatic (flame colors), while smoke recognition is achromatic (luminance and texture), so channel ablations dissociate them cleanly.
why_important: Justifies decoupling fire and smoke heads and predicts which corruptions (night IR cameras are grayscale) silently kill which capability in deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Channel-ablation dissociation between the two amorphous classes, framed as a deployment-relevant diagnostic, appears unreported.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern VFM features may encode fire via bloom and shape of glow, keeping grayscale performance high.
default_community_belief: Fire and smoke are treated as siblings degraded by the same corruptions; color is considered one cue among many rather than fire's load-bearing cue.
falsifiable_prediction: Grayscale input will cut fire IoU by more than 20 points but smoke IoU by fewer than 5; hue rotation will show the same asymmetry.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate any promptable or fine-tuned segmenter on fire and smoke test sets under grayscale, hue-rotate, and channel-swap transforms; compare per-class deltas.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: grayscale eval on 30 fire and 30 smoke images.
main_risk: Fire datasets often contain smoke and vice versa; contaminated labels can smear the dissociation.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: A linear probe on local power-spectrum slope beats a linear probe on deep VFM features for smoke detection, showing the backbone discards the best cue.
problem: We assume deep features subsume simple signal statistics; for scattering media this may be false, and nobody has run the head-to-head.
core_hypothesis: Smoke locally flattens the image power spectrum in a characteristic way; ViT pretraining objectives have no reason to preserve this statistic, so deep features are worse than the raw statistic.
why_important: A concrete existence proof that VFMs destroy task-critical low-level statistics would justify hybrid inputs (image plus signal statistics) for amorphous targets.
why_possibly_novel: Spectral statistics for smoke were used in pre-deep-learning detectors; resurrecting them as an adversarial baseline against frozen VFM probes is the new twist.
why_it_might_be_wrong: VFMs may retain low-level statistics in early layers or register dimensions, so the right deep probe wins once layers are swept.
default_community_belief: Frozen foundation features are assumed to dominate handcrafted features on essentially every visual task now.
falsifiable_prediction: Patch-level smoke/no-smoke linear probing on handcrafted spectral-slope features will exceed the AUROC of a linear probe on frozen final-layer SAM or DINO features on at least one public smoke set.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract 32x32 patches from a labeled smoke set, compute spectral-slope features and frozen VFM features, train logistic regressions on both, compare AUROC with confidence intervals.
fastest_falsification: One day: both probes on one dataset, patch level.
main_risk: Deep features may win easily, making this a negative result; still publishable as a sanity check but less exciting.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: SAM's smoke performance versus opacity is a sharp phase transition, not a gradual decline, revealing an internal edge-detectability threshold.
problem: Deployment risk assessment needs to know at what smoke density a model starts working; the shape of the performance-vs-opacity curve is unknown.
core_hypothesis: The decoder needs boundary contrast above a fixed internal threshold; below it, masks are junk, above it they are decent, with a narrow transition, like a psychometric function.
why_important: A stable threshold turns into an operational rule (detectable at optical density X), enabling principled sensor placement and expectation setting for early-fire detection.
why_possibly_novel: Psychometric-function analysis of segmentation models on parametric opacity sweeps appears absent from smoke literature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging over spatially varying alpha within one plume may smear any per-pixel threshold into an apparently gradual curve.
default_community_belief: Performance is assumed to degrade smoothly with target difficulty; abrupt regime changes are not part of the standard mental model.
falsifiable_prediction: IoU vs composited alpha will fit a sigmoid with a transition width under 0.15 alpha units, rather than a linear ramp; the threshold alpha will be stable across backgrounds.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite one real plume matte over 20 backgrounds at 10 alpha levels; run fixed prompts; fit sigmoid vs linear models to IoU curves and compare fit quality.
fastest_falsification: One day with an existing smoke-matte composite pipeline; 5 alpha levels suffice for curve shape.
main_risk: Threshold may vary wildly with background luminance, killing the stable-threshold half of the claim while the sigmoid shape survives.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Training with an ignore band over the smoke transition zone beats training on hard labels there, at identical data volume.
problem: Standard training treats every GT pixel as equally trustworthy, but smoke transition pixels are label noise by construction, and their gradient contribution may be actively harmful.
core_hypothesis: Hard labels in the ambiguous band teach the model arbitrary annotator whims; masking that band from the loss removes noise without removing signal.
why_important: A free training-recipe improvement applicable to every amorphous class, testable in a day, with direct impact on the many small smoke datasets people train on.
why_possibly_novel: Ignore bands exist in some benchmarks for evaluation; using annotator-disagreement-calibrated ignore bands as a training recipe for scattering media seems unstudied.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transition pixels, though noisy, may carry the only supervision about mask extent, so ignoring them could unmoor the boundary entirely.
default_community_belief: More supervised pixels are better; discarding labeled pixels is seen as wasting annotation money.
falsifiable_prediction: A model trained with a morphological ignore band (say 7px around GT boundary) will match or beat the hard-label model on core-region IoU and beat it on boundary F-score measured against consensus-of-annotators GT.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the same small segmentation model twice on one smoke dataset (hard labels vs banded labels), evaluate on a held-out set relabeled by 3 annotators.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day: two trainings on one dataset plus a 50-image triple-annotated eval slice.
main_risk: The band width is a hyperparameter that could be tuned to flatter the hypothesis; needs a width sweep and a pre-registered metric.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Shallow ViT layers separate smoke from background better than deep layers, because deep layers explain smoke away as illumination.
problem: Everyone fine-tunes from final-layer features by default; for atmospheric phenomena the information may peak early and be progressively destroyed.
core_hypothesis: Deep layers are invariance machines: they normalize away haze-like appearance changes to stabilize object identity, which is exactly wrong when haze is the target.
why_important: Directly actionable: attach smoke heads to early-mid features; also a clean instance of the invariance-vs-detection tension in foundation models.
why_possibly_novel: Layer-wise probing is common, but the specific inversion prediction for scattering media (early peak) versus objects (late peak), tested on segmentation backbones, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Smoke semantics (contextual plausibility of smoke here) may live late even if smoke appearance lives early, making late layers win on real data.
default_community_belief: Deeper features are assumed richer for all dense tasks; feature choice is an afterthought behind architecture choice.
falsifiable_prediction: Layer-wise linear probes for smoke presence on frozen SAM/DINO backbones will peak before the network midpoint and decline monotonically afterward, unlike object classes which peak late.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe every 2nd layer of one frozen backbone for patchwise smoke classification on one dataset; plot AUROC vs depth alongside an object-class control.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day for a full layer sweep on one dataset.
main_risk: Probe capacity and patch alignment details can flip conclusions; must fix probe protocol and repeat across 2 backbones minimum.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Object-centric pretraining makes VFM features of hazy background patches look like clean background, actively erasing translucent occluders.
problem: We lack direct feature-space evidence that VFMs suppress translucent media rather than merely under-representing them.
core_hypothesis: Pretraining rewards recognizing the occluded object despite haze, so the representation maps hazy-background patches near clean-background patches, leaving little linear smoke signal.
why_important: If suppression strengthens with scale, bigger foundation models will get worse at smoke, an important scaling caveat for safety-critical perception.
why_possibly_novel: Feature-similarity analysis of translucent-occluder suppression, with a scale trend prediction, seems absent; most scaling analyses only report task scores.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Larger models may represent both the object and the haze in superposition, so smoke signal could grow with scale instead.
default_community_belief: Scaling foundation models is assumed to improve all downstream perception, including rare categories, via better features.
falsifiable_prediction: Cosine similarity of features(background plus synthetic smoke) to features(clean background) will exceed similarity to features(pure smoke on gray), and the effect will strengthen with backbone depth and with model scale.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build triplets (clean bg, bg plus alpha-composited smoke, smoke on neutral) for 200 scenes; compute the similarity inequality rate across 3 model sizes of one family.
fastest_falsification: One day: 50 triplets, one model family at 2 sizes, count inequality violations.
main_risk: Synthetic compositing artifacts might dominate similarity structure; needs a small real-smoke paired subset (same camera, before/after smoke) as anchor.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Surveillance-trained smoke segmenters run on positional priors: rotating the image collapses them far more than it collapses object segmenters.
problem: Reported smoke accuracy may be inflated by scene-layout shortcuts (smoke near horizon or above sources) that fail exactly when cameras or scenes change.
core_hypothesis: Because appearance evidence for smoke is weak, trained models load heavily on position and scene-context features, more than object models do.
why_important: Quantifies a deployment fragility (new camera angles) and gives a cheap audit any practitioner can run before shipping.
why_possibly_novel: Position-shortcut audits exist for classification; applying them as a standard fragility audit for amorphous-target segmenters seems new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Horizontal flips may show near-zero degradation, and vertical effects may be entirely attributable to legitimate buoyancy priors rather than shortcuts.
default_community_belief: Test-time flips and rotations are treated as benign augmentations; models are assumed roughly equivariant after standard training.
falsifiable_prediction: A 90-degree rotation or vertical flip at test time will cost smoke-trained models at least 2x the IoU it costs comparable object segmenters, and patch-position randomization probes will show higher position decodability from smoke-model features.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 2 public smoke models and 2 object models under rotation/flip transforms on their own test sets; compare relative degradation.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: flip/rotate eval on one public smoke model.
main_risk: Rotation also breaks smoke physics cues (plumes rise), so some degradation is legitimate; need to separate physics-prior loss from layout-shortcut loss via horizontal flip controls.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: SAM's mask for a glass object is determined more by what is behind the glass than by the glass itself.
problem: Transparent-object segmentation failures are reported as scores, without isolating the causal driver: the object's own cues versus the transmitted background content.
core_hypothesis: VFM features at glass pixels are dominated by transmitted background; swapping the background behind identical glass changes the predicted mask more than swapping the glass changes it.
why_important: Establishes a background-sensitivity index as the primary failure metric for transparent objects and motivates background-suppression front-ends.
why_possibly_novel: Controlled background-swap causal analysis for promptable segmenters on real glass appears rare; most transparent-object work reports benchmark scores only.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Specular highlights and rims may anchor masks strongly enough that background swaps change little.
default_community_belief: Transparent objects are hard because they lack texture; the dominant role of transmitted content is acknowledged qualitatively but not measured as the main causal factor.
falsifiable_prediction: In controlled captures (same glass, 10 backgrounds), the variance of SAM masks across backgrounds will exceed the variance across 10 different glasses on one background, measured by mean pairwise IoU.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Photograph 5 glasses against 10 posters on a fixed rig (or composite via existing matting datasets), run fixed prompts, decompose mask variance into background vs object factors.
fastest_falsification: One afternoon with 2 glasses, 5 backgrounds, a tripod, and fixed prompts.
main_risk: A lab rig underrepresents wild refraction and clutter; composites may leak matting artifacts.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: The refraction-induced warp field of the background is the strongest transparent-object cue, and ViTs are nearly blind to it.
problem: Architectures for transparent segmentation add capacity but rarely add the one signal that physically defines transparency: local geometric distortion of the transmitted scene.
core_hypothesis: Patch embeddings are trained to be robust to small warps, so the refraction signal is discarded at the tokenizer; an explicit warp-field estimate reintroduces it cheaply.
why_important: If a physics-defined channel beats data scaling, it redirects the field from architecture tweaks toward cue engineering for ambiguous materials.
why_possibly_novel: Distortion cues appear in classic glass detection literature; making warp-blindness of ViTs the explicit hypothesis and testing the channel against a data-scaling control seems new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern backbones may already encode distortion implicitly at scale, making the extra channel redundant.
default_community_belief: Better backbones and more annotated data are the accepted route; input-cue engineering is considered legacy thinking.
falsifiable_prediction: Feeding an estimated local-distortion map (from flow against an inpainted undistorted background, or from repeated patterns) as an extra input channel will improve transparent-object IoU more than doubling fine-tuning data, at equal compute.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one public transparent-object dataset, train the same model with and without a distortion-proxy channel and with 2x data; compare the three runs.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days for the three-arm comparison on a small model.
main_risk: Estimating the warp field in the wild without knowing the undistorted background may be as hard as the original task (circularity).

judge_flags.title: Refraction warp field is the key transparent-object cue and ViTs are blind to it

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Removing specular highlights collapses SAM on glass, showing masks are anchored to reflections rather than to the object.
problem: It is unclear which residual cue lets models find glass at all; without knowing the anchor cue, robustness claims are guesswork.
core_hypothesis: Sparse specular highlights act as the de facto keypoints for glass; delete them and the model loses the object entirely, revealing brittle single-cue dependence.
why_important: Predicts systematic failure under diffuse lighting (overcast, softbox retail lighting) and motivates highlight-invariant training augmentation.
why_possibly_novel: Highlight ablation as a causal probe with matched-area controls on promptable segmenters appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rim contours (dark edges at silhouettes) may be the true anchor, in which case highlight removal changes little.
default_community_belief: Glass difficulty is blamed on transparency in general; the load-bearing role of highlights is assumed minor or unexamined.
falsifiable_prediction: Inpainting specular highlights (or capturing cross-polarized) will drop glass IoU by over 30 points, while the same-area random inpainting elsewhere on the glass drops it by under 10.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Detect highlights via intensity thresholding on 100 glass images, inpaint them and matched control regions, rerun identical prompts, compare deltas.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: 30 images, threshold-based highlight inpainting, before-after IoU.
main_risk: Inpainting introduces its own artifacts that the model may key on; cross-polarized capture of a small real set is the clean but slower control.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Transparent and amorphous targets fail on opposite axes: glass fails in the interior, smoke fails at the boundary, and this two-axis taxonomy predicts which fix works.
problem: Ambiguous-object failures are lumped together, so remedies are prescribed blindly across materially different failure geometries.
core_hypothesis: Glass has crisp boundaries but misleading interiors (transmitted content), smoke has honest interiors but undefined boundaries; decomposing error into interior vs boundary components will separate the classes almost perfectly.
why_important: A validated failure taxonomy lets practitioners choose fixes from a lookup rather than trial and error, and gives failure mining a coordinate system.
why_possibly_novel: Error decomposition metrics exist, but using the interior/boundary plane as a material-driven failure taxonomy with fix-response predictions appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Real errors may be dominated by whole-instance misses (detection failures), which live on neither axis and flatten the taxonomy.
default_community_belief: Hard transparent-ish categories are treated as one long tail; benchmarks average over them without a failure-geometry axis.
falsifiable_prediction: On a scatter plot of interior-error vs boundary-error fractions, transparent instances and smoke instances will form clusters separable with over 90 percent accuracy by a linear boundary; interior-targeted fixes (context suppression) will help glass but not smoke, and vice versa for boundary-targeted fixes.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute interior and boundary error components for SAM outputs on one transparent and one smoke dataset; test cluster separability; then apply one fix per axis and check the predicted interaction.
fastest_falsification: One day: run decomposition on existing predictions for both datasets, plot, and eyeball separability.
main_risk: Thin glass (stemware) has almost no interior, degenerating the decomposition; needs instance-size stratification.

judge_flags.title: Two-axis failure taxonomy: glass fails interior, smoke fails boundary

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Training transparent-object models with rim-band supervision only (ignore the interior) matches full-mask supervision, because interior labels are noise.
problem: Full-mask supervision forces the model to memorize that transmitted backgrounds are foreground, which may be unlearnable and may corrupt the features.
core_hypothesis: All learnable evidence for glass lives in a thin rim band (contours, highlight lines, distortion gradients); interior pixels supply gradient noise that slows or misdirects learning.
why_important: Cuts effective annotation requirements (rim-only polygons are cheaper) and clarifies where the information actually is for transparent materials.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary-focused losses exist as auxiliary terms; making rim-only the sole positive supervision, with topological infill, appears untested for transparency.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interior consistency (this weird content moves with the object) may be real signal that rim-only training throws away.
default_community_belief: Denser supervision is better; discarding the majority of positive pixels should obviously hurt.
falsifiable_prediction: A model whose positive loss is restricted to a 15px rim band, with interiors filled at inference by closing the rim, will reach at least parity full-mask IoU with the fully supervised model, and beat it on backgrounds unseen in training.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train identical small models on one transparent dataset under full-mask vs rim-band supervision; evaluate on standard split plus a background-shifted split.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days for the paired training run on a small architecture.
main_risk: Rim-closing at inference fails for occluded or truncated objects, capping achievable IoU regardless of feature quality.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Adding monocular depth as an input channel actively hurts transparent-object segmentation: a clean negative-transfer case.
problem: Multi-modal fusion is assumed helpful, but monocular depth predictors place glass at the depth of the transmitted background, injecting confidently wrong geometry.
core_hypothesis: The depth channel asserts hole where glass is, and the segmenter learns to trust depth on the majority of (opaque) pixels, so it inherits the depth model's transparency blindness at exactly the pixels that matter.
why_important: A documented negative-transfer example warns the growing everything-plus-depth pipeline trend and motivates transparency-aware depth uncertainty channels instead.
why_possibly_novel: Depth-for-segmentation ablations rarely stratify by material class; the specific per-class harm prediction appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The network may learn that depth discontinuities around rims are a glass giveaway, turning the flawed channel into net positive signal.
default_community_belief: Auxiliary geometric channels are assumed neutral-to-helpful; more input signal should not hurt a learner that can ignore it.
falsifiable_prediction: RGB-plus-predicted-depth training will underperform RGB-only on transparent classes by a measurable margin (2-plus IoU) while improving or matching on opaque classes in the same benchmark.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the same model on a dataset containing both transparent and opaque classes, with and without a monocular-depth input channel; report per-class deltas.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days: paired training on one mixed-class dataset.
main_risk: Result depends on which depth model is used; needs 2 depth predictors to claim generality.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Mirror-versus-window confusion is auto-diagnosable: check whether the predicted region contains the camera-side scene.
problem: Models confuse mirrors (reflective) with windows/glass (transmissive), but there is no automatic way to know which confusion occurred, so error analyses stay manual.
core_hypothesis: The content inside a mirror region correlates with the camera-side scene while window content does not; a simple content-matching probe can label each error as mirror-type or window-type without human review.
why_important: Turns a manual failure-analysis chore into an automatic mining tool for reflective/transmissive confusions, enabling large-scale audits.
why_possibly_novel: Mirror detection research exists; using camera-side content correlation as an automatic error-attribution tool for segmentation failures seems new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature similarity may be dominated by style (indoor lighting) making everything look correlated, collapsing the probe's discrimination.
default_community_belief: Mirror/window disambiguation is treated as needing dedicated architectures; error attribution is done by manual inspection.
falsifiable_prediction: A retrieval-style probe (feature similarity between the predicted region and the rest of the image versus an inpainted scene extension) will classify mirror-vs-window regions with over 80 percent accuracy against human labels.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect 200 mirror and 200 window instances from public datasets, run the probe, validate attribution accuracy against labels.
fastest_falsification: One day with existing mirror and glass datasets and a frozen feature extractor.
main_risk: Wide-angle scenes where the mirror reflects content also visible to the camera break the correlation logic.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Clicking the rim of a glass yields far better SAM masks than clicking its center, the reverse of opaque objects, motivating class-conditional prompt policies.
problem: Prompt-placement heuristics (click the center) are inherited from opaque objects and may be systematically wrong for transparent ones.
core_hypothesis: The rim is the only region whose features belong to the glass; center clicks land on transmitted background features and prompt the wrong object.
why_important: Immediately deployable guidance for SAM-assisted annotation of transparent objects, and a building block for learned prompt-placement policies.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-position studies exist in aggregate; the predicted sign flip conditioned on material class appears undocumented.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM's prompt encoding may spread attention broadly enough that placement inside the instance barely matters.
default_community_belief: Center-of-mass clicks are the default assumed-optimal single prompt for any instance.
falsifiable_prediction: Rim-band clicks will beat centroid clicks by at least 15 IoU points on transparent instances, while centroid beats rim on opaque instances in the same images.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a transparent-object dataset, evaluate centroid vs rim-band vs random-interior prompts with SAM; repeat on opaque controls from the same scenes.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 50 transparent instances, two prompt policies, compare.
main_risk: Rim clicks may snap to the background object boundary instead (shared contour), capping rim-prompt gains.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Liquid fill level flips the topology of SAM's glass masks (full = one blob, empty = ring), a controllable axis for systematic failure mining.
problem: Failure mining lacks controllable, physically meaningful axes; fill level is a cheap real-world dial that plausibly modulates segmentation topology.
core_hypothesis: Liquid changes interior appearance from transmissive to refractive-opaque, so the model's implicit grouping switches regimes at a predictable fill threshold, producing topology errors rather than smooth degradation.
why_important: Demonstrates a template for physical-parameter failure mining (dial a real variable, observe discrete model regime shifts), applicable beyond glassware.
why_possibly_novel: Fill level as a controlled experimental variable for segmentation failure analysis appears absent from the literature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Topology may vary chaotically with viewpoint and lighting, showing no consistent fill threshold.
default_community_belief: Failure cases are mined by scraping hard examples from the wild, not by physically parameterized lab sweeps.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping fill from 0 to 100 percent on fixed glasses will show a discrete switch in predicted mask topology (Euler number change) for most glasses, at a fill level that is consistent within glass type.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Photograph 10 glasses at 5 fill levels on a fixed rig, run fixed prompts, record mask topology and IoU vs fill.
fastest_falsification: One afternoon with a tripod, 3 glasses, water, and 5 fill levels.
main_risk: Effects may be dominated by liquid color/turbidity rather than fill geometry, requiring the sweep to fix liquid type.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: An RGB-to-polarization-cue predictor, trained once on a small polarized dataset, transfers as a frozen adapter that improves transparent segmentation everywhere.
problem: Polarization strongly reveals glass but requires special hardware, so it is ignored by mainstream pipelines that run on ordinary RGB.
core_hypothesis: The mapping from RGB context to coarse polarization cues (where degree-of-polarization is likely high) is learnable, and even a coarse predicted cue channel carries glass evidence that RGB features lack.
why_important: If physics cues can be distilled from small paired datasets into RGB-only predictors, a whole family of hardware-bound signals becomes software.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-modal distillation is established; distilling polarization specifically as a portable adapter for transparency, evaluated on standard RGB benchmarks, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Degree-of-polarization depends on light geometry unobservable from single RGB images, so the predictor may only learn dataset-specific correlations that do not transfer.
default_community_belief: Polarization is a hardware modality; without the sensor, the cue is considered unavailable.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding the predicted-polarization channel to a transparent-object segmenter will improve IoU by a margin that survives ablation against an equal-capacity randomly initialized extra channel, on datasets with no polarization data.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the cue predictor on any available polarized image set, freeze it, bolt onto a small segmenter, run the ablation-controlled comparison on one RGB transparent benchmark.
fastest_falsification: Three GPU-days: small predictor, small segmenter, one benchmark with ablation control.
main_risk: Predicted polarization may just re-encode highlights already visible in RGB, adding no independent information.

judge_flags.reason: RGB-to-polarization predictor + segmenter pairing; an RGB-derived cue cannot add information beyond RGB (data-processing inequality), so 'carries evidence RGB features lack' is ill-posed as stated.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: IoU hides the worst failure on fences and meshes: models output topologically solid masks for perforated objects, measurable by Euler-number mismatch.
problem: Thin semi-transparent lattices (fences, screens, meshes) are scored with region IoU, which barely penalizes filling all the holes, so benchmarks reward topologically wrong answers.
core_hypothesis: Models trained and evaluated with area metrics learn to fill perforations; a topology-aware metric will reveal near-universal failure invisible to IoU, and topology-aware training will fix it at small IoU cost.
why_important: For robotics and AR, filled masks of see-through lattices cause wrong occlusion and grasping decisions; the metric blind spot actively steers the field wrong.
why_possibly_novel: Topology metrics exist in medical imaging; importing Euler-mismatch auditing to transparent lattice classes and quantifying the IoU-topology dissociation appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern high-resolution models may already preserve perforations more than expected, making the mismatch rare.
default_community_belief: IoU (plus boundary F) is considered sufficient to characterize segmentation quality across categories.
falsifiable_prediction: On mesh-like instances, over 80 percent of predicted masks will have Euler numbers differing from GT by an order of magnitude, while IoU for the same masks looks acceptable (above 0.6).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select mesh/fence instances from public datasets, compute IoU and Euler mismatch for a few models' predictions, plot the dissociation.
fastest_falsification: One day, mostly spent relabeling 30 mesh instances with true perforations.
main_risk: GT annotations themselves often fill the holes, making honest topology evaluation impossible without relabeling a subset.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Fire masks track the sensor's saturation contour, not the flame: exposure bracketing moves the predicted boundary.
problem: Flame cores clip to pixel maximum, so the image contains a sensor artifact boundary that may be what models actually segment, making fire extent estimates camera-dependent.
core_hypothesis: Models anchor fire boundaries on the clipped-highlight contour because it is the highest-contrast edge available; change exposure and the model's fire changes size accordingly.
why_important: Fire-size estimates feed fire-spread models and alarm severity levels; exposure-coupled masks make those estimates artifacts of camera settings.
why_possibly_novel: Exposure sensitivity of fire segmentation, with the saturation-contour tracking mechanism, appears unmeasured; datasets rarely include bracketed captures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may key on flame color gradients outside the clipped core, keeping masks stable across exposure.
default_community_belief: Fire is considered an easy bright-object segmentation case; masks are assumed to reflect flame extent, not sensor clipping.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a plus-minus 2EV exposure bracket of the same flame, predicted fire mask area will vary by over 30 percent, tracking the saturation contour area, while human annotations of flame extent vary far less.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture (or find HDR footage of) flames with bracketed exposures, run a fire segmenter on each bracket frame, correlate predicted area with saturated-pixel area.
fastest_falsification: One evening with a gas stove, tripod, manual exposure bracketing, and any fire segmentation model.
main_risk: Auto-exposure in most footage prevents clean brackets; may need a small controlled burn or gas stove capture session.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Lens bloom halos are systematically included in fire masks, and a cheap deglaring preprocessor removes most of the over-segmentation.
problem: On cheap CCTV optics, bright flames produce glare halos; whether models count halo as fire determines large area errors, but nobody attributes error to optics vs model.
core_hypothesis: Since training data mixes halo-annotated and halo-excluded labels, models split the difference and include halo probabilistically, inflating masks most on the cheapest cameras.
why_important: Separates optics-induced error from model error, and offers a deployment fix that requires no retraining of the segmenter.
why_possibly_novel: Glare-aware evaluation of fire segmentation appears absent; optics quality is not a variable in any fire benchmark I am aware of.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Halo pixels may genuinely help detection recall at night, so removing them could hurt the metric that matters (event detection).
default_community_belief: Fire over-segmentation is attributed to model coarseness; optical glare is treated as noise rather than a structured, correctable error source.
falsifiable_prediction: Predicted-fire over-extension will correlate positively with a glare-extent estimate (from streak/halo detectors) across cameras, and applying a deglaring network before segmentation will cut over-segmentation by half without hurting recall.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Film the same flame with a clean lens and a smeared/cheap lens, compare mask inflation, then test a deglaring preprocessor on the smeared footage.
fastest_falsification: One afternoon: same flame, clean vs petroleum-jelly-smeared filter, compare masks.
main_risk: Deglaring may erase faint true flame regions along with halo, trading precision for recall in a way that nets zero.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Video fire models ignore flame flicker entirely: temporal downsampling to 5fps costs them nothing, proving the strongest physical cue goes unused.
problem: Flame flicker (roughly 10Hz and harmonics) is a classic handcrafted fire cue, but it is unknown whether end-to-end video models exploit it or average it away.
core_hypothesis: Standard video architectures with frame-rate-agnostic training smooth over flicker frequencies, so their fire evidence is purely appearance-based and frame rate has almost no effect.
why_important: Shows a concrete case where end-to-end learning fails to discover a known physical signal, and provides the cheap fix (handcrafted spectral channel).
why_possibly_novel: Flicker features are pre-deep-learning lore; the falsifiable claim that modern video models do not use flicker, tested via frame-rate ablation, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models might exploit flicker via inter-frame differences even at coarse rates, so downsampling could hurt more than predicted.
default_community_belief: End-to-end video models are assumed to learn whatever temporal cues matter, given enough data.
falsifiable_prediction: Reducing input frame rate from 30 to 5fps will change video fire segmentation IoU by under 2 points, while adding an explicit per-pixel temporal-spectrum feature will improve it by more than 5 points on hard (small, distant) fires.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one video segmenter at 30/15/5fps on fire clips; then retrain with a flicker-band energy channel and compare on small-fire subsets.
fastest_falsification: One day: frame-rate ablation on existing fire video clips with one pretrained video segmenter.
main_risk: Rolling shutter and video compression already distort flicker, so even the handcrafted channel may find little exploitable signal in real footage.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: A two-layer MLP on raw chromaticity rivals fine-tuned foundation models for daytime flame pixels at a thousandth of the compute.
problem: The field assumes fire segmentation needs deep semantics, but flame pixels may be almost linearly separable in chroma space, making heavy models unjustified for the flame-pixel part of the task.
core_hypothesis: Daytime flame color occupies a compact chromaticity locus few natural materials enter; most of what deep models add is context filtering of the few chroma impostors.
why_important: Right-sizes the problem: if chroma does 90 percent of the work, edge devices need only a tiny impostor-rejection module, not a foundation model.
why_possibly_novel: Color-rule fire detectors are classic; the honest head-to-head against modern fine-tuned VFMs with an impostor-stratified analysis appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Smoke occlusion, motion blur, and white-hot cores may push many flame pixels off the chroma locus, letting the VFM win everywhere.
default_community_belief: Simple color baselines are considered obsolete and are rarely run against modern models under matched protocols.
falsifiable_prediction: A pixelwise chroma MLP will reach within 10 IoU points of a fine-tuned VFM on daytime flame segmentation, and the VFM's advantage will concentrate entirely in impostor-heavy scenes (sunsets, orange objects).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the chroma MLP and fine-tune a VFM segmenter on the same fire dataset; evaluate both, stratifying test scenes by presence of fire-colored distractors.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day: both models on one dataset with a distractor-tagged eval split.
main_risk: Public fire datasets over-represent easy large flames, flattering the MLP; needs a hard-scene subset to be meaningful.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Fire reflections on windows, water, and metal are the dominant false-positive class of fire segmenters, and they are separable by context, not appearance.
problem: Fire false positives are reported in aggregate; if reflections dominate, appearance-only improvements will never fix them because reflections are appearance-identical to fire.
core_hypothesis: Reflected fire matches real fire in chroma and flicker, so appearance models must fail; the separating signal is contextual (support surface, geometry, paired source visibility).
why_important: Redirects false-alarm reduction from appearance tuning to context modeling, and defines a hard-negative category worth dedicated collection.
why_possibly_novel: Reflection FPs are anecdotal in fire-alarm practice; quantifying their share and proving in-feature-space inseparability appears novel.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Slight polarization, blur, and geometry cues might leak into deep features, making reflections separable in-feature after all.
default_community_belief: False positives are treated as a data problem: collect more hard negatives and retrain, assuming appearance separability exists.
falsifiable_prediction: In an FP audit of any deployed fire model on urban footage, reflection FPs will account for over 30 percent of high-confidence errors, and their embeddings will be inseparable from true fire (probe AUROC under 0.6) while surface-context features separate them (AUROC over 0.8).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a fire segmenter over footage rich in glass and water at night, manually audit top-500 FPs into categories, probe separability in feature space vs with context features.
fastest_falsification: One day auditing FPs of any public fire model on night city footage.
main_risk: The FP mixture depends heavily on footage domain; the 30 percent share may hold for cities and fail for forests.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Fire segmentation is secretly two different tasks split by scene luminance, and a hard day/night gate with two heads beats one unified head.
problem: Single models are trained for fire across all lighting, but the cue structure inverts between day (fire is a textured colored region) and night (fire is the light source), possibly causing destructive averaging.
core_hypothesis: Day and night fire occupy nearly disjoint feature regimes; a unified head compromises both, while trivially gating on mean scene luminance lets two specialized heads each exploit their regime.
why_important: A cheap architectural pattern for any class whose appearance regime flips with illumination (fire, headlights, emergency strobes), plus a diagnostic for regime-averaging harm.
why_possibly_novel: Mixture-of-experts is standard; the specific claim that scene luminance is the single dominant gating variable for fire, verifiable with a trivial gate, appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The unified model may already implement a soft gate internally, leaving no headroom for the explicit version.
default_community_belief: One sufficiently large model is assumed to internalize lighting regimes without explicit gating.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched parameters, the gated two-head model will beat the unified model by at least 4 IoU points overall, with the gain concentrated in the dimmest and brightest scene quintiles.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Split any fire dataset by scene luminance, train unified vs luminance-gated two-head versions of the same model, compare per-quintile IoU.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days: paired training on one dataset with luminance-stratified evaluation.
main_risk: Twilight and mixed-lighting scenes straddle the gate; a hard gate may create a new failure band at the threshold.

judge_flags.reason: Two heads + luminance gate is a mixture-of-experts architecture permutation.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Training fire models with amodal labels (fire extent including smoke-occluded parts) improves even the visible-flame segmentation.
problem: Fires self-occlude with their own smoke; models trained on visible-flame labels learn fragmented, unstable fire concepts that flicker with occlusion.
core_hypothesis: Amodal supervision forces the model to bind flame fragments into one physical fire, and this binding regularizes visible-region predictions too.
why_important: Counterintuitive supervision transfer with practical payoff: amodal labels are cheap to add (annotators extrapolate) and would improve the metric everyone already uses.
why_possibly_novel: Amodal segmentation is studied for rigid objects; amodal supervision for self-occluding emissive phenomena, with the modal-improvement claim, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The model may learn to overpredict fire under any smoke, wrecking precision in smoke-without-fire scenes.
default_community_belief: Labels should match the desired output; training on unobservable extent is seen as injecting hallucination.
falsifiable_prediction: A model trained with amodal fire masks will beat the modal-trained model on modal (visible-only) evaluation by 3-plus IoU points on heavily smoke-occluded scenes, not just on amodal metrics.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Relabel 500 smoky fire images with amodal extent, train modal vs amodal versions of one model, evaluate both on a modal-labeled occlusion-stratified test set.
fastest_falsification: Three days including the relabeling sprint on a small subset.
main_risk: Amodal fire extent is poorly defined even for humans; annotator variance may swamp the effect.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: White-hot flame cores are segmented worse than colored flame edges because saturated white matches sky, lights, and paper in feature space.
problem: Within-flame error structure is unexamined: models may systematically miss the hottest (whitest) core regions while finding colored fringes, inverting the physical importance ordering.
core_hypothesis: Saturated white pixels carry no chromatic fire evidence and match many benign classes, so per-pixel fire probability dips inside the core, producing donut-shaped predictions.
why_important: Core misses corrupt fire-intensity estimates and downstream severity triage; the donut signature is also an easy automatic failure-mining probe.
why_possibly_novel: Within-instance radial error profiles for fire appear unreported; standard metrics average over the instance and hide the donut.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Context aggregation in modern decoders may fill cores reliably, making donuts rare curiosities rather than a systematic failure.
default_community_belief: The bright core is assumed to be the easy part of fire; misses are expected at wispy flame edges instead.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-pixel recall as a function of distance from flame center will be non-monotonic (lower at core than at mid-flame) for most models, and donut-topology predictions will appear in over 20 percent of large-flame instances.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On large-flame instances from public sets, compute radial recall profiles and count hole-in-mask topologies across 3 models.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: radial recall profile on 50 large flames with one model.
main_risk: GT masks may themselves exclude blown-out cores inconsistently, confounding the measurement.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Binary masks are a category error for smoke: training as alpha matting and thresholding afterward beats direct binary training even on binary IoU.
problem: Smoke is a continuous density field forced into binary labels, and it is unknown whether the binarization should happen in the label space (status quo) or the output space (matting).
core_hypothesis: Binary targets make the model waste capacity memorizing arbitrary annotator thresholds; a soft-target model learns the density field and any threshold of it beats the binary model at its own game.
why_important: Would flip the default output format for all amorphous classes and reframe dozens of smoke-segmentation papers as optimizing the wrong objective.
why_possibly_novel: Matting for smoke has been attempted; the specific claim that soft training wins on the binary metric itself, under matched capacity and data, appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Soft targets dilute gradient signal at decision-relevant pixels, so the binary model may remain better exactly at the threshold that matters.
default_community_belief: Match the training target to the evaluation format: binary metrics imply binary training targets.
falsifiable_prediction: A matting-style model trained on soft pseudo-alpha (from composites or annotator averaging), thresholded at a single global value, will beat an identically sized binary-trained model on binary IoU on the same test set.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build soft targets by averaging 3 annotators (or via composites), train soft vs binary variants of one model, evaluate both with binary IoU at swept thresholds.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days using composite-generated alpha as soft targets on one dataset.
main_risk: Obtaining honest soft targets at scale is the bottleneck; annotator-average alpha on real smoke is expensive.

judge_flags.title: Binary masks are a category error for smoke; matting formulation wins even on binary IoU

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Humans disagree on binary smoke boundaries but agree on relative opacity ordering, so ranking annotation is the consistent (and cheaper) protocol.
problem: Smoke annotation is noisy and expensive, and the noise may be an artifact of asking a question (where is the boundary) that has no answer, rather than of task difficulty.
core_hypothesis: The perceptual quantity humans share about smoke is ordinal density (patch A is smokier than patch B), so pairwise comparisons will show high inter-annotator agreement where binary boundaries show low agreement.
why_important: Annotation protocol redesign is the highest-leverage intervention for a data-starved field; consistency determines everything downstream.
why_possibly_novel: Ranking-based annotation is known in aesthetics and depth; applying it to scattering-media segmentation with an agreement-vs-protocol study appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pairwise comparisons scale quadratically and per-comparison cost may eat the claimed budget advantage.
default_community_belief: Segmentation annotation means drawing masks; protocol alternatives are considered exotic and are rarely costed against mask drawing.
falsifiable_prediction: Inter-annotator agreement for pairwise patch opacity comparisons will exceed 85 percent while binary boundary agreement (boundary F between annotators) on the same images stays low, and a model trained on rankings will match binary-trained models using half the annotation budget.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Have 5 annotators do both protocols on 50 images; measure agreement per protocol; train a small ranking-supervised model vs binary baseline at matched labeling hours.
fastest_falsification: Two days with 3 annotators on 30 images comparing agreement statistics only.
main_risk: Converting ordinal labels to a dense mask still requires calibration anchors, reintroducing some binary-style decisions.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Chroma-keyed real smoke composited over new backgrounds gives exact alpha supervision that beats hand-annotated wild data of equal size.
problem: Hand-annotated smoke labels are noisy binary approximations; lab-captured plumes over known backing give physically exact alpha, but nobody has tested which data source trains better wild-smoke models.
core_hypothesis: Label exactness beats domain authenticity for smoke: exact-alpha composites teach density structure that noisy wild labels cannot, and background randomization covers the domain gap.
why_important: Would redirect data investment from annotation farms to one-time capture rigs, a large cost restructuring for the field.
why_possibly_novel: Smoke compositing for augmentation exists; the controlled composites-vs-wild-labels head-to-head at matched budget, evaluated on consensus-relabeled wild data, appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Composite images have telltale statistics (lighting mismatch) that models exploit as shortcuts, then fail in the wild.
default_community_belief: Real in-domain data with human labels is assumed to beat any composite/synthetic source at equal volume.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched image counts, a model trained on exact-alpha composites will beat a wild-binary-trained model on a held-out wild test set relabeled by annotator consensus, on both soft and binary metrics.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or source chroma-keyed plume footage, composite 5k images, train paired models (composite vs 5k wild-labeled), evaluate on a common consensus test set.
fastest_falsification: Three GPU-days plus one day of compositing using any existing keyed smoke stock footage.
main_risk: Lab plumes (smoke machines) differ physically from combustion smoke in color and dynamics, capping transfer.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: A frozen pretrained dehazing network's transmission map, inverted and thresholded, is a zero-training smoke segmenter competitive with trained baselines.
problem: Smoke segmentation and image dehazing model the same physics (scattering media) from opposite directions, yet the fields do not share tools; a strong free baseline may be sitting unused.
core_hypothesis: Dehazing networks already estimate per-pixel transmission (one minus smoke alpha under a scattering model), so their intermediate output is a smoke density map obtained with zero smoke-specific training.
why_important: A strong zero-training baseline recalibrates the field's sense of progress and provides free pseudo-labels for bootstrapping.
why_possibly_novel: The physics link is obvious in hindsight but I am not aware of dehazing transmission maps being evaluated as smoke segmenters.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transmission estimates may be so entangled with scene depth (hazier equals farther) that the map segments distance, not smoke.
default_community_belief: Task-specific training is assumed necessary; adjacent-field models are not considered candidate baselines for segmentation papers.
falsifiable_prediction: Thresholded inverse-transmission from an off-the-shelf dehazing model will achieve at least 70 percent of the IoU of dedicated trained smoke segmenters on at least one public smoke benchmark.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run 2 public dehazing models on a smoke test set, extract transmission, sweep one threshold, report IoU against dedicated baselines.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: one dehazing model, one smoke dataset, one threshold sweep.
main_risk: Dehazing models assume global atmospheric haze and may suppress or distort localized dense plumes, breaking the transmission estimate exactly on-target.

judge_flags.title: Frozen dehazing transmission map as zero-training smoke segmenter

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: On static cameras, smoke alpha is recoverable unsupervised by decomposing each frame into a background layer plus a smoke overlay constrained by neighboring frames.
problem: Unsupervised smoke extraction from video is unsolved, yet static-camera footage (most CCTV) massively overdetermines the problem via temporal background redundancy.
core_hypothesis: With background estimated from temporal medians, per-pixel smoke alpha and color follow from a two-layer compositing equation solved per frame with smoothness priors, no labels needed.
why_important: Unlocks unlimited pseudo-alpha supervision from ordinary surveillance archives, feeding every other soft-supervision idea in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: Background subtraction for smoke exists as detection; solving explicitly for continuous alpha via the compositing equation with temporal background appears less explored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Smoke color is unknown per pixel, making the decomposition underdetermined where smoke is thick, exactly where accuracy matters for alarms.
default_community_belief: Continuous alpha is assumed to require matting supervision or special capture; classical background models are used only for binary change masks.
falsifiable_prediction: The analysis-by-synthesis alpha will achieve rank correlation above 0.7 with composited GT alpha on synthetic static-camera sequences, and thresholding it will beat zero-shot SAM on real static-camera smoke clips.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement median-background plus per-pixel alpha solve on synthetic composites over static backgrounds, measure alpha recovery, then eyeball-transfer to 20 real CCTV smoke clips.
fastest_falsification: Two days: synthetic static-camera benchmark plus the closed-form solve.
main_risk: Auto-exposure drift, shadows, and moving non-smoke objects violate the two-layer model and may dominate errors in real footage.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Models trained on binary smoke labels are confidently wrong in the transition band; disagreement-weighted label smoothing fixes calibration for free.
problem: Alarm systems consume smoke-probability maps, but the probability outputs of binary-trained models in ambiguous regions may be meaningless, and nobody measures band-local calibration.
core_hypothesis: Cross-entropy on hard labels in the ambiguous band teaches arbitrary high-confidence outputs there; smoothing labels in proportion to annotator disagreement restores honest probabilities without hurting core accuracy.
why_important: Downstream alarm thresholds assume calibrated probabilities; band miscalibration converts directly into false alarms or missed early smoke.
why_possibly_novel: Label smoothing and calibration are standard tools; targeting them at annotator-disagreement structure of amorphous boundaries, with band-local ECE as the metric, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Global temperature scaling after training might fix band ECE just as well, making the training-time fix redundant.
default_community_belief: Calibration is evaluated globally if at all; segmentation training recipes ignore where label noise is concentrated.
falsifiable_prediction: Expected calibration error computed only within the boundary band will be at least 3x the core-region ECE for hard-label models, and disagreement-weighted smoothing will cut band ECE by half with under 1 point IoU change.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-annotator smoke subset, train hard vs disagreement-smoothed models, report band-local and core-local ECE plus IoU.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day given any triple-annotated smoke subset (even 100 images).
