main_risk: Requires multi-annotator data; simulating disagreement via boundary distance may bake in the conclusion.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Off-the-shelf hair/fur matting models, given a trimap from a coarse smoke detector, outperform dedicated smoke segmentation architectures.
problem: Smoke segmentation reinvents soft-boundary machinery that the matting community perfected for hair and fur; the recomposition (detector for where, matting for how much) is untested.
core_hypothesis: Matting models encode generic soft-transition priors that transfer to smoke; localization is the only smoke-specific part, and a weak detector suffices for it.
why_important: Decomposing the task changes what needs to be researched (only the detector) and imports a mature toolchain for free.
why_possibly_novel: Matting-for-smoke exists in graphics contexts; the zero-smoke-training transfer claim with a detector-generated trimap pipeline appears new for recognition benchmarks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Trimap quality from a weak detector may bottleneck the pipeline so hard that end-to-end wins regardless of matting quality.
default_community_belief: Task-specific end-to-end models are assumed to dominate; pipeline recomposition with frozen cross-task modules is out of fashion.
falsifiable_prediction: Coarse-detector-plus-frozen-matting pipelines will beat end-to-end smoke segmenters on boundary-band accuracy (measured against consensus labels) on at least one public benchmark, without any smoke-specific matting training.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate trimaps by dilating/eroding a weak smoke detector's masks, run 2 public matting models, compare band-accuracy against 2 dedicated smoke models.
fastest_falsification: One day: trimap generation plus frozen matting on 50 test images.
main_risk: Matting priors are tuned to thin structures with hard cores (hair); smoke's everywhere-soft structure may violate their assumptions.

judge_flags.reason: Coarse detector + off-the-shelf matting model is a Module A+B pipeline as stated.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Smoke density estimates from cross-lens parallax on dual-camera phones give free weak supervision for opacity.
problem: Opacity supervision is scarce; billions of dual-lens phone captures encode small-baseline parallax that interacts measurably with translucent media, an untapped label source.
core_hypothesis: For semi-transparent smoke, cross-view correspondence confidence degrades in proportion to opacity (background match visible through thin smoke, lost in thick smoke), yielding an ordinal opacity signal from stereo matching residuals.
why_important: Opens a passive, hardware-free (for phone data) supervision channel for a data-starved problem.
why_possibly_novel: Stereo through scattering media is studied in physics-based vision; harvesting matching-confidence as weak opacity labels for learning appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Small phone baselines may make parallax effects smaller than sensor noise for typical smoke distances.
default_community_belief: Opacity labels must come from annotation or synthesis; passive geometric cues for translucency are not part of the supervision toolbox.
falsifiable_prediction: Stereo-matching confidence maps over smoke will correlate (rank correlation above 0.5) with composited GT alpha in controlled dual-view captures, enough to serve as weak supervision that measurably improves a downstream matting model.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture dual-view smoke scenes (two phones on a bar), compute matching-confidence maps, correlate with composite-calibrated alpha, then train a model with and without this weak signal.
fastest_falsification: One day with two phones, a smoke machine, and an off-the-shelf stereo matcher.
main_risk: Textureless backgrounds destroy matching confidence with or without smoke, confounding the signal in many real scenes.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: On static cameras, a thresholded per-pixel temporal-variance map beats zero-shot SAM at smoke segmentation, an embarrassing baseline the field skips.
problem: Papers benchmark heavy models on single frames while most deployment cameras are static and video-rich; the strength of trivial temporal baselines is unreported, so claimed progress may not clear it.
core_hypothesis: Smoke's defining wild signature is sustained low-amplitude temporal variation over otherwise static background, which a variance filter captures better than any single-frame appearance model.
why_important: Establishes the honest floor for video smoke work; anything below this baseline is negative progress regardless of architecture novelty.
why_possibly_novel: Motion cues for smoke are classic; positioning temporal variance as a formal adversarial baseline against foundation models, with published numbers, appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern zero-shot models may handle dense smoke well enough that the variance map only wins on thin wisps, netting a smaller or reversed gap.
default_community_belief: Foundation models are assumed to dominate hand-crafted signals across settings, so trivial baselines are omitted from comparisons.
falsifiable_prediction: A 2-second per-pixel standard-deviation map with one learned threshold will exceed zero-shot SAM's smoke IoU on static-camera clips by at least 10 points, while costing six orders of magnitude less compute.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 50 static-camera smoke clips with masks on selected frames, run the variance baseline and zero-shot SAM, report IoU and compute.
fastest_falsification: Half a day on 20 clips with existing annotations.
main_risk: Any camera shake or moving foliage floods the variance map; the baseline may only win on tripod-clean footage.

judge_flags.title: Temporal-variance map beats zero-shot SAM on static cameras

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Memory-based video segmenters shrink smoke masks over time: memory anchors to the dense core and refuses the plume's diffuse growth.
problem: Video object segmentation assumes the target maintains appearance identity, but smoke grows, thins, and disperses, and how memory mechanisms cope is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Feature memory built from early dense-smoke frames matches poorly to later diffuse smoke, so masks progressively under-segment as the plume evolves, with error growing monotonically in time.
why_important: Time-correlated under-segmentation means alarm severity is underestimated exactly as fires grow, the worst possible error correlation for safety.
why_possibly_novel: Video-tracker drift is studied for objects; the systematic directional bias (shrinkage on growing scattering media) and its safety implication appear unexamined.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Memory updating may actually chase the diffuse boundary outward, causing over-segmentation instead; either direction is informative but refutes shrinkage.
default_community_belief: Video memory models are assumed to handle gradual appearance change via memory updates; drift is treated as symmetric noise, not directional bias.
falsifiable_prediction: For SAM2-style trackers initialized on frame one, the ratio of predicted to GT mask area will decay with clip time, losing at least 30 percent by 30 seconds on growing plumes, while solid-object tracks show no such trend.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a memory-based video segmenter on 30 growing-plume clips with sparse GT frames, plot area ratio and IoU vs time, compare against rigid-object controls.
fastest_falsification: One day: 10 clips, area-ratio-vs-time plot.
main_risk: Ground-truthing plume growth needs annotation of late diffuse frames, which is itself unreliable, muddying the trend measurement.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Topology-change frames (plume splitting or merging) account for the majority of video smoke tracking failures, a countable and mineable event class.
problem: Tracking metrics average over frames, hiding whether failures are diffuse or concentrated at discrete physical events like splits and merges that violate object-permanence assumptions.
core_hypothesis: Video segmenters carry a one-target-one-blob prior; frames where smoke topology changes force a model decision that usually breaks the track, so failures cluster tightly around these events.
why_important: Turns amorphous-target tracking failure from a vague deficiency into a specific, detectable event class that architectures can be designed and tested against.
why_possibly_novel: Identity switches are studied in multi-object tracking of discrete objects; topology-change events of continuous media as the failure driver appears unformalized.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Failures may instead concentrate at contrast minima (smoke passing in front of matching backgrounds), swamping any topology effect.
default_community_belief: Tracking failures on hard targets are attributed to appearance ambiguity in general, without a discrete-event failure model.
falsifiable_prediction: Aligning failure onsets (IoU drop over 0.2) with automatically detected topology-change frames will show over 60 percent of failures within 1 second of such events, versus under 20 percent expected under uniform failure timing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Detect connected-component count changes in GT (or pseudo-GT) over 30 clips, align with tracker failure onsets, run the timing-concentration test.
fastest_falsification: One day on 10 manually event-annotated clips.
main_risk: Topology changes in pseudo-GT may themselves be segmentation artifacts, creating circularity; needs a manually verified event subset.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Optical-flow divergence separates expanding smoke from moving solid objects, a one-channel cue that cuts moving-object false positives.
problem: Motion-based smoke detectors fire on any moving region (cars, people, flags); the specific kinematic signature of expansion is unused as an explicit discriminator.
core_hypothesis: Smoke plumes exhibit sustained positive flow divergence (sources expanding), while rigid movers show near-zero divergence with strong advection, so a divergence map is a cheap class-evidence channel.
why_important: Moving-object FPs dominate real-world alarm noise on roads and industrial sites; a physics-grounded channel is more robust than appearance patching.
why_possibly_novel: Flow features for smoke exist in older literature; isolating divergence as the load-bearing invariant and quantifying its FP reduction on modern pipelines appears fresh.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Turbulent eddies produce alternating divergence signs that cancel under averaging, leaving little net signal.
default_community_belief: Deep spatiotemporal features are assumed to subsume any handcrafted kinematic quantity worth having.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding a temporal-averaged flow-divergence channel to a motion-based smoke detector will cut moving-object false positives by over 40 percent at fixed recall on mixed traffic-plus-smoke footage.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute flow divergence on smoke and traffic clips, add as input channel to a small detector, compare FP rates at matched recall against the no-divergence baseline.
fastest_falsification: One day: divergence statistics on 20 smoke vs 20 traffic clips, ROC of a threshold rule.
main_risk: Flow estimates inside low-texture smoke are unreliable, so the divergence signal may be noisiest exactly where it is needed.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Classical background subtraction plus SAM prompting (change-blob centroid as click) beats both parts alone, even on stabilized moving-camera footage.
problem: SAM lacks temporal grounding and background models lack shape understanding; the trivial composition is untested as a smoke video baseline, especially off static cameras.
core_hypothesis: Background models solve where (temporal anomaly) and SAM solves what shape (spatial support), and their errors are nearly independent, so the composition dominates each component.
why_important: Defines a strong, nearly free system baseline for video smoke that new methods must beat, and tests how far stabilization stretches static-camera tricks.
why_possibly_novel: Both components are ancient; the specific composition evaluated as a baseline for amorphous targets on moving cameras appears unreported.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM may reject change-blob prompts that land on thin smoke (see-through failure), inheriting the worst of both components instead of the best.
default_community_belief: Pipeline compositions of classical and foundation components are considered engineering, not research, so they go unmeasured and unpublished.
falsifiable_prediction: The hybrid will beat background subtraction alone by over 10 IoU (shape quality) and SAM-with-grid-prompts alone by over 10 IoU (localization), and retain most of its margin after electronic stabilization on handheld clips.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement median-background change detection, feed blob centroids to SAM as prompts, evaluate on static and stabilized handheld smoke clips against both components.
fastest_falsification: One day: hybrid vs components on 20 static clips.
main_risk: Stabilization residual motion may flood the change mask on handheld video, restricting the claim back to static cameras.

judge_flags.reason: Background subtraction + SAM prompting is the classic classical-CV+SAM combo.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: A two-band temporal filter (high-frequency flicker for fire, low-frequency drift for smoke) improves joint fire-smoke segmentation more than doubling model size.
problem: Fire and smoke have oppositely structured temporal signatures, but shared video backbones process both with one temporal receptive strategy, potentially serving neither.
core_hypothesis: Explicitly decomposing input video into fast (5-15Hz) and slow (0.1-1Hz) band energies hands each class its natural evidence channel, worth more than generic capacity.
why_important: A compute-free accuracy trade that matters for edge deployment, and a demonstration that class-specific temporal priors beat brute scale for periodic-vs-drift phenomena.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal filtering for fire is classic; the band-split-versus-scale controlled trade-off on modern architectures appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The learned model may already recover band structure internally, so the explicit channels add redundancy, not information.
default_community_belief: Scaling model capacity is the default lever; input-space temporal engineering is assumed subsumed by learned spatiotemporal kernels.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding the two band-energy channels to a small video segmenter will improve joint fire-plus-smoke mean IoU more than replacing the backbone with one of double the parameters, at equal training data.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train small model, small model plus band channels, and 2x model on the same fire-smoke video data; compare mean IoU and per-class deltas.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days for the three-arm training on one dataset.
main_risk: Video compression at typical bitrates may have already destroyed the high band, nullifying the fire channel on real footage.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Video smoke segmenters fall off a cliff below 10fps, a silent killer since most CCTV records at 1-5fps.
problem: Academic video models are trained and tested at 24-30fps while deployment cameras often store 1-5fps; the degradation curve across this gap is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: Temporal modules learn motion statistics tuned to training frame intervals; smoke's slow drift becomes temporal aliasing at low fps, breaking learned correspondences non-gracefully below a threshold.
why_important: Identifies a deployment-fidelity gap that invalidates video-model gains for the dominant installed camera base, and motivates frame-rate augmentation as standard practice.
why_possibly_novel: Frame-rate robustness is studied for action recognition; the smoke-specific degradation curve and its comparison against static baselines appear unmeasured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Smoke moves slowly enough that even 1fps may preserve its drift signature, making degradation gentle and the cliff nonexistent.
default_community_belief: Video models are assumed to degrade gracefully with frame rate, and evaluation frame rate is rarely reported at all.
falsifiable_prediction: Performance vs frame rate will show a knee: under 5 points IoU loss from 30 to 10fps, then over 15 additional points lost from 10 to 2fps, while single-frame baselines stay flat by construction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Temporally subsample test clips at 30/10/5/2/1fps, evaluate 2 video smoke models and 1 single-frame model, plot the curves.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: subsample eval of one model at 4 frame rates.
main_risk: Low-fps behavior depends on whether models are also retrained at low fps; both eval-only and retrain arms are needed for a fair claim.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Averaging SAM masks over five registered consecutive frames improves smoke IoU for free: smoke moves coherently while its errors do not.
problem: Zero-shot single-frame smoke masks are noisy, but the cheapest possible temporal aggregation (mask averaging after registration) has no published numbers for amorphous targets.
core_hypothesis: SAM's per-frame errors on smoke are high-variance and weakly correlated across frames, while the true smoke support is temporally coherent, so simple averaging cancels error faster than it blurs signal.
why_important: A zero-training deployment upgrade and a probe of the error-correlation structure of foundation models on unstable targets.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal test-time augmentation is standard elsewhere; its unusual effectiveness regime on amorphous targets (where per-frame variance is extreme) is the untested part.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM's smoke errors may be systematic (same wrong background object every frame), in which case averaging entrenches rather than cancels them.
default_community_belief: Zero-shot failures on hard categories are assumed to need better models, not trivial ensembling of the same model.
falsifiable_prediction: Majority-vote or mean-probability fusion over 5 frames will add at least 8 IoU points over single-frame SAM on static-camera smoke, with gains shrinking but persisting (over 3 points) on stabilized handheld clips.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run SAM per-frame with fixed prompts on 30 clips, fuse over sliding windows of 3/5/9 frames, compare against single-frame on annotated keyframes.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 10 clips, 5-frame fusion, keyframe IoU comparison.
main_risk: Fast-evolving smoke violates the static-support assumption within the window, so window size may trade error cancellation against motion smear with no good setting.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Deep ensembles are confidently and unanimously wrong on smoke: epistemic uncertainty is low where error is highest, proving the failure is bias, not variance.
problem: The fix-it playbook (more data, bigger ensembles) assumes failures are variance-like; if smoke failure is a shared inductive bias, that playbook cannot work and we should know now.
core_hypothesis: All ensemble members inherit the same edge-seeking prior from architecture and pretraining, so they agree on the same wrong smoke masks, yielding low disagreement exactly at systematic failures.
why_important: Distinguishes fixable-by-data failures from architectural bias, redirecting effort from data scaling toward inductive-bias surgery for amorphous targets.
why_possibly_novel: Uncertainty-error decoupling is documented in OOD contexts; pinning it on amorphous targets specifically, with the bias-not-variance diagnosis, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Smoke's ambiguity may inject enough label and prediction noise that disagreement stays high everywhere, restoring the correlation trivially.
default_community_belief: Ensemble disagreement is treated as a reliable error flag, and scaling data or members is assumed to chip away at any failure.
falsifiable_prediction: On smoke pixels with high error, ensemble mutual disagreement will be no higher than on correctly segmented pixels (uncertainty-error correlation below 0.2), whereas on object classes the correlation is substantially positive.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a 5-member ensemble on a smoke dataset, compute pixelwise disagreement and error, compare their correlation against an object-class control ensemble.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days for a small 5-member ensemble on one dataset.
main_risk: Conclusions may be ensemble-recipe dependent (seed-only vs data-resampled ensembles), requiring both variants.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: For rejecting bad smoke masks, max-softmax is beaten by a trivial input statistic (local contrast), an indictment of learned confidence on amorphous targets.
problem: Selective prediction (declining to output when unsure) is the responsible deployment mode, but nobody has checked whether learned confidence even beats input-only statistics for amorphous classes.
core_hypothesis: Learned confidence on smoke reflects the model's miscalibrated self-assessment, while failure is actually driven by measurable input conditions (contrast, clutter), so the input statistic ranks risk better.
why_important: If input statistics outrank learned confidence, deployed systems should gate on cheap image measurements, and confidence research for amorphous classes needs rebooting.
why_possibly_novel: Selective-prediction baselines are standard in classification; the input-statistic-beats-confidence claim for amorphous dense prediction appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Max-softmax may encode contrast implicitly and add model-specific information on top, keeping it ahead.
default_community_belief: Learned confidence, whatever its flaws, is assumed to beat model-blind input heuristics at predicting the model's own errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Risk-coverage curves using local-contrast-based rejection will dominate max-softmax rejection over most coverage levels on smoke segmentation, whereas softmax wins comfortably on object classes.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute both rejection scores on a smoke test set for one model, plot risk-coverage curves, repeat on an object dataset as control.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: both scores plus risk-coverage curves on existing predictions.
main_risk: The best input statistic may vary per dataset, making the claim recipe-dependent unless a fixed statistic wins everywhere.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Training smoke models to also predict the annotator-disagreement map improves the main mask, not just the uncertainty output.
problem: Multi-annotator information is usually collapsed to majority masks, discarding the disagreement structure that might be the most informative supervision about smoke's nature.
core_hypothesis: Predicting disagreement forces the representation to model the density gradient explicitly (disagreement lives where density transitions), which sharpens the main head's boundary decisions.
why_important: Gives a concrete reason to collect and keep multi-annotator smoke labels, changing dataset construction economics.
why_possibly_novel: Auxiliary uncertainty heads exist; sourcing the auxiliary target from human disagreement specifically for amorphous classes, with main-task gain as the claim, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The auxiliary task may steal capacity in small models, hurting rather than helping the main head at practical sizes.
default_community_belief: Annotator disagreement is noise to be averaged out, not a supervision signal worth a dedicated head.
falsifiable_prediction: A two-head model (mask plus disagreement) will beat the single-head model trained on the same majority masks by over 2 points boundary F-score on consensus test labels, with the gain persisting when the disagreement head is discarded at inference.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-annotator smoke dataset, train single-head vs two-head variants, evaluate main-task metrics on consensus labels.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day on a small multi-annotator subset, accepting wide error bars.
main_risk: Multi-annotator smoke datasets are scarce and small; the effect may not reach significance at available scale.

judge_flags.reason: 'Auxiliary head improves main task' is the aux-task-roulette pattern.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Smoke is familiar-but-not-understood: OOD detectors on VFM features call smoke images in-distribution even though task error is OOD-grade.
problem: Deployment safety nets rely on OOD detection to flag inputs the model will fail on; if smoke passes those nets while failing the task, the safety architecture has a hole with a specific shape.
core_hypothesis: Smoke is abundant in pretraining imagery (so feature-density OOD scores look normal) yet unrepresented in mask-supervision structure (so task competence is absent), decoupling familiarity from competence.
why_important: Names and measures a failure category (familiar-incompetent) that current reliability stacks structurally cannot catch, motivating competence-aware flagging.
why_possibly_novel: The distinction between input-distribution familiarity and task competence is discussed abstractly; a concrete measurable demonstration via smoke appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Smoke may actually score as OOD under mask-conditioned scores (energy of decoder outputs), in which case the right stack already catches it.
default_community_belief: OOD scores are treated as a proxy for expected competence: in-distribution implies the model probably works.
falsifiable_prediction: Standard feature-based OOD scores will rank smoke images as more in-distribution than many object images on which the model performs far better, yielding near-zero or negative correlation between OOD score and task error across categories.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute standard OOD scores and per-image task error for mixed categories including smoke; plot score vs error and report the categorical decoupling.
fastest_falsification: One day with precomputed features, 2 OOD scores, and existing error maps.
main_risk: Different OOD methods may disagree; the claim needs 3-plus detector families to survive as a statement about the paradigm rather than one method.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: On smoke benchmarks, model-to-human IoU often exceeds human-to-human IoU, putting reported rankings below the annotation noise floor.
problem: Smoke leaderboards report differences of 1-3 IoU points without ever measuring inter-annotator IoU, so nobody knows whether reported progress is statistically meaningful.
core_hypothesis: For amorphous targets, the annotation noise floor is so high that a large fraction of published method deltas are indistinguishable from relabeling variance.
why_important: Establishes the significance bar for the whole subfield; without it, architecture papers may be publishing noise.
why_possibly_novel: Noise-floor audits exist for some benchmarks (saliency, edges); smoke and fire benchmarks appear never to have been audited this way.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotators given identical detailed instructions may agree far more than expected, validating the benchmarks and refuting the noise-floor concern.
default_community_belief: Benchmark GT is treated as fixed truth, and any IoU improvement is treated as real progress worth publishing.
falsifiable_prediction: On a re-annotated subset of any public smoke benchmark, mean human-human IoU will fall below 0.75, and the confidence interval implied by relabeling variance will cover the gaps between several published method pairs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Have 3 annotators independently relabel 100 test images of one smoke benchmark, compute human-human IoU distribution, compare against published method gaps.
fastest_falsification: Two days: 50 images, 3 annotators, one benchmark.
main_risk: Findings may vary by dataset; a single-benchmark audit invites this-dataset-only dismissals, so 2 benchmarks are safer.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Adding a boundary ignore band to smoke evaluation reorders method rankings, showing current comparisons hinge on unknowable pixels.
problem: Methods may win benchmarks by better matching annotator whims in the ambiguous band rather than by better smoke understanding, and current evaluation cannot tell the difference.
core_hypothesis: A sizable share of inter-method IoU differences is concentrated in the transition band; excluding it flips at least some published orderings, exposing whim-fitting.
why_important: Directly changes how the subfield should score itself; a one-line evaluation change with leaderboard-level consequences.
why_possibly_novel: Ignore-band evaluation exists in matting and some parsing tasks; applying it as a ranking-stability audit for smoke leaderboards appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Method differences may genuinely live in the core (detection ability), leaving rankings stable under band exclusion.
default_community_belief: Rankings are assumed robust to reasonable evaluation-protocol tweaks; the transition band is small enough to ignore.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a set of public smoke models with band-ignore IoU (band width set by annotator disagreement) will change the sign of at least one pairwise ranking among the top methods and shrink average gaps by over 40 percent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate 4-plus public smoke models under standard and band-ignore IoU on one benchmark; compare rankings and gap distributions.
fastest_falsification: Half a day with released predictions or checkpoints of a few methods.
main_risk: If no ranking flips, the result is a (still useful) robustness confirmation rather than a headline finding.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Most of the gap between smoke methods is a global density-threshold offset: one calibrated bias parameter per model erases the SOTA ladder.
problem: Methods are compared as monoliths; if their differences reduce to segmenting at different implicit density cutoffs, the field is comparing thresholds, not understanding.
core_hypothesis: Each model internalizes a different effective opacity threshold from its training labels; aligning thresholds post hoc (one scalar per model, fit on validation) collapses most inter-method differences.
why_important: If true, method development should target detection and shape fidelity, not boundary placement, and papers must report threshold-calibrated comparisons.
why_possibly_novel: Threshold sensitivity is known generally; the claim that it explains the bulk of inter-method variance on amorphous benchmarks is specific and untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may differ mainly in which plumes they find at all, a difference no global threshold can erase.
default_community_belief: IoU differences between methods reflect architectural and training substance, not recoverable scalar offsets.
falsifiable_prediction: After per-model optimal global threshold or mask dilation-erosion calibration, the spread of IoU across published smoke methods will shrink by over half, and the best-vs-median gap will fall within the annotation noise floor.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 5 public smoke models, fit one morphological calibration parameter each on validation, re-evaluate on test, compare calibrated vs raw spreads.
fastest_falsification: One day given saved predictions from a handful of methods.
main_risk: Requires access to several models' outputs; results could differ by benchmark difficulty profile.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Pixel IoU and event-level alarm F1 rank smoke models differently, so the field's metric does not measure the product's objective.
problem: Deployment success is counted in correctly raised and suppressed alarms per video, but research success is counted in pixel overlap; the assumption that one orders models like the other is untested.
core_hypothesis: Event-level performance is dominated by behavior on small early plumes and persistence of detections, which pixel IoU averages away, so the two metrics decouple across models.
why_important: Justifies (or refutes) an event-level benchmark standard for smoke, aligning academic incentives with the safety application paying for the research.
why_possibly_novel: The metric-objective mismatch is folklore in industry; a quantified decoupling study across public models appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models good at pixels may be uniformly good at events too, yielding high correlation and defending the status quo.
default_community_belief: Pixel metrics are treated as the finest-grained truth from which all coarser operational metrics follow monotonically.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a model zoo evaluated on long videos with event annotations, Spearman correlation between pixel IoU and event F1 will be below 0.5, and the IoU-best model will not be the event-F1-best model.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate event windows on 40 long clips, evaluate 5 models for both metrics with a fixed event-matching rule, compute rank correlation.
fastest_falsification: Two days including lightweight event annotation of 20 clips.
main_risk: Event definitions (onset tolerance, minimum duration) inject researcher degrees of freedom; the protocol must be preregistered and sensitivity-analyzed.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Three annotation instructions (visible smoke, hazard-level smoke, plume envelope) produce GTs that differ more than competing architectures do.
problem: Smoke datasets are labeled under unstated definitions of what counts as smoke; the size of the instruction effect relative to the architecture effect has never been measured.
core_hypothesis: The instruction is the largest unacknowledged experimental variable in smoke segmentation: instruction-induced GT variance exceeds the variance across model families trained on any one instruction.
why_important: Forces instruction disclosure as a reporting standard and explains cross-dataset transfer failures as definitional, not distributional.
why_possibly_novel: Instruction effects are studied in NLP annotation; a controlled instruction experiment for amorphous visual GT appears absent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotators may collapse all instructions to the same perceptual routine (label what looks smoky), making instruction variance small.
default_community_belief: Datasets are treated as interchangeable samples of the same underlying task called smoke segmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-instruction GT IoU on identical images will be lower than cross-architecture prediction IoU under a fixed instruction, and a model trained under one instruction will drop over 15 IoU points when evaluated under another.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Label 100 images under 3 instructions with 3 annotators each, quantify instruction vs annotator vs architecture variance components with trained models per instruction.
fastest_falsification: Scaled-down pilot: 30 images, 2 instructions, 2 annotators, variance decomposition.
main_risk: Requires a real annotation budget (about 900 image-labelings); confounds between annotator pools and instructions must be randomized.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: For early smoke smaller than 0.5 percent of the frame, centroid localization error predicts alarm utility; IoU is statistically useless at that scale.
problem: The most safety-relevant smoke instances are tiny, where a few boundary pixels swing IoU wildly, yet evaluation treats all instance sizes with the same overlap metric.
core_hypothesis: At tiny scales, the operationally sufficient statistic is where the model thinks the smoke is (for camera-zoom or human verification), so distance-based localization metrics track downstream utility while IoU tracks pixel luck.
why_important: Fixes evaluation where it matters most (early detection) and would change how tiny-instance performance is reported across smoke papers.
why_possibly_novel: Small-object metric critiques exist for boxes; the utility-anchored validation of alternative metrics for tiny amorphous masks appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Raters may actually punish sloppy extents even at tiny scales, keeping IoU competitive as a utility proxy.
default_community_belief: IoU with size-stratified reporting is considered adequate; metric validity at tiny scales is not questioned.
falsifiable_prediction: For sub-0.5-percent-area instances, correlation between IoU and human-judged alarm usefulness will be near zero, while centroid-distance and hit-or-miss metrics will correlate above 0.6.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect model predictions on tiny-smoke instances, have raters judge usefulness for verification workflows, correlate judgments with candidate metrics.
fastest_falsification: One day: 100 tiny instances, 2 raters, 3 candidate metrics.
main_risk: Usefulness judgments depend on the assumed downstream workflow; needs 2 distinct workflow framings to generalize.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: A density-weighted boundary metric agrees with human judgments of smoke mask quality where standard boundary F-measure fails.
problem: Boundary F-measure assumes a trustworthy GT contour; smoke has none, so the metric punishes defensible boundaries and rewards whim-matching, but no replacement has been validated.
core_hypothesis: Weighting boundary agreement by local GT confidence (annotator agreement or estimated density gradient) yields a metric that orders masks the way humans do on amorphous targets.
why_important: Every amorphous-target paper needs a boundary metric; a validated one becomes core evaluation infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: Weighted metrics exist (trimap-based matting losses); a human-validated boundary metric designed for scattering media appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human orderings on smoke masks may be too inconsistent for any metric to match, capping all metrics at similar agreement.
default_community_belief: Boundary F with a pixel tolerance is considered the finished answer to boundary evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: On triplets of masks per image ranked by humans, the density-weighted metric will match human ordering over 75 percent of the time versus under 60 percent for standard boundary F at any tolerance.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 150 human-ranked mask triplets on smoke images, compute agreement rates for candidate and baseline metrics.
fastest_falsification: Two days including the small ranking study.
main_risk: The metric needs density or disagreement estimates at evaluation time, limiting adoption where only single-annotator GT exists.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Bayesian optimization over a parametric smoke renderer finds a low-dimensional failure manifold of any frozen segmenter.
problem: Failure cases for smoke models are collected opportunistically from the wild, giving anecdotes rather than a systematic map of where and why models break.
core_hypothesis: Model failure is governed by a handful of interpretable rendering parameters (opacity, color offset from background, backlight, texture scale), so black-box search in renderer space recovers a compact, human-readable failure manifold.
why_important: A compact failure manifold converts testing from enumeration to geometry, enabling coverage claims (we tested the manifold) that wild data can never support.
why_possibly_novel: Parametric adversarial testing exists for faces and driving; applying renderer-space failure geometry to scattering media, with the low-dimensionality claim, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Failure structure may be high-dimensional and model-specific, with no shared compact manifold to find.
default_community_belief: Failure analysis means collecting hard real examples; synthetic search is distrusted as testing the renderer, not the world.
falsifiable_prediction: Search over an 8-parameter smoke renderer will find failure regions explained by at most 3 principal parameter directions covering over 80 percent of failure-boundary variance, consistent across 2 different segmenters.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a simple composite renderer, run Bayesian optimization against a frozen model's IoU, fit the failure-boundary geometry, repeat for a second model and compare.
fastest_falsification: Two days: coarse grid search over 4 renderer parameters against one model.
main_risk: Renderer realism limits transfer: manifold directions found in synthetic space may not predict wild failures, requiring a wild-validation step.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Failure cases mined against SAM transfer to other vision foundation models at high rates, indicating shared pretraining blind spots rather than architecture quirks.
problem: Each model's failures are studied in isolation; whether amorphous-target failures are properties of models or of the shared training paradigm is unknown but determines whether fixing one model fixes the field.
core_hypothesis: Web-scale pretraining distributions and object-centric supervision recipes overlap so heavily that hard smoke and transparency cases fail across model families, not just within one.
why_important: High transfer means failure datasets are durable community assets and the fix must target data and supervision, not architecture; low transfer means ensembles cheaply patch the hole.
why_possibly_novel: Adversarial-example transferability is classic; transferability of naturally mined amorphous-target failures across VFM families appears unmeasured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Different prompt mechanisms and decoders may fail on disjoint image subsets, yielding low transfer and refuting the shared-blind-spot story.
default_community_belief: Failures of a specific model are treated as that model's problem; evaluation practice implicitly assumes independence across models.
falsifiable_prediction: Of the worst-percentile failure images mined against SAM, over 70 percent will also fail (IoU below half of dataset mean) on at least 2 other independently trained segmentation-capable VFMs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine bottom-decile smoke and glass failures against SAM, evaluate the same items on 3 other models, report transfer rates against matched random controls.
fastest_falsification: One day: 100 mined failures, 2 additional models, transfer-rate table.
main_risk: Models share data lineages (LAION-style corpora), so high transfer may reflect data commonality rather than paradigm-level inevitability, limiting interpretation.

judge_flags.title: SAM-mined failures transfer across vision foundation models

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Fewer than ten embedding clusters cover over 90 percent of a smoke detector's false positives, making targeted negative collection tractable.
problem: False-positive reduction proceeds by ad hoc hard-negative scraping without knowing the FP distribution's structure; if FPs are few-cluster concentrated, collection can be planned like a checklist.
core_hypothesis: Smoke FPs arise from a small taxonomy of physical look-alikes (clouds, fog banks, steam vents, dust, glare, headlight beams, white walls in motion blur), so unsupervised clustering of FP embeddings will find a compact cover.
why_important: Converts false-alarm engineering from whack-a-mole to a bounded checklist, with measurable per-category closure.
why_possibly_novel: Slice discovery is an active area; the specific claim of low FP cardinality for smoke, validated by targeted-fix closure, appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: FPs in the wild may be dominated by scene-specific one-offs (weird textures) that never cluster, validating the long-tail pessimism.
default_community_belief: The false-positive long tail is assumed effectively unbounded, justifying endless data collection cycles.
falsifiable_prediction: Clustering high-confidence FPs from any deployed-style smoke model over diverse footage will yield under 10 clusters covering over 90 percent of FPs, with human-nameable semantics per cluster, and per-cluster targeted negatives will cut that cluster's FP rate by over half without raising others.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a smoke model over varied unlabeled footage, collect top FPs, cluster embeddings, name clusters, then fine-tune with negatives from one cluster and measure per-cluster deltas.
fastest_falsification: One day on any public model plus a few hours of diverse video.
main_risk: Cluster granularity is analyst-dependent; the under-10 claim needs a principled model-selection criterion to be falsifiable rather than rhetorical.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Inpainting away the smoke source (chimney, flames) while keeping the smoke collapses model predictions, exposing source-context crutches.
problem: Models may detect smoke largely by detecting its plausible sources; this context reliance is invisible in standard evaluation and dangerous for sourceless smoke (smoldering, off-frame origins).
core_hypothesis: A significant fraction of smoke evidence used by trained models is source co-occurrence, so deleting the source with the smoke untouched will cut predicted smoke confidence disproportionately versus deleting matched control regions.
why_important: Sourceless smoke (early smoldering, wind-carried plumes) is a critical alarm case; quantifying the context crutch predicts real missed alarms and motivates counterfactual augmentation.
why_possibly_novel: Counterfactual context editing is used for classifier interpretation; deploying it as a systematic segmentation failure-mining tool for smoke appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may rely mostly on smoke texture after all, showing small drops and refuting the crutch narrative for modern architectures.
default_community_belief: Context use by segmenters is considered a feature, not a measurable liability with a specific failure population attached.
falsifiable_prediction: Source-inpainted images will show over 30 percent mean drop in predicted smoke probability inside unchanged GT smoke regions, versus under 10 percent for size-matched control inpainting elsewhere.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 100 images with visible sources, inpaint sources and controls, run 3 smoke models, compare confidence drops within untouched smoke GT.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: 30 images, one model, source vs control inpainting.
main_risk: Inpainting artifacts near the smoke may leak into its appearance; a spatial buffer and artifact controls are mandatory.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Auto-captioning failure images and mining over-represented caption n-grams yields actionable failure slices for amorphous targets.
problem: Failure sets are unstructured image piles; without nameable slices, teams cannot prioritize fixes or collect targeted data, and amorphous-target failures resist attribute schemas designed for objects.
core_hypothesis: Language descriptions surface latent failure conditions (backlit, sunset, foggy morning, steam over kettle) that correlate with error, and slices defined by caption terms are coherent enough that per-slice fine-tuning fixes them without hurting the rest.
why_important: Provides a scalable, semi-automatic failure taxonomy pipeline for exactly the classes where manual attribute schemas fail.
why_possibly_novel: Language-based slice discovery exists for classification; validating slice actionability (fix one slice cleanly) for amorphous segmentation appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Slices may be confounded (sunset correlates with distance and resolution), so slice fixes could fail to isolate causal conditions.
default_community_belief: Failure analysis for segmentation is done by visual inspection and manual tagging when done at all.
falsifiable_prediction: At least 5 caption-derived slices will show error rates over 2x the corpus mean, and targeted fine-tuning on one slice will cut its error by over 30 percent while global performance changes by under 1 point.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Caption a failure corpus and a control corpus, mine differentially frequent terms, define top slices, run one slice-targeted fine-tune, measure slice and global deltas.
fastest_falsification: One day: caption 500 failures plus 500 controls, inspect the differential n-gram table.
main_risk: Captioners may systematically under-describe atmospheric conditions, missing the failure-relevant vocabulary entirely.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: The corruption-robustness fingerprint of smoke segmentation is qualitatively unlike object segmentation, and synthetic fog actually raises smoke recall.
problem: Robustness benchmarking applies one corruption suite with one expectation (performance drops); for smoke the same corruptions change the class evidence itself, and the response structure is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: Corruptions interact with smoke's identity: fog and haze corruptions inject smoke-like evidence (raising recall, cratering precision), while blur barely matters; the resulting response fingerprint is diagnostic of what a model thinks smoke is.
why_important: Corruption fingerprints become a cheap behavioral assay for classifying what cue a smoke model relies on, without opening the model.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption benchmarks are standard; reading the corruption-response profile as a cue-attribution diagnostic for amorphous classes appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may treat synthetic fog as globally distinct from smoke (uniform vs structured), leaving recall unchanged and killing the fingerprint idea.
default_community_belief: Corruptions degrade performance monotonically; robustness is a scalar to maximize, not a structured response to interpret.
falsifiable_prediction: Under standard corruption suites, smoke models will show recall increases (over 5 points) under fog corruption with simultaneous precision collapse, a signature absent in object segmentation, and the fingerprint will differ measurably between texture-reliant and contrast-reliant models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 3 smoke models under a corruption ladder, decompose deltas into precision and recall components, compare fingerprints against 2 object models.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: fog-corruption ladder on one model with precision-recall decomposition.
main_risk: Corruption implementations of fog vary; conclusions must be shown stable across at least 2 fog synthesis recipes.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Labeling the most ambiguous smoke images is worse than labeling mid-ambiguity ones: active learning's acquisition logic inverts on amorphous targets.
problem: Active learning acquires the most uncertain samples, but for smoke the most uncertain samples are often objectively unlabelable, so the standard loop may buy noise with its budget.
core_hypothesis: Annotation quality collapses on high-ambiguity smoke images, and the product of informativeness times label quality peaks at mid ambiguity, inverting the acquisition ranking.
why_important: Changes active-learning practice for every ambiguous-boundary domain and links label-noise theory to acquisition design.
why_possibly_novel: Noise-aware active learning exists in theory; a demonstration that the practical optimum is interior on a real amorphous task appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern annotation tooling (zoom, video context) may keep label quality acceptable even on ambiguous images, preserving the standard ranking.
default_community_belief: Maximum-uncertainty acquisition is the default; label quality is assumed roughly constant across acquired samples.
falsifiable_prediction: Fine-tuning on top-ambiguity-ranked images (by ensemble disagreement) will underperform fine-tuning on mid-ambiguity images at equal budget by over 3 IoU points on a consensus-labeled test set.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rank an unlabeled pool by disagreement, label top and middle tranches with the same annotators, fine-tune identical models on each, evaluate on consensus labels.
fastest_falsification: Two days including labeling 2 tranches of 100 images.
main_risk: The effect entangles annotator skill and instruction quality; needs annotator randomization across tranches.

judge_flags.title: Active-learning acquisition logic inverts on amorphous targets

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: For sim-to-real smoke segmentation, matching the camera's noise and compression pipeline matters more than matching scattering physics fidelity.
problem: Synthetic smoke pipelines invest in physically accurate rendering, but the binding constraint for transfer might be mundane sensor realism, and nobody has ranked the fidelity axes.
core_hypothesis: Models key on low-level statistics; if synthetic smoke lacks the target camera's noise, demosaicing, and compression artifacts, it is detectably synthetic regardless of scattering accuracy, and transfer suffers accordingly.
why_important: Tells synthetic-data builders where to spend effort, potentially replacing expensive volumetric rendering with cheap composites plus sensor simulation.
why_possibly_novel: Sensor-realism effects are known in other sim-to-real work; the explicit fidelity-axis ranking for participating media appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For thin smoke, scattering fidelity controls exactly the faint structures that matter, so physics could win after all.
default_community_belief: Physical rendering accuracy is assumed to be the main driver of synthetic-data quality for physics-driven phenomena like smoke.
falsifiable_prediction: In an ablation grid (scattering fidelity x sensor-pipeline fidelity), adding sensor simulation to crude single-scatter renders will improve real-world IoU more than upgrading crude renders to multiple-scattering under a clean pipeline.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate 4 synthetic training sets crossing 2 scattering levels with 2 sensor-pipeline levels, train identical models, evaluate all on one real smoke test set.
fastest_falsification: Three GPU-days for the 2x2 grid with a small model.
main_risk: Interaction effects may dominate main effects, muddying the headline ranking.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Open-vocabulary segmenters give wildly different masks for smoke, steam, vapor, and haze on the same image, and the variance is a class-ambiguity fingerprint.
problem: Text-prompted segmentation is deployed as if category names were stable handles, but amorphous phenomena have overlapping vocabularies, and prompt-synonym sensitivity is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: For solid objects, synonyms converge to similar masks; for scattering media, the text embedding differences translate into large mask differences, revealing that the model has no unified concept underneath the words.
why_important: Prompt-synonym variance determines whether text-prompted pipelines can be trusted for atmospheric hazards, and offers a label-free ambiguity audit for any category.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is studied for classification robustness; the mask-level synonym-variance audit contrasting amorphous vs solid categories appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Text encoders may map the synonyms nearly on top of each other, making masks agree and localizing the problem elsewhere.
default_community_belief: Category names are treated as interchangeable pointers to a learned concept; synonym choice is considered a detail.
falsifiable_prediction: Mean pairwise mask IoU across 6 near-synonym prompts will be below 0.5 for smoke-like regions and above 0.8 for object classes with equal synonym counts, across at least 2 open-vocab segmenters.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run 2 open-vocab segmenters with synonym prompt sets on mixed test images, compute per-category inter-synonym mask IoU distributions.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 6 prompts, 30 images, one model.
main_risk: Synonym sets are researcher-chosen; a principled synonym-selection protocol (thesaurus plus frequency matching) is needed to avoid cherry-picking.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Steam and smoke are visually indistinguishable near their sources in RGB, so any model separating them must be reading context, testable by cropping it away.
problem: Steam-vs-smoke discrimination is demanded by industrial deployments (steam is benign), and models appear to do it, but whether the discrimination is physical or contextual is unknown and safety-relevant.
core_hypothesis: Both are condensed or particulate scattering media with overlapping appearance distributions near sources; classifiers achieving separation rely on source objects and scene context, so context-free crops will collapse them to chance.
why_important: If separation is contextual, deployments must not trust plume-only evidence (night, zoomed cameras), and datasets should be relabeled with confidence tiers near sources.
why_possibly_novel: The context-dependence of this specific safety-critical distinction, with matched human controls, appears unmeasured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Subtle physical differences (droplet vs particle scattering, dissipation profile) may survive in crops, letting models exceed the predicted ceiling.
default_community_belief: Steam-vs-smoke is treated as a solvable appearance classification problem, evidenced by reported benchmark accuracies.
falsifiable_prediction: Steam-vs-smoke classifiers scoring above 85 percent on full frames will fall below 60 percent on tight crops containing only the plume, while human experts show a similar (not larger) drop, confirming the information is genuinely absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build full-frame and plume-only crop versions of a steam-plus-smoke set, train or evaluate classifiers on both, run a small human study on the crops.
fastest_falsification: One day: crop-eval of an existing classifier plus a 30-minute human test.
main_risk: Crop-induced resolution and framing artifacts could depress performance for trivial reasons; controls with object classes are required.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Wildfire smoke detectors are horizon-geometry cheaters: vertical flipping collapses their smoke-vs-cloud discrimination.
problem: Smoke-vs-cloud separation is the core difficulty of early wildfire camera systems, and reported accuracy may rest on layout priors (clouds live above the skyline) that fail under camera tilt or unusual weather.
core_hypothesis: Models learn that plume-shaped things touching the terrain are smoke and detached white masses in the sky region are clouds; geometry manipulation that preserves appearance will break the discrimination.
why_important: Identifies a shortcut that predicts real failure modes (valley fog below skyline, low stratus touching ridges) that plague deployed lookout systems.
why_possibly_novel: Position-shortcut audits are known generally; the horizon-geometry mechanism for the smoke-cloud dyad and its link to documented deployment nuisances appears unformalized.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models trained with strong augmentation may already be geometry-robust, showing minimal flip degradation.
default_community_belief: Wildfire model errors on clouds are attributed to appearance similarity, not to reliance on scene geometry priors.
falsifiable_prediction: Vertical flips or synthetic horizon shifts will cut smoke-vs-cloud discrimination (AUROC) by over 0.15 for wildfire models, while barely affecting texture-based control classifiers trained without positional input.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a wildfire smoke model on flip and horizon-shift transformed test sets, compare degradation against an appearance-only baseline model.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: flip-eval on any public wildfire smoke classifier or segmenter.
main_risk: Flipping also inverts smoke buoyancy cues that are legitimate physics; horizon-shift synthesis (relabeling skyline height) is the cleaner but harder manipulation.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: The true fog-vs-smoke discriminator is the spatial gradient of density, and a handcrafted density-gradient feature beats CLIP embeddings at this distinction.
problem: Fog triggers smoke alarms in camera systems; the fields lack a principled account of which measurable quantity separates a localized plume from a global atmospheric condition.
core_hypothesis: Fog density varies smoothly over large scales while smoke density has strong local gradients near its source and edges; a scale-normalized density-gradient statistic captures this physics while generic semantic embeddings do not.
why_important: Provides a physics-grounded, interpretable anti-fog module for alarm systems and a counterexample to embeddings-solve-everything practice.
why_possibly_novel: Fog detection and smoke detection exist separately; the explicit gradient-of-density formulation as the separating statistic, benchmarked against VFM embeddings, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: CLIP may encode fogness vs smokiness through co-occurring scene semantics well enough to win despite lacking the physical variable.
default_community_belief: Semantic embeddings are assumed to encode whatever separates visually similar categories, given a linear probe.
falsifiable_prediction: A logistic classifier on density-gradient features (from estimated transmission maps) will beat a linear probe on frozen CLIP features by over 10 AUROC points on fog-vs-smoke frame classification.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate transmission maps on fog and smoke frame collections, compute multi-scale gradient statistics, train both probes, compare AUROC.
fastest_falsification: One day: both probes on assembled fog and smoke frames.
main_risk: Transmission estimation itself may fail differently on fog vs smoke, smuggling the answer into the feature and complicating interpretation.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Industrial dust false positives are temporally structured (activity-driven), so a time-context prior halves them without touching the vision model.
problem: Dust from vehicles, machinery, and material handling is a leading FP source for industrial smoke systems, and fixes are attempted purely in appearance space where dust and smoke overlap heavily.
core_hypothesis: Dust events co-occur with observable operational context (moving machinery in frame, work hours, repeated locations), giving a conditional prior that separates dust from smoke better than appearance refinements do.
why_important: Demonstrates that for some confusions the cheapest reliable information is not in the pixels of the event, reshaping how alarm stacks are engineered.
why_possibly_novel: Context priors are standard in some surveillance analytics; a controlled comparison against appearance fine-tuning for the dust-smoke confusion appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dust may be less temporally predictable than assumed (wind-driven), leaving the context prior with little signal.
default_community_belief: False-positive reduction is a vision problem: collect the confusing cases and retrain the model.
falsifiable_prediction: A context model (time-of-day, co-detected machinery motion, location recurrence) multiplied onto an unchanged smoke detector will cut dust FPs by over 50 percent at fixed smoke recall on industrial footage, beating an appearance-only fine-tune of equal effort.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On industrial footage with audited alarms, fit the context prior, compare FP reduction against a dust-hard-negative fine-tune using the same labeling budget.
fastest_falsification: Two days on any labeled industrial alarm log with timestamps.
main_risk: Context priors risk suppressing true fires that co-occur with activity (the most likely ignition times), requiring careful recall accounting.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Language-supervised encoders inherit idiomatic smoke (cigarettes, chimneys), predicting a measurable performance ladder across smoke sub-types.
problem: Pretraining text pairs the word smoke with photogenic sub-types; whether this skews downstream segmentation across sub-types (cigarette vs wildfire wisp vs smoldering haze) is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Retrieval frequency of each smoke sub-type in image-text pretraining predicts zero-shot segmentation quality ordering on those sub-types, indicating performance is allocated by caption statistics, not visual difficulty.
why_important: Establishes caption statistics as a quantitative predictor of where open-vocab models will fail, enabling pre-deployment risk maps without labeled data.
why_possibly_novel: Pretraining-frequency effects are documented for classification; extending the analysis to sub-type structure within one amorphous category, with difficulty controls, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Visual difficulty may dominate so strongly (wisps are just harder) that frequency adds no predictive power after controls.
default_community_belief: Zero-shot performance differences are attributed to visual difficulty, with pretraining composition treated as unmeasurable background.
falsifiable_prediction: Estimated sub-type frequency (via retrieval sampling from an accessible image-text corpus) will rank-correlate above 0.7 with zero-shot sub-type segmentation IoU, and the correlation will survive controlling for visual difficulty proxies like contrast and size.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define 6 smoke sub-types, estimate corpus frequencies by retrieval, evaluate zero-shot segmentation per sub-type on a curated set, run the controlled correlation.
fastest_falsification: Two days: frequency estimates plus zero-shot eval on 6 sub-type buckets.
main_risk: Sub-type frequency estimation from retrieval is noisy and corpus-dependent; needs two corpora for stability.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Attribute prompts (semi-transparent gray turbulent region) beat category prompts (smoke) precisely on rare smoke sub-types where category priors are weakest.
problem: Category names bundle appearance priors that mismatch rare sub-types; whether attribute-level language can substitute for missing category coverage in segmentation is an open, testable question.
core_hypothesis: Attribute prompts route through compositional visual-language features that generalize where category embeddings are over-committed, producing an interaction: attributes lose on common sub-types, win on rare ones.
why_important: Gives a practical zero-data lever for tail sub-types and probes whether compositional language grounding survives into dense prediction.
why_possibly_novel: Attribute-based zero-shot classification is established; the frequency-conditioned interaction effect for segmentation of amorphous matter appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense heads may ignore attribute tokens entirely, making both prompt families equivalent modulo noise.
default_community_belief: The category name is assumed to be the strongest available text handle for any class, with attributes as weaker paraphrases.
falsifiable_prediction: On a sub-type-stratified smoke set, attribute prompts will underperform category prompts on high-frequency sub-types by a few points but outperform them by over 10 IoU points on the rarest stratum, in at least 2 open-vocab models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify a smoke set by sub-type frequency estimates, evaluate category vs attribute prompt batteries per stratum, test the interaction statistically.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: two prompt batteries on 30 rare-sub-type images.
main_risk: Attribute prompts may segment all soft gray regions (fog, dust) indiscriminately, winning IoU on rare smoke while destroying precision in mixed scenes.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: A gravity-aware positional encoding helps smoke segmentation on average but hurts on downdrafts and inversions, and the trade is quantifiable.
problem: Buoyancy (smoke rises) is an obvious prior to inject, but priors help until they lie; the field lacks a worked example quantifying the help-hurt ledger of a physics prior on real distribution tails.
core_hypothesis: Encoding gravity direction improves aggregate metrics via easier plume completion, while creating a new structured failure on the physical exceptions, and the net is positive only if exceptions are rarer than the prior's gain threshold.
why_important: Provides the template cost-benefit analysis the community needs before physics priors are adopted in safety systems, where tail cases are exactly the emergencies.
why_possibly_novel: Physics-informed vision usually reports aggregate gains; explicit exception-set accounting of a prior's induced failures appears rare to absent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The model may learn to ignore the encoding when appearance contradicts it, showing gains without the predicted exception cost.
default_community_belief: Physics priors are presumed safe regularizers whose failures are negligible relative to their gains.
falsifiable_prediction: The gravity-encoded model will gain 2-plus IoU overall but lose 10-plus IoU on a curated exception set (inversion layers, downward venting, wind-flattened plumes) versus the baseline model.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with and without gravity-direction conditioning on one smoke dataset, evaluate on standard test plus a hand-curated 100-image exception set.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days plus one day of exception-set curation.
main_risk: Curating enough genuine exception images is laborious; synthetic exceptions may not convince.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: An advection-consistency loss (masks should warp along smoke flow plus grow at sources) improves temporal stability without any extra labels.
problem: Video smoke predictions flicker frame to frame, and temporal-consistency losses built for rigid objects (pure warping) are wrong for media that grow and disperse.
core_hypothesis: Modeling mask evolution as advection by optical flow plus a nonnegative source term matches smoke physics closely enough to serve as an unsupervised regularizer that reduces flicker and improves accuracy on unlabeled video.
why_important: Separates the right physics (transport plus sources) from the borrowed physics (rigid warping) in video regularization, with free unlabeled-data gains.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal consistency losses are standard; the source-term extension for growing media, evaluated against the rigid-warp version, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The source term may act as an escape hatch that lets the loss excuse any inconsistency, nullifying its regularization value.
default_community_belief: Temporal consistency means warp-and-match; growth terms are not part of standard consistency objectives.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding the advection-consistency loss on unlabeled clips will reduce temporal flicker (frame-to-frame IoU variation) by over 30 percent and improve keyframe IoU by 2-plus points versus both no-consistency and rigid-warp-consistency baselines.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train three variants (none, rigid-warp, advection-plus-source) on one labeled set plus unlabeled clips, compare stability and keyframe accuracy.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days for the three-arm comparison on a small model.
main_risk: Optical flow inside smoke is unreliable, so the loss may propagate flow errors into masks and net negative on turbulent plumes.

judge_flags.reason: 'New physics-consistency loss improves metrics' is a loss-addition permutation as stated.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: A per-pixel single-scattering color test (smoke color must be a convex mix of ambient light and transmitted background) reranks SAM proposals into much better smoke masks.
problem: Segmenter proposals are ranked by learned confidence, which fails on smoke; the compositing physics of scattering media provides a checkable constraint that could rank proposals instead.
core_hypothesis: True smoke regions satisfy the convex-combination constraint against locally estimated background and ambient color, while false proposals (walls, clouds through windows, background objects) violate it measurably.
why_important: A modular, interpretable physics verifier that upgrades any proposal-based segmenter for scattering media, and a template for constraint-based reranking generally.
why_possibly_novel: Physics-based verification of learned proposals for smoke appears unexplored; scattering models are used for dehazing, not for scoring segmentation hypotheses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Many false proposals (white walls, haze) may satisfy the constraint too, giving the score little discriminative power.
default_community_belief: Proposal ranking is a learned-confidence problem; physical constraints are not part of modern segmentation stacks.
falsifiable_prediction: Reranking SAM everything-mode proposals by a physics-consistency score will improve best-selected-proposal smoke IoU by over 10 points versus confidence ranking, without touching the model.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the consistency score with median-filtered background estimates, rerank proposals on a smoke dataset, compare selected-mask IoU under both rankings.
fastest_falsification: One day: score existing proposals on 50 images and compare rankings.
main_risk: Background color under thick smoke is unobservable, so the test may only discriminate for thin-to-medium smoke.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: An 8x8-pixel thermopile array fused with an RGB fire segmenter eliminates most reflection and sunset false positives at trivial hardware cost.
problem: Fire false positives (reflections, sunsets, orange lights) are appearance-inseparable in RGB, and full thermal cameras are considered the expensive fix, so most deployments run RGB-only and eat the false alarms.
core_hypothesis: The FP classes emit no heat, so even an extremely coarse thermal prior (single-digit-dollar thermopile arrays) provides the missing bit, and fusion needs no retraining beyond a validation-fit gate.
why_important: Quantifies the cheapest possible cross-modal fix for the largest fire-alarm nuisance class, with direct product implications.
why_possibly_novel: RGB-thermal fusion research uses full-resolution thermal imagers; the extreme-low-resolution regime and its sufficiency question appear unstudied.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sun-heated surfaces and machinery create warm FPs of their own, and distance attenuates flame signal below coarse-sensor noise floors quickly.
default_community_belief: Meaningful thermal fusion requires imaging-grade thermal sensors; coarse point sensors are dismissed as insufficient for vision tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: Gating RGB fire detections on coarse thermal evidence will remove over 80 percent of reflection and sunset FPs while retaining over 95 percent of true fire detections within the sensor's range, in bench trials.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bench-test a thermopile-plus-camera rig against real flames, reflected flames, and displays showing fire footage; measure gated vs ungated detector performance.
fastest_falsification: Two days with off-the-shelf parts and a candle, a mirror, and a monitor.
main_risk: Thermopile range and field-of-view limits may exclude the long-distance scenarios where false positives actually occur in deployments.

judge_flags.reason: Thermopile + RGB fusion is a sensor-fusion engineering combo.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: The difference image between RGB and NIR channels is the strongest single smoke feature available to consumer sensors, because smoke fades in NIR.
problem: Smoke's wavelength-dependent scattering (stronger at shorter wavelengths) is textbook physics, yet mainstream smoke segmentation uses RGB alone even though many surveillance cameras capture NIR at night or on demand.
core_hypothesis: Registered RGB-minus-NIR contrast isolates wavelength-dependent scatterers (smoke) from wavelength-flat occluders (solid objects, most fog droplets are larger and flatter spectrally), giving a near-direct smoke image.
why_important: Thin smoke is the early-warning regime that RGB models miss; a physically grounded channel targeting exactly that regime has outsized safety value.
why_possibly_novel: Multispectral smoke physics is known in remote sensing; exploiting the RGB-NIR difference on commodity surveillance hardware for segmentation appears underexplored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Water-vapor-rich smoke and large-particle smoke may scatter too flatly across the RGB-NIR gap for the difference to register.
default_community_belief: Smoke segmentation is an RGB problem; spectral solutions are assumed to require specialized multispectral hardware.
