falsifiable_prediction: A threshold on the registered spectral-difference channel will outperform an RGB-only trained segmenter on thin smoke (alpha under 0.4) in paired captures, and adding the channel to training will improve thin-smoke IoU by over 10 points.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture paired RGB-NIR smoke scenes with a dual-mode camera, compute difference channels, evaluate thresholding and channel-augmented training against RGB baselines.
fastest_falsification: One day with a day-night camera whose IR-cut filter can be toggled, plus a smoke source.
main_risk: Registration errors between RGB and NIR optics create edge artifacts that could dominate the faint smoke signal.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Requiring a co-detected adjacent shadow validates dense smoke plumes and rejects cloud false positives whose shadows are elsewhere.
problem: Cloud-vs-smoke false positives persist in wide-area monitoring; single-region appearance analysis ignores that dense plumes and clouds cast differently located shadows.
core_hypothesis: A dense plume near the ground casts a shadow adjacent to its base, while cloud shadows are displaced far from the cloud's image position; shadow-plume geometric consistency is therefore a discriminative, physics-grounded validator.
why_important: Adds an orthogonal validation channel using already-available pixels, and formalizes a trick human fire lookouts report using.
why_possibly_novel: Shadow analysis exists for object insertion and sun estimation; using shadow-plume geometry as a smoke validator appears unpublished.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Thin and moderate plumes cast no visible shadow, so the validator may only work for plumes already easy to classify.
default_community_belief: Cloud rejection is pursued through appearance and temporal modeling of the region itself, not through inter-region physical consistency.
falsifiable_prediction: A shadow-consistency filter will reject over 50 percent of cloud FPs while rejecting under 10 percent of true dense-plume detections on sunny-scene footage, with failure concentrated (predictably) on overcast days.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On sunny wildfire-camera footage with audited detections, implement shadow detection near plume bases, measure the accept-reject confusion of the geometric consistency rule.
fastest_falsification: One day of rule prototyping on 50 sunny detections.
main_risk: The validator abstains on overcast scenes (no shadows), limiting coverage to sunny conditions, which must be reported honestly.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: A single rotatable polarizing filter separates real fire from reflected fire: direct flame emission is unpolarized, reflections are partially polarized.
problem: Reflected fire (windows, water, glossy floors) defeats appearance-based fire detection, and no deployable low-cost physical discriminator exists in current systems.
core_hypothesis: Reflections acquire partial polarization at dielectric surfaces while flame emission does not, so two captures at orthogonal polarizer angles reveal which fire-colored regions are reflections by their intensity modulation.
why_important: A physically principled, few-dollar fix for a failure class that pure learning approaches cannot separate in principle (the pixels are genuinely fire-colored).
why_possibly_novel: Polarization for reflection removal is established in graphics; its targeted use as a fire-vs-reflection discriminator in detection systems appears unexplored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Motion-flicker synchronization between a flame and its reflection may already suffice for separation, making the hardware unnecessary.
default_community_belief: Reflection false positives are treated as a data problem for retraining rather than a physically separable signal class.
falsifiable_prediction: The polarization-modulation depth of reflected-fire regions will exceed that of direct-flame regions by a factor of 3 or more in bench captures across common surfaces (glass, water, painted metal), enabling a threshold rule with over 90 percent separation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture flame plus its reflections through a rotating polarizer, compute per-region modulation depth, test the separation rule across surfaces and angles.
fastest_falsification: One afternoon: candle, window, polarizing filter, tripod.
main_risk: Modulation depends on viewing angle relative to Brewster geometry; grazing and normal incidence reflections may evade the rule.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Real smoke motion follows turbulent spatiotemporal spectra that flags, water, and foliage do not, enabling a physics-signature classifier of moving regions.
problem: Motion-based smoke detectors confuse any textured non-rigid mover (flags, steam-free water, foliage); discriminating by motion appearance has plateaued.
core_hypothesis: Turbulent plumes exhibit characteristic energy-cascade statistics in their spatiotemporal frequency content that other non-rigid movers lack, and a classifier on these spectra outperforms appearance-based motion classification for the same compute.
why_important: Adds a physically interpretable motion signature to the failure-mining toolkit and directly attacks the moving-distractor FP class.
why_possibly_novel: Turbulence statistics appear in fluid imaging literature; their use as a discriminative feature against the specific FP taxonomy of smoke detection seems new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Wind-driven foliage and water also show broadband quasi-turbulent spectra, possibly overlapping smoke's signature entirely.
default_community_belief: Learned spatiotemporal features are assumed to capture any useful motion regularity without physics-motivated feature design.
falsifiable_prediction: A spectra-based classifier will separate smoke motion from flag, water, and foliage motion with AUROC over 0.85 on clips where an optical-flow-appearance baseline scores under 0.75.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect clip sets of the four motion classes, compute 3D spectral features on dense patches, train small classifiers on spectra vs flow-appearance features, compare.
fastest_falsification: Two days: spectra extraction and a linear classifier on 40 clips per class.
main_risk: Camera compression and frame rates may destroy the spectral bands where the cascade signature lives.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Depth-conditioned smoke models degrade gracefully on out-of-scale scenes while depth-free models fail silently, testable with forced-perspective footage.
problem: Smoke size and distance are entangled in monocular views; models presumably resolve scale from scene context, but their behavior when scale cues mislead (miniatures, forced perspective, unusual lenses) is unknown and relevant to camera diversity.
core_hypothesis: Providing coarse scene depth lets models normalize plume scale physically, so depth-conditioned models generalize across focal lengths and scene scales where context-only models rely on spurious scale correlates.
why_important: Camera heterogeneity is a core deployment reality; understanding scale robustness determines whether one model can serve varied installations.
why_possibly_novel: Depth conditioning is common for objects; the scale-disentanglement question for volumetric media across lens configurations appears unstudied.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Data diversity may indeed suffice, with the depth channel adding nothing but complexity.
default_community_belief: Scale invariance is assumed to emerge from data diversity without explicit geometric conditioning.
falsifiable_prediction: On a test set spanning focal lengths and staged forced-perspective scenes, the depth-conditioned model's IoU variance across scale conditions will be under half the depth-free model's, with the depth-free model showing systematic misses of very close large plumes.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models (with and without monocular-depth conditioning), evaluate on a scale-diverse test set including staged near-lens smoke and distant plumes.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days plus a staged capture session with near-lens smoke.
main_risk: Monocular depth estimates on smoke itself are unreliable, so conditioning may inject noise exactly on-target (echoing the transparent-object depth problem).

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: ViT attention entropy over smoke regions is anomalously high, making attention-entropy maps a zero-shot smoke saliency signal.
problem: Zero-shot localization of amorphous matter lacks any signal source; internal attention statistics might already encode where the model finds nothing to latch onto.
core_hypothesis: Attention distributions from tokens in structured regions concentrate on informative neighbors, while tokens inside texture-poor scattering media attend diffusely, so per-token attention entropy elevates over smoke.
why_important: A label-free smoke prior extracted from any deployed ViT for free, and a window into how transformers represent featureless regions.
why_possibly_novel: Attention maps are mined for object saliency; entropy (rather than magnitude) as an amorphousness signal appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Registers or attention sinks may absorb the diffuse attention, flattening entropy differences between smoke and structure.
default_community_belief: Internal attention statistics are visualization material, not quantitative localization signals for unseen categories.
falsifiable_prediction: Thresholded attention-entropy maps from a frozen ViT will localize smoke with AUROC above 0.7 against GT masks, beating feature-norm and reconstruction-error baselines on the same backbone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract per-layer attention entropy on smoke datasets from 2 frozen ViTs, evaluate localization AUROC across layers against baselines.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: entropy maps vs GT on 30 images from one backbone.
main_risk: Sky, walls, and other flat regions share high entropy, so specificity may be too low without combining cues.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Register tokens make smoke localization worse: global tokens absorb haziness as image-level style, draining it from patch features.
problem: Architectural conveniences adopted for object tasks (register tokens absorbing global signals) may specifically harm classes whose evidence is a global-looking veil, and nobody has checked.
core_hypothesis: Haze and smoke read as global photometric style, exactly what register tokens learn to soak up, so backbones with registers encode less smoke evidence in patch tokens than register-free counterparts.
why_important: Reveals that architecture choices benign for objects can silently trade away atmospheric perception, informing backbone selection for hazard tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Register tokens are new enough that their class-conditional side effects on dense prediction of scattering media appear unexamined.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cleaner patch tokens might actually preserve smoke evidence better, reversing the predicted gap.
default_community_belief: Registers are considered pure quality improvements that clean up patch features for all dense tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear probes for pixelwise smoke on patch tokens will score measurably worse (over 5 AUROC points) on register-equipped variants than on matched register-free variants of the same architecture family, while object probing shows no such gap.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe patch tokens from register and non-register variants of one model family for smoke and object classes; additionally probe the registers themselves for global haze level.
fastest_falsification: One day: paired probing on one family with and without registers.
main_risk: Register and non-register checkpoints differ in more than registers (data, recipes), confounding attribution without careful pairing.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Synthetic haze moves all patch embeddings along one linear direction, and projecting it out erases smoke detectability while restoring background recognition, a hard trade-off.
problem: Dehazing-style invariance and smoke detection are opposite goals, but whether they compete for the same representational subspace, or can coexist, is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Haze is encoded near-linearly in VFM feature space; the same direction carries both the nuisance (for recognition) and the signal (for smoke detection), so any linear intervention trades one task against the other one-for-one.
why_important: Establishes whether atmospheric perception and recognition robustness can be jointly optimized in one representation or structurally require separate channels.
why_possibly_novel: Linear concept directions are well studied for attributes; the two-sided intervention analysis showing a signal-nuisance identity for haze appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The representation may store haze redundantly, so projection hurts detection less than predicted, happily refuting the hard trade-off.
default_community_belief: Robustness to atmospheric degradation and detection of atmospheric phenomena are pursued independently, assumed compatible within one backbone.
falsifiable_prediction: A single direction fit on hazy-clean pairs will (a) transfer across scenes, (b) restore over half the recognition accuracy lost to haze when projected out, and (c) simultaneously drop smoke-probe AUROC by over 15 points.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit the haze direction on synthetic pairs, apply projection interventions, measure recognition and smoke-probe metrics before and after across held-out scenes.
fastest_falsification: One day: fit direction on 200 synthetic pairs, run both probes pre and post projection.
main_risk: Haze may be encoded nonlinearly or multi-directionally, making the single-direction framing a strawman.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Self-supervised (DINO-style) features segment smoke better zero-shot than segmentation-supervised features, because mask supervision teaches boundaries smoke does not have.
problem: Pretraining choice for amorphous-target transfer is made by general benchmark reputation, but supervision that sharpens object boundaries may actively unfit features for boundary-free matter.
core_hypothesis: Mask-supervised training collapses within-object variation and sharpens edges, discarding density gradients; SSL objectives preserve photometric structure that smoke segmentation needs.
why_important: Backbone selection is the first decision of every applied project; a class-conditional reversal would change defaults for atmospheric and medical-diffuse domains alike.
why_possibly_novel: SSL-vs-supervised comparisons abound for objects; the predicted ranking reversal on amorphous matter appears undocumented.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation tuning may add grouping abilities that help even boundary-free targets, keeping supervised backbones on top everywhere.
default_community_belief: Segmentation-supervised features are assumed strictly better starting points for any segmentation-flavored downstream task.
falsifiable_prediction: Zero-shot smoke localization via feature clustering will rank SSL backbones above segmentation-tuned backbones of similar scale on at least 2 smoke datasets, reversing their ranking on object datasets.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cluster patch features from 3 SSL and 3 supervised backbones on smoke images, measure best-cluster IoU against GT, compare orderings on smoke vs objects.
fastest_falsification: One day: fixed clustering protocol on 2 backbones per family, one smoke dataset.
main_risk: Clustering protocol choices (k, layer) may drive results; a fixed protocol swept identically across backbones is essential.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Amorphous regions are underrepresented in promptable-segmentation training masks relative to their pixel frequency, and this representation gap predicts per-class zero-shot failure.
problem: We suspect data imbalance causes amorphous failures but have no measurement of how mask-annotation practices sample different matter types relative to their actual pixel prevalence.
core_hypothesis: Annotation pipelines favor delineable things, so smoke, haze, and translucent matter appear in masks far below their pixel-frequency in natural images, and zero-shot performance across matter types tracks this sampling ratio.
why_important: Converts the data imbalance is the cause intuition into a measured, predictive quantity that data-collection efforts can target directly.
why_possibly_novel: Class imbalance is measured for named categories; a matter-type audit of mask corpora against natural pixel prevalence appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Zero-shot failure may track intrinsic ambiguity rather than sampling, leaving the correlation weak even if undersampling is confirmed.
default_community_belief: Web-scale mask corpora are assumed approximately representative of visual reality, with rare-category gaps at the entity level, not the matter level.
falsifiable_prediction: Estimating matter-type pixel prevalence (via classification of random patches) and mask coverage (via auditing everything-mode outputs and public mask corpora) will show amorphous matter undersampled by over 5x, and the undersampling ratio will rank-correlate above 0.6 with zero-shot IoU across matter types.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Audit a large public mask corpus and a random natural-image sample for matter-type coverage, compute ratios, correlate with measured zero-shot performance per type.
fastest_falsification: Two days: coverage audit on a corpus subsample plus existing per-type performance numbers.
main_risk: Matter-type taxonomies are fuzzy and the patch classifier defining prevalence introduces its own bias; sensitivity analysis across taxonomies is required.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Smoke opacity is linearly decodable from frozen VFM patch features even though mask decoders never use it: the information exists but is unread.
problem: It is unknown whether amorphous-segmentation failure is an encoding failure (density not represented) or a decoding failure (represented but unused by mask heads), and the answer dictates the fix.
core_hypothesis: Backbone features retain graded opacity information from pretraining on hazy scenes, but binary-mask decoders were never trained to read it; a linear regression probe will therefore recover alpha where full systems fail.
why_important: If density is already encoded, cheap decoder retrofits (probe-guided heads) can unlock amorphous segmentation without touching backbones, a huge cost saving.
why_possibly_novel: Probing for continuous physical variables (opacity) rather than class membership in segmentation backbones appears unexplored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Features may genuinely lack graded opacity (invariance erased it), making this an encoding failure and the probe result negative.
default_community_belief: Segmentation failure is read as the model cannot see the category, conflating representation absence with readout absence.
falsifiable_prediction: A ridge-regression probe on frozen patch features will predict composited GT alpha with rank correlation above 0.6 on scenes where the full segmentation pipeline scores near-zero IoU, demonstrating encode-decode dissociation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build alpha-annotated composites, fit ridge probes per layer on frozen features, compare probe alpha quality against end-to-end pipeline masks on the same images.
fastest_falsification: One day: layer-swept ridge probes on 500 composite patches.
main_risk: Probe success on composites may reflect compositing statistics rather than true opacity encoding, requiring a small real-smoke validation set.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Background diversity beats plume diversity: at fixed budget, few plumes over many backgrounds trains better smoke models than many plumes over few backgrounds.
problem: Smoke data collection allocates effort between capturing varied smoke and varying scenes, with no evidence about which axis buys generalization.
core_hypothesis: Models overfit background-smoke co-occurrence more than plume morphology, so background variation attacks the dominant shortcut while plume variation adds redundant appearance samples.
why_important: Directly reallocates collection budgets (backgrounds are nearly free; plume captures are expensive), potentially cutting data costs severalfold.
why_possibly_novel: Factorized data-scaling studies exist for objects and faces; the background-vs-plume factorial for scattering media appears undone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Plume morphology diversity may be exactly what separates smoke from steam and dust, making plume variety the binding constraint after all.
default_community_belief: Target-appearance diversity is assumed to be the precious axis; backgrounds are considered incidental context.
falsifiable_prediction: Composite datasets with 10 plumes x 1000 backgrounds will train models beating 1000 plumes x 10 backgrounds by over 8 IoU on wild tests, despite identical image counts.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the two factorial composite datasets, train identical models, evaluate on wild footage; add intermediate ratios for the response curve.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days with 2x2 factorial pilot datasets.
main_risk: Composite realism limits external validity; a small real-data replication (subsampling existing datasets by scene) is needed as anchor.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Binary copy-paste smoke augmentation teaches edge shortcuts: models detect the paste boundary, not the smoke, and alpha-aware pasting removes the shortcut.
problem: Copy-paste is the default cheap augmentation, but hard-edged smoke pastes create an artifact (impossible sharp smoke boundary) that models can exploit, inflating training metrics while harming deployment.
core_hypothesis: Networks preferentially learn the high-signal paste edge; models trained with binary pastes will fire on paste-edge-like artifacts and underperform on real soft-boundary smoke relative to alpha-blended pasting.
why_important: A widespread augmentation practice may be quietly poisoning smoke models; the artifact-probe methodology also generalizes to auditing other augmentations.
why_possibly_novel: Copy-paste artifacts are acknowledged folklore; constructing artifact-only probe sets to quantify the shortcut for amorphous classes appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Random paste diversity may prevent the edge shortcut from forming, showing equal real-data performance for both variants.
default_community_belief: Copy-paste augmentation is treated as robustly beneficial, with artifacts assumed to be averaged away by volume.
falsifiable_prediction: Binary-paste models will score over 20 points higher on artifact-only probes (empty scenes with paste-shaped sharp edges) than alpha-paste models, and over 5 points lower on real smoke test sets.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models with binary vs alpha pasting, evaluate both on real test data and on synthesized artifact-probe images.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day: paired training plus a 100-image artifact probe.
main_risk: Alpha mattes for pasting require decent smoke mattes to begin with, a mild circularity resolvable with lab captures.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Blackbody-temperature-swept synthetic flames close the day-night fire generalization gap better than collecting more single-regime real data.
problem: Fire models trained on daytime-rich data fail at night and vice versa; collecting balanced real fire data is dangerous and slow, and it is unknown whether physical color modeling can substitute.
core_hypothesis: The day-night gap is primarily a flame color-and-exposure distribution shift that a physically parameterized renderer (temperature, exposure, tone curve sweeps) covers more systematically than opportunistic real collection.
why_important: Provides a safe, cheap route to lighting-condition robustness for a data-limited safety domain, with a physics-grounded recipe.
why_possibly_novel: Synthetic fire data exists; framing the day-night gap as a color-temperature-exposure manifold to be swept parametrically, with the controlled comparison, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gap may be dominated by background context shift rather than flame appearance, which the sweep does not address.
default_community_belief: Domain gaps are closed by collecting in-domain real data; parametric synthesis is a stopgap, not a preferred fix.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding temperature-and-exposure-swept synthetic flames to daytime real data will recover over 60 percent of the night-performance deficit, beating the addition of an equal count of extra daytime real images (which will recover under 10 percent).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train three arms (day-only, day plus synthetic sweep, day plus extra day data), evaluate all on a night fire test set.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days for the three-arm study with an existing renderer or even 2D flame sprites.
main_risk: Night fire scenes differ in more than flame appearance (sensor gain noise, light bleeding), so color sweeps may hit a ceiling early.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Smoke models tolerate dilated ground truth far better than eroded ground truth, so biasing annotation outward is a free training win.
problem: Annotator guidance must pick a bias direction for uncertain smoke extents, but the loss landscape's asymmetry to over- vs under-labeling has never been measured for amorphous targets.
core_hypothesis: Missing supervision on true smoke pixels (erosion) actively teaches smoke-is-background, while extra background pixels labeled smoke (dilation) add soft, low-gradient noise, so equal-pixel-budget dilation harms much less than erosion.
why_important: Converts directly into annotation guidelines (when unsure, include it) with measurable model improvements at zero extra cost.
why_possibly_novel: Label-noise robustness is studied symmetrically; the directional asymmetry claim for diffuse-boundary classes with actionable annotation guidance appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dilation may destroy precision on thin plumes surrounded by sky, where extra labeled pixels are proportionally huge.
default_community_belief: Label errors in either direction are treated as equivalent noise to be minimized; annotation guidance says be accurate, not be biased outward.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained with GT dilated by k pixels will lose under 2 IoU versus clean-GT training, while erosion by the same k will lose over 8 IoU, evaluated against consensus test labels, across two architectures.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train models on systematically dilated and eroded versions of one dataset at 3 magnitudes each, evaluate all against consensus labels.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day: 3 dilation and 3 erosion levels on one dataset, one architecture.
main_risk: Asymmetry magnitude may depend on class prior and loss function (cross-entropy vs dice), requiring both losses for a robust recipe claim.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Temporal-variance pseudo-labels from static cameras pretrain smoke models that beat human-label-only training with a fraction of the annotation.
problem: Human smoke annotation is the cost bottleneck, while unlabeled static-camera footage with detectable smoke motion is effectively unlimited and unused.
core_hypothesis: Noisy-but-plentiful motion-derived pseudo-masks teach smoke appearance at scale, and a small human-labeled set then calibrates extent conventions, dominating human-only pipelines at fixed cost.
why_important: A practical recipe that could shift the whole subfield's data economics toward harvesting surveillance archives.
why_possibly_novel: Motion pseudo-labels are used in video object discovery; the cost-controlled comparison against pure human labeling for smoke appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The pseudo-label bias toward moving smoke may systematically miss smoldering and distant smoke, capping wild performance below the human-data baseline.
default_community_belief: Weak pseudo-labels are assumed too noisy to beat curated human data for boundary-sensitive dense prediction.
falsifiable_prediction: Pretraining on 50k pseudo-labeled frames plus fine-tuning on 500 human-labeled images will beat training on 5000 human-labeled images alone by over 5 IoU on a common test set, at under half the labeling cost.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate pseudo-labels on public static-camera footage, run the two-arm cost-matched comparison with one architecture.
fastest_falsification: Three GPU-days including pseudo-label generation on available footage.
main_risk: Pseudo-label failure modes (missing static dense smoke, including moving distractors) may teach biases that fine-tuning cannot fully unwind.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Adding hard-negative scenes (fog, sunsets, steam) without any new positives improves smoke-detector precision more than doubling the positive set.
problem: Data budgets default to collecting more smoke, but deployed failure is dominated by false positives on look-alikes, suggesting the negative set is the real deficiency.
core_hypothesis: The decision boundary's bad side is under-specified: models have seen too few labeled non-smoke look-alikes, so negative-set enrichment moves the boundary where errors actually occur.
why_important: Rebalances collection guidance for every applied smoke project and quantifies the value of negatives, which current dataset papers barely count.
why_possibly_novel: Hard-negative mining is standard; the budget-allocation claim (negatives beat positives at the margin for this domain) with cost-matched arms appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern pretrained backbones may already know the look-alikes well enough that negative enrichment saturates immediately.
default_community_belief: Dataset value is measured in positive instances; negatives are whatever background comes along with them.
falsifiable_prediction: At fixed training size, replacing half the added positives with curated hard negatives will improve precision at 90 percent recall by over 15 points compared to positives-only enrichment, on an FP-rich evaluation stream.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a base dataset, add equal-count positives vs hard negatives vs a mix, train identical models, evaluate precision-recall on held-out footage rich in distractors.
fastest_falsification: Two GPU-days with a three-arm cost-matched training comparison.
main_risk: Gains depend on matching the negative taxonomy to the test distribution; mismatched negatives could show no effect and muddy the general claim.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Standard weather augmentation (synthetic fog and haze) is label poison for smoke training: it injects unlabeled positives into the negative class.
problem: Robustness recipes apply fog augmentation universally, but for smoke tasks the augmented haze is visually in-class while labeled as background, a direct contradiction fed to the loss.
core_hypothesis: Fog-augmented negatives teach the model to suppress exactly the thin-scattering appearance that early smoke shows, measurably reducing thin-smoke recall while nominally improving robustness scores.
why_important: Identifies a silent recipe bug plausibly present in many published smoke models, fixable by deleting one line of the augmentation config.
why_possibly_novel: Augmentation-task interference is known abstractly; this concrete class-collision case and its magnitude for smoke appear unreported.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fog augmentation might actually work as useful hard-negative training, improving precision more than it costs recall.
default_community_belief: Weather augmentation is a robustness best practice with no task-specific contraindications.
falsifiable_prediction: Removing fog and haze transforms from the augmentation stack will improve thin-smoke recall by over 8 points at matched precision, while other augmentations (blur, noise, color jitter) show no such interaction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models differing only in fog-augmentation presence, evaluate thin-smoke recall and overall metrics; sweep fog intensity for a dose-response curve.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day: paired training on one dataset with and without fog augmentation.
main_risk: The effect may be small if fog augmentation is rare in practice or if models distinguish global synthetic fog from local plumes anyway.

judge_flags.title: Weather augmentation is label poison for smoke training

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Video compression at CCTV bitrates deletes thin smoke from the signal: smoke segmentation collapses below a bitrate threshold where object segmentation barely notices.
problem: Models are developed on high-quality footage but deployed behind aggressive H.264/H.265 encoders whose quantization is designed to discard exactly the low-contrast texture smoke consists of.
core_hypothesis: Encoder rate allocation treats faint smoke as noise-like detail and removes it first, so smoke-task degradation versus bitrate is much steeper than object-task degradation, with a knee at typical CCTV settings.
why_important: Quantifies a deployment gap that no amount of model improvement can cross (the information is gone), redirecting effort to camera-side settings and bitrate-aware training.
why_possibly_novel: Compression robustness studies exist broadly; the class-conditional steepness claim for scattering media, tied to encoder psychovisual models, appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Smoke's low-frequency mass may survive quantization well, with only fine wisps lost, making the curve gentler than predicted.
default_community_belief: Compression is treated as mild uniform degradation, handled adequately by augmentation, with no class-specific catastrophe expected.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-encoding a smoke test set across a bitrate ladder will show smoke IoU dropping over 15 points between 4 and 1 Mbps at 1080p while object IoU drops under 3 points on the same ladder, and the loss will concentrate on low-alpha smoke.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-encode one smoke and one object dataset at 5 bitrates, evaluate fixed models, plot degradation curves stratified by smoke opacity.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: one dataset, 3 bitrates, one model, opacity-stratified deltas.
main_risk: Encoder implementations differ; conclusions need 2 codecs and 2 preset families to support general claims.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Dirty-lens and condensation artifacts are the dominant long-duration smoke false positives, and a permanence filter (smoke cannot be static for hours) removes them without model changes.
problem: Deployed smoke systems generate persistent false alarms from lens contamination that looks locally identical to haze, and fixes are attempted in appearance space where the classes genuinely overlap.
core_hypothesis: The separating variable is temporal permanence at scene scale: real smoke evolves or clears within minutes, while contamination is quasi-static for hours and locks to lens coordinates rather than scene coordinates under camera motion.
why_important: Contamination alarms erode operator trust and cause alarm fatigue; an appearance-free fix is robust exactly because it does not compete with smoke appearance.
why_possibly_novel: Lens-artifact detection exists for autonomous driving; formalizing permanence and mount-frame locking as the discriminator against smoke appears new for alarm systems.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models may already suppress contamination via subtle focus cues, making the filter redundant.
default_community_belief: False-positive reduction is pursued by improving the vision model rather than by modeling the sensor's own failure modes.
falsifiable_prediction: A two-rule filter (persistence beyond a time constant, plus invariance to pan-tilt motion) will remove over 90 percent of contamination alarms while delaying or suppressing under 1 percent of true smoke events in labeled deployment logs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On recorded footage with contamination and smoke events (or staged smudges), implement the filter and measure the removal-vs-suppression trade.
fastest_falsification: One day with a smudged lens, a smoke source, and the two-rule prototype.
main_risk: Slow smoldering scenarios can produce quasi-static haze for long periods, colliding with the permanence rule at exactly the highest-stakes cases.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Auto-exposure feedback makes fires self-hiding: the flame drives exposure down and the surrounding smoke becomes invisible, so alarm latency depends on camera AE policy more than on the model.
problem: End-to-end detection latency is attributed to model quality, ignoring that the camera's control loop reacts to fire by re-exposing the scene, actively degrading the evidence available to any model.
core_hypothesis: When a bright flame enters the frame, AE reduces gain and exposure, crushing the dim smoke regions into noise; different AE policies therefore change achievable detection latency more than swapping between competitive models does.
why_important: Moves a chunk of the smoke-detection problem from ML to camera configuration, offering deployments an immediate latency improvement lever.
why_possibly_novel: Sensor-control interactions with detection are studied for autonomous driving exposure; the fire-specific self-hiding feedback loop appears undocumented.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern local-tone-mapping pipelines may preserve shadow detail well enough that AE policy differences barely matter.
default_community_belief: Camera ISP behavior is treated as a fixed benign preprocessing stage; benchmark footage is taken as representative of deployment sensing.
falsifiable_prediction: In controlled ignition captures across 3 AE policies (default, highlight-priority, locked), the spread of time-to-detection across policies for one fixed model will exceed the spread across 3 leading models under one fixed policy.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stage repeatable ignition scenarios recorded simultaneously by cameras with different AE settings, run fixed models, compare latency distributions.
fastest_falsification: One day with two identical cameras (one locked exposure) and a controlled flame.
main_risk: Staged ignitions are logistically heavy; simulation via HDR footage re-rendered under AE models is the fallback with weaker external validity.

judge_flags.title: Auto-exposure makes fires self-hiding

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Smoke detectability follows a measurable pixels-per-plume scaling law, letting deployments compute maximum detection distance per camera instead of guessing.
problem: Camera placement for smoke monitoring is designed by rules of thumb; there is no validated function mapping sensor resolution, optics, and distance to expected detection performance.
core_hypothesis: Model recall depends on angular resolution of the plume in a smooth, law-like way (recall as a function of plume pixels), stable enough across scenes to invert into an operational range envelope.
why_important: Converts model evaluation into engineering specifications (coverage maps, camera counts), the missing link between benchmarks and installations.
why_possibly_novel: Resolution-performance relationships are studied ad hoc; a validated invertible scaling law for amorphous-target detection with field verification appears absent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectability may be dominated by contrast rather than size at long range, making pixels-per-plume the wrong master variable.
default_community_belief: Detection range is established empirically per installation; performance is not assumed to follow an invertible law worth publishing.
falsifiable_prediction: Recall curves versus plume pixel size, measured by synthetic downscaling and verified on natural distance-varied captures, will collapse onto one master curve per model (R-squared over 0.8), and the curve will predict held-out field-trial detection ranges within 20 percent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Downscale-and-composite plumes at controlled pixel sizes, measure recall curves, then validate against captures of one real smoke source at 5 distances.
fastest_falsification: Two days: synthetic size ladder plus one outdoor distance session.
main_risk: Atmospheric visibility and background clutter may shift the curve per scene, breaking the single-master-curve claim into families.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Distilling a foundation smoke segmenter into an edge model loses the ambiguous transition band first, and soft-alpha distillation targets fix exactly that loss.
problem: Edge deployment requires distillation, but where in the image the student loses fidelity is unmeasured; for smoke the loss may concentrate in the safety-relevant faint regions.
core_hypothesis: Hard-label distillation transfers confident core predictions but discards the teacher's graded uncertainty structure in transition bands, which is most of the useful signal for early smoke; distilling soft probability maps preserves it.
why_important: Edge devices are where smoke detection actually runs; band-concentrated distillation loss means deployed models are worst exactly at early-warning sensitivity.
why_possibly_novel: Distillation losses are compared globally; region-conditional distillation-gap analysis tied to amorphous class structure appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Capacity limits may force the student to lose band fidelity regardless of target softness, making the fix ineffective.
default_community_belief: Distillation quality is a single number; where the student differs from the teacher is rarely asked, and soft targets are seen as a minor refinement.
falsifiable_prediction: The student-teacher IoU gap will be over 3x larger in transition-band regions than in core regions under hard distillation, and soft-target distillation will close over half the band gap at equal student size.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Distill one teacher into a small student with hard vs soft targets, decompose student-teacher agreement by band vs core regions on smoke test data.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-day: one distillation pair, region-decomposed agreement analysis.
main_risk: Band definitions require decent GT or teacher-confidence proxies; conclusions should be shown under both definitions.

territory: Smoke / fire / ambiguous (transparent) object segmentation + failure mining
one_line: Rolling-shutter banding under flame flicker creates a spurious texture that video fire models key on, failing silently on global-shutter cameras.
problem: Most training footage comes from rolling-shutter sensors whose interaction with flame-driven illumination flicker produces banding patterns; models may adopt this sensor artifact as fire evidence, breaking on other sensor types.
core_hypothesis: Banding is a reliable, learnable fire correlate in rolling-shutter data, so models weight it; on global-shutter or synchronized-lighting footage the cue vanishes and recall drops for scenes where flames are partially occluded and banding was carrying the detection.
why_important: A concrete instance of sensor-artifact shortcut learning in safety systems, with a clear audit (cross-shutter evaluation) that certification processes could adopt.
why_possibly_novel: Rolling-shutter effects are studied for geometry; their role as a learned spurious cue for fire detection appears unexamined.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Flicker-induced banding may be too faint after compression to be learnable, in which case cross-shutter performance will match.
default_community_belief: Sensor readout architecture is assumed irrelevant to high-level recognition; nobody stratifies fire benchmarks by shutter type.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained on rolling-shutter-dominated data will lose over 10 points recall on matched global-shutter captures of the same scenes, and adding synthetic banding to global-shutter test frames will restore most of the loss, confirming the cue.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture flames with paired rolling and global shutter cameras, evaluate public fire models on both, run the synthetic-banding restoration test.
fastest_falsification: One day with a candle, one rolling-shutter and one global-shutter camera (or a phone and an industrial cam).
main_risk: Banding visibility depends on flame size, ambient light, and exposure time; the effect may be too small outside dim scenes to matter.
